Numeric and notation inconsistencies are preserved rather than silently reconciled. Visual inspection covers pages 1–10; pages 11–14 are text-only.

claims.statement: WebShop's product corpus contains 1,181,436 Amazon products spanning five categories, collected using 113 sub-category names as queries; this scale describes the simulated corpus, not the number of evaluation tasks.

The benchmark has 12,087 instructions split i.i.d. into 10,587 training, 1,000 development, and 500 test instances; harder category-based generalization splits are proposed rather than evaluated in the supplied main text.

Search imitation generates queries from the instruction without prior-search or visited-item context; BART search training uses 1,421 instruction-search pairs extracted from 1,012 human training trajectories.
IL+RL freezes BART and supplies ten generated search candidates to the action-choice model, rather than directly fine-tuning unrestricted text generation with reinforcement learning.

On the simulated test comparison reported over three trials, IL+RL has the highest agent Task Score, 62.4, while IL has the highest agent Success Rate, 29.1%; IL+RL success is 28.7%, so the best model depends on the metric.

RL fine-tuning raises average task score but reduces the option component from 45.2 to 38.9; the authors associate this with reduced exploration. The reported average trajectory length is inconsistent: 4.5 in Table 2 versus 4.8 in the explanatory paragraph.

The choice oracle sees hidden reward information and exhaustively explores result products and options. On 500 test instructions, BART-query oracle success is 57.6%, compared with ordinary IL's 29.1%, under substantially more privileged and expensive conditions.

Zero-shot transfer uses 100 sampled test instructions on Amazon and eBay without fine-tuning and with manual scoring. IL+RL achieves Score/SR 65.9/25% on Amazon and 62.3/21% on eBay; these are real-site task-performance results, not security results.
The complete product-type matching formula cannot be assessed from the supplied pages because the authors defer TextMatch to Appendix A.5, which was not supplied.

For security research, the documented pathway from webpage/product observations and candidate action text to executable search/choose decisions identifies possible surfaces for a future threat model. This is analyst inference, not evidence that those surfaces are exploitable.

The supplied study evaluates shopping performance, ablations, diagnostics, and transfer; it does not directly compare adversarial vulnerability of web agents with standalone LLMs. A comparative security conclusion is unsupported by these supplied experiments.

The explicitly enumerated demonstration collections total 1,566: 1,012 training + 54 development + 500 test. This does not reconcile with the abstract's 'over 1,600'; additional demonstrations are not identified in the supplied material.

research.title: WorkArena: How Capable are Web Agents at Solving Common Knowledge Work Tasks?
research.research_question_relevance: MEDIUM confidence, analyst inference: the paper documents the operational connections that make browser agents security-relevant—external observations, executable actions, enterprise record changes, orders, identity switching, and information transmission. It does not establish that web agents are more vulnerable than standalone LLMs. The comparative security hypothesis remains UNKNOWN because no matched standalone baseline, adversarial evaluation, or attack-success metric is supplied.
research.attack_surface: MEDIUM confidence, analyst inference: candidate surfaces are HTML/AXTree/screenshot observations, chat and error information entering prompts, model-generated browser actions, optional arbitrary Python execution, navigation, enterprise data writes, catalog submission, impersonation, and outgoing user messages. These are documented interfaces or capabilities, not demonstrated exploit paths. Table 1's evaluated agents use bid-only actions; unrestricted Python is an environment option.
research.method: HIGH confidence: benchmark and systems development plus empirical capability evaluation. WorkArena has 33 task types and 19,912 available instances on ServiceNow. BrowserGym uses Chromium, CDP, and Playwright. GPT-4o, GPT-3.5, and Llama3-70B configurations are selected through random search on WorkArena and MiniWoB, then reevaluated with a different seed. Evaluation uses ten seeds per WorkArena/MiniWoB task, one per WebArena task, a 15-step limit, and 1,000 stratified-bootstrap mean samples. Tables 3–5 report feature ablations; GPT-4o-V adds a Set-of-Mark screenshot.
research.limitations: HIGH confidence for source boundaries: no direct comparative security study, formal threat model, attack workload, validated defense, or standalone-LLM security baseline. Some tasks may exceed the 15-step limit; prompts are truncated; model-specific configurations and context budgets vary. Oracle solutions may be nonoptimal. Synthetic knowledge content and limited task seeds constrain generalization. Repository code and raw outputs were not inspected. Textual inconsistencies and unreadable exact Figure 4 statistics remain explicit.

claims.statement: WorkArena contains 33 task types and 19,912 unique instances covering core ServiceNow interactions; available instances are distinct from evaluated episodes.
WorkArena goals come from human-designed templates populated with predefined values and are intended to provide all information required for task completion.

BrowserGym supports configurable high-level actions and can alternatively permit arbitrary Python including the Playwright API; this environment capability was not the bid-only action configuration selected for the main evaluated agents.
ServiceNow page HTML is reported to range from 40k to 500k tokens after basic cleaning; WorkArena and WebArena agents therefore use AXTrees rather than HTML.
Table 2 reports WorkArena success rate ± standard error of 42.7% ± 1.5 for GPT-4o, 41.8% ± 1.7 for GPT-4o-V, 6.1% ± 1.3 for GPT-3.5, and 17.9% ± 1.5 for Llama3 under the final evaluation protocol.
All four agents have 0.0% reported success in Table 2's six-task list-filter category; list-sort results are nonzero and must not be merged into the zero-success claim.

Evaluation uses a 15-step episode limit, and the authors acknowledge that some WorkArena tasks may require more steps unless multi-action mode is used; selected main configurations disable multi-action mode.

The protocol uses ten seeds per task for WorkArena and MiniWoB, one per WebArena task, and 1,000 stratified-bootstrap mean samples; reported uncertainty is standard error rather than a confidence interval.
Removing thinking in Table 5 lowers Llama3 from 59.8% to 48.6% on MiniWoB and from 20.0% to 8.5% on WorkArena; these ablation baselines use a different seed from Table 2.

The GPT-4o-V condition adds a Set-of-Mark screenshot while retaining the other flags of the selected GPT-4o agent; aggregate point-estimate improvements on MiniWoB and WebArena are small, and aggregate WorkArena performance decreases.
WorkArena's knowledge base comprises 100 GPT-4-generated articles; question variants are checked using GPT-3.5 and revised if necessary, while generated alternative answer formats support validation.

The authors identify workplace web-agent privacy concerns because sensitive information may need to be transmitted; this is an impact-statement concern, not a measured exfiltration or vulnerability result.

Analyst inference: the combination of external page observations and executable browser actions identifies security-relevant observation-to-action boundaries, but the paper does not demonstrate attacks against those boundaries or establish greater vulnerability than standalone LLMs.

Analyst inference: record creation, catalog ordering, and user impersonation give web-agent mistakes potentially consequential effects on enterprise state and identity; these benchmark capabilities do not establish unauthorized access or a successful exploit.

The supplied paper evaluates web-task capability and feature ablations, not comparative security vulnerability of web agents versus standalone LLMs; it supplies no standalone security baseline, defined adversarial workload, or attack-success metric.

Analyst-derived: GPT-4o's final WorkArena success exceeds GPT-3.5 by 36.6 percentage points, calculated as 42.7 minus 6.1, and Llama3 by 24.8 percentage points, calculated as 42.7 minus 17.9; these are differences in point estimates, not significance-test results.
Oracle action counts are based on hand-coded solutions that may not be optimal; they should not be interpreted as exact minimum agent-step requirements.

research.title: WorkArena++: Towards Compositional Planning and Reasoning-based Common Knowledge Work Tasks
research.research_question_relevance: MEDIUM confidence, analyst inference: the paper informs 'Why Are Web AI Agents More Vulnerable Than Standalone LLMs?' by documenting how browser agents integrate page-resident instructions, target interface elements, change enterprise records, and sometimes misjudge resulting state. It does not compare standalone LLMs with web agents, measure adversarial vulnerability, or establish that one is more vulnerable.
research.attack_surface: Analyst-inferred candidate surfaces include ticket descriptions, knowledge-base instructions, accessibility-tree content, screenshot-to-element grounding, action identifiers, and record-changing frontend operations. These are legitimate workflow inputs and interfaces in the paper; no attacker control, injection payload, exploitation result, or validated security boundary is supplied.
research.method: Benchmark and systems study: 341 ServiceNow workflows at L2 and L3 yield 682 tasks; coded oracles and validators support reproducible curricula of 235 instances per level. Five agent variants operate through restricted BrowserGym actions under a 50-step cap. Evaluation includes a 15-person human study on 98 instances, qualitative trace analysis, oracle action-length characterization, and an L1 context-length ablation.
research.limitations: Safety and malicious-behavior robustness are explicitly outside scope. The environment is ServiceNow only; the human sample is small and biased; human and agent action budgets differ; model context budgets vary; qualitative errors lack prevalence estimates. Task-count, offboarding, and context-configuration inconsistencies remain unresolved. Repository and supplementary artifacts were not reviewed.

claims.statement: WorkArena++ presents 341 workflows at two instruction levels, yielding 682 tasks; L2 supplies explicit chat instructions whereas L3 uses tickets and knowledge-base guidance.
Tasks use coded oracles and validators; validators inspect task completion and return binary success rather than accepting the agent's own completion claim.
The reproducible agent curriculum contains 235 configured task instances at each of L2 and L3, with meta-seeds 0–9 reserved for evaluation.
Baseline agents are limited to 50 time steps, making reported success conditional on a practical execution budget.
Table 2 reports zero observed L3 success for all five agent variants on 235 instances; L2 overall success is 3.0 ± 1.1% for GPT-4o and 3.8 ± 1.3% for GPT-4o-v, with the other three variants at zero.
The human study uses 15 participants and a smaller 98-instance curriculum; its high success supports feasibility for that sample rather than exhaustive human validation of every task type.
The human-agent comparison has an action-budget asymmetry: humans have no explicit action limit, whereas agents have a 50-step limit.
The human cohort is not representative of general users: 11 of 15 participants had ServiceNow employment history, although employment did not necessarily imply product familiarity.
Qualitative errors include falsely believing an overwritten field remains correct, showing a divergence between the agent's progress account and actual page state.

For security research, the example of mistaking a ticket's assignment description for fulfilled work suggests a relevant instruction-versus-state failure mechanism, but it is not an adversarial attack demonstration.
The paper explicitly excludes assessment of safety and robustness against malicious behaviors; it therefore does not establish comparative vulnerability against standalone LLMs.
The trace-generation mechanism records BrowserGym observations and coded oracle actions; the supplied paper does not report an experiment measuring fine-tuning gains from those traces.
The context-length ablation is conducted on WorkArena L1, and the authors caution against expecting the same context insensitivity for more complex tasks.
The L2 overall point-estimate difference between GPT-4o-v and GPT-4o is 0.8 percentage points, calculated as 3.8% minus 3.0%; this is not a reported statistically established improvement.

quality.limitations: Quotation presence and page bounds do not prove claim entailment or full coverage.

research.title: AUTOSCRAPER: A Progressive Understanding Web Agent for Web Scraper Generation
research.research_question_relevance: ANALYST INFERENCE — MEDIUM confidence for architectural relevance; UNKNOWN confidence for comparative vulnerability. The paper illustrates a workflow in which webpage HTML influences LLM-generated XPath, parser outputs feed back into reasoning, and a selected extraction sequence is reused. These interfaces can inform questions about content manipulation and propagation of erroneous rules. The work does not directly compare the security of web agents and standalone LLMs; its direct-extraction comparison measures extraction performance rather than attack susceptibility.
research.attack_surface: ANALYST INFERENCE — Candidate interfaces for a future security analysis are preprocessed HTML input, extraction and thought history, LLM-generated XPath submitted to a parser, step-back judgments, and synthesis selection over candidate sequences and results. No attacker capabilities, malicious-content conditions, privileged actions, exfiltration paths, or demonstrated exploit are reported. Removal of script/style nodes and non-class attributes is preprocessing, not an evaluated security defense.
research.method: Two-phase scraper generation: progressive top-down XPath selection with step-back DOM-context recovery, followed by selection among candidate sequences using their extraction results across seed pages. Evaluation covers SWDE, Extended SWDE, and DS1 with eight LLMs, COT and Reflexion baselines, six case-outcome categories, mean per-case extraction metrics, synthesis ablation, seed-count variation, direct and supervised comparisons, runtime amortization, golden-label generation, action lengths, and predicate fragility. Main seed counts are 3, 3, and 1 respectively; DS1 omits synthesis.
research.limitations: Author-stated boundaries include vertical-page extraction, limited transfer to broad interactive environments, backbone dependence, non-generalizable layouts, missed multi-valued information, and XPath fragility. Analyst observations include absent security experiments, absent main-result confidence intervals, incomplete reproduction settings, unclear sample accounting, DS1 166/186-page inconsistency, Extended inventory 297/294 discrepancy, eight/ten runtime-domain mismatch, and pseudocode ambiguities. Text-only inspection applies to pages 9–11 and 17; external implementation and supplementary artifacts were not reviewed.

claims.statement: AUTOSCRAPER is a two-phase scraper-generation framework using progressive generation over HTML structure and synthesis based on multiple pages.
An action sequence executes XPath expressions in order; intermediate expressions prune the page and the final expression extracts the target value.
The main experiments use three seed webpages for SWDE and Extended SWDE, one for DS1, and a maximum retry parameter of five; these conditions must accompany interpretation of the reported scores.
On SWDE, GPT-4-Turbo with AUTOSCRAPER reports Correct 71.56%, Un-executable 4.06%, and macro-F1 88.69, compared with Reflexion's 67.50%, 10.94%, and 82.40 respectively.

Synthesis does not improve every metric: Gemini Pro AUTOSCRAPER on SWDE has F1 54.91 and Un-executable 34.38% with synthesis, versus F1 56.48 and Un-executable 31.56% without it, while Correct improves from 39.46% to 42.81%.
Direct extraction outperforms AUTOSCRAPER for seven of the eight tested models on SWDE; GPT-4-Turbo is the sole reverse case. This is an extraction-performance comparison, not a security comparison.
The authors report a mean runtime break-even threshold of 19.5 pages for GPT-4-Turbo; Table 6 lists eight domain thresholds averaging 19.5, although the experimental prose says ten domains.
The framework is explicitly limited to information extraction on vertical web pages and is not demonstrated to transfer readily to broader interactive environments such as Mind2Web or WebArena.

The authors identify incomplete extraction of multi-valued attributes as a remaining failure mode, including restaurant addresses and university contact numbers distributed across several page locations.
DS1 uses one webpage for inference and another for evaluation and omits synthesis, so its results test progressive generation rather than the complete two-phase configuration.
Extended SWDE contains exceptions to universal superiority: CodeLlama AUTOSCRAPER F1 is 12.52 versus Reflexion 16.01, and GPT-4-Turbo AUTOSCRAPER Correct is 64.11% versus Reflexion 64.81%.
The authors acknowledge XPath fragility even for GPT-4-Turbo; their analysis concerns reuse failures from predicates tied to specific page information rather than demonstrated adversarial attacks.

Analyst inference: passing HTML and extraction history into an LLM, then executing generated XPath and selecting reusable sequences, identifies interfaces worth examining in a security study. The supplied paper does not demonstrate that these interfaces are exploitable or more vulnerable than standalone LLMs.

The supplied study does not answer why web AI agents are more vulnerable than standalone LLMs: its explicit research questions address scraper performance, framework improvement, accuracy, and efficiency, and its experiments report no adversarial security comparison.
Analyst-derived: on SWDE with GPT-4-Turbo, AUTOSCRAPER's macro-F1 exceeds Reflexion by 88.69 − 82.40 = 6.29 score points. This is an absolute difference, not a relative percentage improvement.

quality.limitations: Quotation presence and page bounds do not prove claim entailment or full coverage.

research.title: Mind2Web 2: Evaluating Agentic Search with Agent-as-a-Judge
research.research_question_relevance: MEDIUM confidence, analyst inference: the paper informs the question 'Why Are Web AI Agents More Vulnerable Than Standalone LLMs? A Security Analysis' through evidence of complex browser environments, long contexts, improper tool invocation, source-memory failures, fabricated URLs, and unsupported synthesis. It is a reliability and benchmark study, not an adversarial security comparison. No standalone tool-free LLM control, attacker model, or attack-success measurement is supplied, so greater comparative vulnerability is not established.
research.attack_surface: Analyst inference only: examined interfaces include agent answers, cited URLs, retrieved webpage text and screenshots, browser interaction, generated tool code, and the evaluator's LLM inputs. These are relevant places to investigate untrusted-content handling, but the paper does not demonstrate exploitation of them. Its attribution framework assumes truthful and credible sources and does not assess source credibility.
research.method: 130 validated tasks across six domains and 24 subdomains; 10 public development tasks and 120 private test tasks; task-specific rubric trees with critical gates, non-critical averaging, and sequential dependencies; Python judges using o4-mini extraction/verification and cached webpage evidence; Claude-3.7-Sonnet initial script generation, debugging, reflection, and two-stage human refinement. Ten systems are evaluated three times per task using April–June 2025 answers; human comparison and error analysis use Subset-30; judge validation uses 15 tasks, two held-out answers each, and 720 leaf checks.
research.limitations: Authors acknowledge limited task scope, assumed source truthfulness, single-page attribution requirements, possible LLM judgment errors, and proprietary-system opacity. Additional analyst observations include unequal agent/human task sets, mixed timing procedures, observational rather than controlled mechanism comparisons, one primary judge-study evaluator with developer adjudication, unavailable reproduction artifacts, and possible completeness/scoring issues in the illustrative script. Original authors are Boyu Gou, Zanming Huang, Yuting Ning, Yu Gu, Michael Lin, Weijian Qi, Andrei Kopanev, Botao Yu, Bernal Jiménez Gutiérrez, Yiheng Shu, Chan Hee Song, Jiaman Wu, Shijie Chen, Hanane Nour Moussa, Tianshu Zhang, Jian Xie, Yifei Li, Tianci Xue, Zeyi Liao, Kai Zhang, Boyuan Zheng, Zhaowei Cai, Viktor Rozgic, Morteza Ziyadi, Huan Sun, and Yu Su; affiliations are The Ohio State University and Amazon AGI. The supplied version is arXiv:2506.21506v2, 3 July 2025.

claims.statement: Mind2Web 2 contains 130 curated tasks; construction of tasks and judge agents together required at least 1,000 hours of human labor.
Each task is evaluated by a dedicated Python judge workflow that checks fine-grained rubric criteria and aggregates their scores upward; Extractor and Verifier tools use o4-mini.
The rubric evaluates both correctness against task requirements and attribution to cited sources; leaf judgments are binary and internal scores are aggregated hierarchically.

Table 3 reports OpenAI Deep Research partial completion 0.54±0.04, success 0.28±0.04, Pass@3 0.40, and time 8.40±0.71 minutes. Human results are 0.79±0.01, 0.54±0.07, 0.83, and 18.40±1.61 minutes, but humans use Subset-30 while agent accuracy uses the private test set.
The authors identify 57 explicitly time-varying tasks. Most systems perform worse on this subset; Operator and humans achieve relatively similar or superior performance compared with other tasks.

Judge validation reports 99.03% correctness from seven actual errors among 720 leaf verifications after adjudicating human mistakes and excluding a conflicting-source case; four of the seven errors involve inaccessible collapsed webpage content.
The evaluator assumes cited sources are truthful and credible; evaluating source truthfulness is outside scope. Therefore verified attribution does not establish independent factual truth.

The benchmark excludes video and non-English tasks, avoids explicitly complex-reasoning or external-tool requirements, excludes extremely rapidly changing answers, and requires attribution checks decomposable into individual webpage verification.

In the Subset-30 error analysis of five representative agents, hallucination is defined as the union of Invalid Attribution and Unsupported Answer. OpenAI Deep Research has a reported rate of 23%; other analyzed agents have rates of at least 50%. These are task-level error rates, not adversarial attack-success rates.
Figure F.12 illustrates Operator reporting an invalid source URL even after visiting the correct page, separating successful navigation from reliable final-answer provenance.

Analyst inference: the authors' discussion of noisy browser environments, complex action spaces, and longer contexts is relevant to possible web-agent failure mechanisms, but it does not establish greater adversarial vulnerability than standalone LLMs.

The supplied study selects agentic search systems with search, browsing, or hybrid capabilities; it provides no controlled standalone tool-free LLM comparator and no adversarial attack evaluation. The user's comparative security question is consequently not directly answered.

System answers were collected between April and June 2025; Hugging Face Open Deep Research used OpenAI o3, while other systems were accessed through web interfaces. Results describe those collection conditions rather than current product performance.

Using Table 3 means, OpenAI Deep Research reaches approximately 68.35% of human partial completion (0.54/0.79×100), 51.85% of human success (0.28/0.54×100), and 45.65% of human time (8.40/18.40×100). These descriptive ratios retain the human-subset and timing caveats.

The example judge script checks each of five author slots against any expected contributor and marks the profile-source node non-critical. No explicit cross-slot uniqueness enforcement is visible, so completeness and scoring behavior require inspection of the unavailable toolkit rather than assuming the example enforces every requested detail.

quality.limitations: Quotation presence and page bounds do not prove claim entailment or full coverage.

research.title: WebDancer: Towards Autonomous Information Seeking Agency
research.research_question_relevance: ANALYST INFERENCE, MEDIUM confidence: The paper is relevant as architectural and reliability evidence for investigating why web-agent security might differ from standalone-model security. External observations guide subsequent reasoning and actions, and tool responses are serialized as user messages. These are interfaces for future security tests. The paper directly compares task performance across base, RAG, and agentic configurations; it does not compare their adversarial vulnerability or establish that web agents are more vulnerable.
research.attack_surface: ANALYST INFERENCE, MEDIUM confidence: Candidate interfaces visible in the current system include search titles/snippets, visited web content, summarizer-produced evidence and summaries, tool-response dialogue context, and generated search/visit arguments. No malicious-content experiment, privilege model, credential exposure, or exploit is supplied. Browser modules and a Python sandbox for external APIs are future proposals and are excluded from the evaluated current surface.
research.method: AUTHOR-REPORTED, HIGH confidence: Four-stage pipeline: synthesize CRAWLQA and E2HQA; sample short/long-CoT ReAct trajectories with rejection sampling and quality filtering; apply observation-masked supervised fine-tuning; apply on-policy DAPO with binary format and model-judged correctness rewards weighted 0.1 and 0.9. Evaluation uses 103 GAIA text-only validation questions and 680 WebWalkerQA test questions, with additional BrowseComp evaluations and training/data ablations.
research.limitations: AUTHOR-REPORTED plus clearly labeled ANALYST OBSERVATIONS: Current tools and short-answer tasks are limited; RL uses a small subset under compute/stability constraints; rollouts are costly; long reasoning can generate invalid or repetitive outputs, nonexistent tools, and redundant actions. Analyst observations include absent security tests, no uncertainty intervals, incomplete reproducibility settings, an action-filter/count contradiction, an unexplained Figure 3 count mismatch, and an unrelated thought in the case study. No absent supplement or external repository was reviewed.

claims.statement: WebDancer proposes a four-stage pipeline combining browsing-data construction, trajectory sampling, supervised fine-tuning for cold start, and reinforcement learning for generalization.

The agent uses search and visit tools plus an answer termination action; search observations contain top-10 titles and snippets, while visit observations contain summarizer-generated evidence and summary.
Supervised training excludes observation-token loss while retaining observations as context for generating the agent's decision steps.
The reported evaluations use 103 questions from GAIA's text-only validation split and 680 questions from the WebWalkerQA test set; these are task-success evaluations rather than attack evaluations.
Under Table 1's Pass@1 conditions, QwQ-32B WebDancer improves over QwQ-32B vanilla ReAct by 13.7 percentage points on GAIA (51.5 minus 37.8) and 23.8 points on WebWalkerQA (47.9 minus 24.1).
The authors report best-model Pass@3 scores of 64.1% on GAIA and 62.0% on WebWalkerQA; these three-attempt results must be distinguished from Table 1's Pass@1 averages.

Table 3 shows a reasoning-style trade-off: Qwen2.5-7B's invalid rate rises from 0.65% with short-CoT to 21.36% with long-CoT, while its Pass@3 rises from 33.98 to 35.92 and its Cons@3 falls from 22.33 to 21.00.

In a same-set memorization stress test, Qwen-7B was fine-tuned on 69 correctly sampled GAIA-development trajectories for 10 epochs, but greedy decoding achieved only 37.4%; this is not a held-out generalization result.
The authors acknowledge hallucinated nonexistent tools and redundant actions after answer confirmation; these are reliability limitations, not measured adversarial attack outcomes.

For the security research question, serializing tool responses as user messages identifies an external-content interface worth examining. The paper does not establish that such content acquires legitimate user authority or demonstrate an exploit.

The case study contains an unresolved goal-coherence mismatch: its fish/USGS question is followed by a Step 2 thought about chinstrap-penguin population differences, although the subsequent visit action concerns the fish.

The supplied study compares information-seeking task performance across direct-model, RAG, and agentic configurations, but provides no threat model, adversarial attack experiment, or measured vulnerability comparison establishing that web agents are more vulnerable than standalone LLMs.

The action-filter description on p. 5 says to remove trajectories with more than two actions, but Table 4 on p. 18 reports mean action counts of 4.56 and 2.31. The supplied work does not reconcile the apparent inconsistency.

The authors identify misinformation from unreliable sources and possible misuse in automated content extraction or surveillance as broader-impact concerns; these are stated risks rather than experimentally quantified harms.

quality.limitations: Quotation presence and page bounds do not prove claim entailment or full coverage.

research.title: WebGPT: Browser-assisted question-answering with human feedback
research.research_question_relevance: ANALYST INFERENCE, MEDIUM confidence: WebGPT is relevant to 'Why Are Web AI Agents More Vulnerable Than Standalone LLMs?' because its browser architecture adds external-source ingestion, evidence selection, and externally executed actions. Its discussion identifies selective references, citation-induced overreliance, and conditional evidence manipulation with broader permissions. It does not directly compare security vulnerability against standalone LLMs. Its actual GPT-3 comparison concerns truthfulness and favors WebGPT under the reported conditions.
research.attack_surface: ANALYST INFERENCE: Potential security-relevant boundaries include Bing queries and result text, fetched pages, HTML/PDF-to-text conversion, indexed links, collected quotations, and browser commands. The implemented external actions are restricted to queries and following existing links. Form submission and direct page editing are absent. Prompt injection, exfiltration, credential theft, and successful privilege escalation are not evaluated.
research.method: Empirical machine-learning and restricted-browser systems study: GPT-3 models of 760M, 13B, and 175B parameters learn from human browser demonstrations; pairwise comparisons train reward models; PPO and best-of-n selection are compared. Main configurations use behavior cloning plus 4, 16, or 64 candidates, temperature 0.8, and at most 100 browsing actions. Evaluations cover ELI5 preferences, TruthfulQA truthfulness/informativeness, TriviaQA extraction, scaling, framing, cultural bias, and contractor surveys.
research.limitations: No formal attacker model or controlled security comparison; current browser lacks direct write actions. Human preference and supportedness do not equal independently established truth. TruthfulQA uses different evaluator types for GPT-3 and WebGPT and truncates WebGPT answers. The framing study is small, cultural bias is a single-question case study, some scaling uses a learned proxy, and smaller-model RL has a disclosed EMA bug. Linked supplementary artifacts were not inspected.

claims.statement: WebGPT fine-tunes GPT-3 to answer long-form questions through a text browser that permits searching and navigating the web.

The evaluated 175B best-of-64 model receives 56% overall preference against browser-using human demonstrators on ELI5, with ties counted as half preferences; this is not an absolute factual-accuracy rate.

The same 175B best-of-64 model receives 69% preference against ELI5 Reddit reference answers under a separate protocol that strips model citations and references and uses new contractors with minimal instructions.

The best WebGPT configuration is reported as 75% truthful and 54% both truthful and informative on TruthfulQA, outperforming base GPT-3 while remaining below human performance; WebGPT uses human scoring and truncated answers.
For 175B models, best-of-64 selection of behavior-cloned answers is preferred to unselected BC 68% of the time, whereas RL is preferred to BC 58%; these are separate comparisons against BC.
The detailed comparison procedure evaluates whether answer claims are supported by reliable references or common knowledge, without requiring independent research into factual accuracy.
The authors acknowledge that citations may make WebGPT appear more authoritative and encourage overreliance even when it produces false statements.
The reference-based reward procedure may incentivize cherry-picking evidence that evaluators find convincing rather than representing the evidence fairly.
The authors' hypothetical live-web risk is that a model with form access could edit Wikipedia to manufacture a credible-looking reference; they do not report this occurring in WebGPT.

The implemented environment limits external interactions to Bing queries and following existing links, excluding direct Wikipedia editing; the authors assess current real-world side-effect exploitation risk as very low.
The hypothesis that WebGPT reduces non-imitative falsehoods relative to GPT-3 was not directly tested because subtle hallucinations were difficult for labelers to identify.
The 60-question framing study gives suggestive evidence of lower accuracy for affirming questions, but its authors consider the sample too small for definitive conclusions.

In the TriviaQA development evaluation, adding WebGPT output to the fine-tuned GPT-3 answer extractor raises total exact match by 10.8 percentage points, calculated as 69.5% minus 58.7%; this evaluates a two-stage system.

Analyst inference: browser integration introduces external-information and external-action pathways relevant to security, but WebGPT supplies no controlled attack experiment establishing greater vulnerability than standalone GPT-3.

Appendix I's validation reward model predicts selection performance well for n at most 64 in the tested setting, while the authors expect sufficiently large n to overoptimize even the validation evaluator.

quality.limitations: Quotation presence and page bounds do not prove claim entailment or full coverage.

research.title: WebSailor: Navigating Super-human Reasoning for Web Agent
research.research_question_relevance: ANALYST INFERENCE, MEDIUM confidence: the paper describes how external search results, retrieved webpages, goal-conditioned summaries, and repeated observations enter an agent's later decision context. These are useful boundaries for studying why web agents might differ from standalone LLMs in security exposure. The paper compares direct inference and browsing for accuracy, not vulnerability, and does not establish that web agents are more vulnerable.
research.attack_surface: ANALYST INFERENCE, MEDIUM confidence for architectural identification; UNKNOWN confidence for exploitability: search-result titles, snippets and URLs; full webpage content retrieved through Jina; Qwen-2.5-72B goal-conditioned page summaries; accumulated tool-response context; and model-based answer judging. No attacker-controlled condition, demonstrated exploit, security objective, or attack success rate is supplied.
research.method: Graph-based SailorFog-QA synthesis with ambiguous clues; successful expert action-observation traces with reconstructed short reasoning; correctness, length and tool-call filtering; observation-masked RFT cold start; DUPO RL with group-relative rewards and duplication of informative batch cases; benchmark and ablation evaluation of Qwen-2.5-based 3B, 7B, 32B and 72B agents using search and visit tools.

Performance evaluation uses heterogeneous baseline provenance, partial benchmark coverage, LLM judging, and no reported confidence intervals. Synthetic answers may be nonunique. claims.statement: WebSailor is an integrated post-training methodology combining high-uncertainty task generation, RFT cold start, and DUPO reinforcement learning.
The agent follows repeated Thought-Action-Observation interactions, with external observations entering the history used for subsequent decisions.
SailorFog-QA deliberately obfuscates question features and relationships to increase initial uncertainty; this is training-data construction rather than a evaluated security attack.

The supervision pipeline discards verbose expert thoughts, retains successful action-observation traces, and reconstructs concise thoughts conditioned on the current action and its subsequent observation.
RFT retains correct-answer trajectories, discards those exceeding 32k tokens, keeps trajectories with more than five tool calls, and masks observation tokens from the loss.

DUPO duplicates informative cases already in the batch after removing zero-variance cases and is reported to achieve approximately 2–3 times speedup over DAPO dynamic sampling; detailed timing conditions are absent.
GAIA evaluation uses 103 cases from its text-only validation subset, so these results do not evaluate the benchmark's full multimodal scope.

Table 1 reports WebSailor-72B scores of 12.0, 30.1, 55.0, and 55.4 on BrowseComp-en, BrowseComp-zh, Xbench-DeepSearch, and the evaluated GAIA subset; it leads the listed open-source rows but not DeepResearch where reported.

On BrowseComp-en, DeepResearch's 51.5 exceeds WebSailor-72B's 12.0 by 39.5 percentage points, calculated as 51.5 minus 12.0; parity therefore does not apply to this strongest listed proprietary comparison.
The authors acknowledge that some synthesized questions may have multiple valid answers, so low pass rates reflect both difficulty and ambiguity.

Figure 4 reports 93.5% and 92.8% pass@1 for WebSailor-72B and WebSailor-32B on a 200-question SimpleQA sample, rather than the full 4,326-question dataset; the scoring aggregation behind some decimal values is unspecified.
The cold-start ablation favors RFT followed by RL over direct RL in the tested Qwen-2.5-instruct-32B setting; it does not establish necessity for every model or training budget.
The authors identify context-limit failures, possible over-thinking, and synchronous RL inefficiency as limitations; RL is limited to 50 training steps.

For security research, the described visit pipeline identifies external webpage retrieval and a goal-conditioned Qwen-2.5-72B summarizer as additional information-processing boundaries. This architectural relevance is analyst inference, not evidence that these boundaries are exploitable.

The supplied study compares direct inference and browsing on information-seeking accuracy, but does not evaluate comparative security vulnerability, attack success, or an explicit attacker threat model.

quality.limitations: Quotation presence and page bounds do not prove claim entailment or full coverage.

research.title: WEBSCRAPER: LEVERAGE MULTIMODAL LARGE LANGUAGE MODELS FOR INDEX-CONTENT WEB SCRAPING
research.research_question_relevance: ANALYST INFERENCE, MEDIUM confidence: the paper provides a concrete architecture for examining how external webpage observations connect to computer actions, network/file tools, delegated parsing, and generated-code execution. research.attack_surface: ANALYST INFERENCE: candidate interfaces include screenshot and HTML ingestion, agent-to-tool decisions, Bash network and filesystem operations, file editing, delegated model inputs, generated Python execution, and output consolidation. These are described capabilities and analytical boundaries, not demonstrated exploit paths; permissions and security controls are unspecified.
research.method: Experimental AI systems study using Anthropic Computer Use with a guiding five-stage prompt and custom Parse/Merge Tools. It compares baseline, prompt-only, and full configurations on six news sites and two e-commerce sites, with temperature 0, clean Firefox starts, 30 reported repetitions, a CI convergence analysis, and a seven-day temporal repeat. News Correctness requires exact URL matching and title/content ROUGE-L scores of at least 0.8; product Correctness is stricter but incompletely defined.
research.limitations: Index-and-content scope; visual-navigation and generated-code failures; difficulty with streaming and advanced virtual scrolling; incomplete benchmark sizes, statistical details, product matching rules, prompt stages, and implementation access; unresolved GPT-o3 versus GPT-o3-mini wording. Figures 1–4 and Tables 1–2 were visually reviewed on pages 1–5; pages 6–7 were text-only. No adversarial evaluation or standalone-LLM control is reported.

claims.statement: The framework targets index-and-content websites, with listing pages linking to individual detail pages, and returns extracted items as structured JSON.
Webscraper enhances Computer Use with specialized parsing and merging tools and a guiding prompt for a five-stage process; the supplied paper does not enumerate those stages.
The Parse Tool sends HTML and user requirements to a reasoning model that generates Python code, then executes the script in a GPT code interpreter environment.
The experiments compare baseline, prompt-only, and prompt-plus-tools configurations at temperature 0, with each run starting a clean Firefox instance.
For news, an article is correct only if its URL exactly matches the reference and both title and content have ROUGE-L scores of at least 0.8.

The authors select 30 runs using diminishing reductions in 95% CI half-width; the supplied document does not specify the interval estimator or reconcile its nine convergence settings with all news configurations.
Figure 3 shows the full system above the baseline and prompt-only configuration on every one of the six news websites; exact bar values and between-method statistical uncertainty are not displayed.
The baseline is reported to have successfully operated LTN pagination only twice in 30 runs; this navigation count is distinct from article-level Correctness.
Table 2 reports baseline/prompt-only/full scores of 0.000/0.040/0.242 on Momo and 0.027/0.138/0.422 on Amazon, under a stricter near-exact product criterion whose tolerance is unspecified.
From Table 2, the full system's absolute gain over baseline is 24.2 percentage points on Momo, calculated as (0.242−0.000)×100, and 39.5 percentage points on Amazon, calculated as (0.422−0.027)×100.

Table 1's full-system seven-day changes are +0.022, +0.025, and 0.000 for Websites 3, 4, and 5, calculated respectively from 0.533−0.511, 0.673−0.648, and 0.820−0.820; these are score changes, not statistical variance estimates.
The authors identify complex navigation and buggy LLM-generated parsing scripts as critical failure modes and limit the framework's applicability to index-and-content architectures.

For the security research question, the described access to webpage observations, filesystem operations, network requests, and generated-code execution identifies candidate interfaces for security analysis, but the paper does not demonstrate that they are exploitable.
The supplied evaluation compares Computer Use configurations on extraction performance; it does not directly compare web agents with standalone LLMs or measure adversarial attack success.
Page 3 names GPT-o3 in the Parse Tool description but OpenAI GPT-o3-mini in the experimental setting; the supplied document does not explicitly reconcile the model names.

The authors report restricting experiments to public information without bypassing access controls, using delayed low-frequency requests, and keeping collected data for academic research rather than redistribution or commercial use.

research.title: WebWalker: Benchmarking LLMs in Web Traversal

research.method: Mixed benchmark and empirical AI systems study: 680 human-refined QA pairs across 1,373 webpages; single-source and two-page multi-source construction with depth-based difficulty; explorer–critic WebWalker compared with ReAct and Reflexion across six listed backbones in zero-shot conditions with a principal 15-action budget; GPT-4 factual grading and correct-execution action counts; additional domain/language, error-category, search-system, RAG-integration, and action-budget analyses.

Table 3 Qwen2.5-7B ReAct overall action count is below all displayed subgroup means; the aggregation remains unresolved.

claims.statement: WebWalkerQA contains 680 queries spanning four real-world scenarios and more than 1,373 webpages according to the contribution statement; Table 1 reports 1,373 webpages.
Dataset construction combines initial GPT-4o annotation with crowdsourced human quality control, filtering, and possible rewriting of questions and answers.
WebWalker separates exploration from criticism: the explorer selects clickable subpage URLs, while the critic accumulates useful information and decides when sufficient evidence exists to answer.
The main WebWalker, ReAct, and Reflexion experiments operate zero-shot with an explorer budget of at most 15 actions; the reported action-count metric includes only correct executions.

Under the principal zero-shot, 15-action setup, GPT-4o WebWalker has the highest Table 3 overall accuracy at 37.50%, with reported successful-execution action count 4.67; GPT-4o ReAct and Reflexion achieve 33.82% and 35.29%.

GPT-4o WebWalker's overall accuracy gain over GPT-4o ReAct is 3.68 percentage points, calculated as 37.50 minus 33.82; this is an absolute percentage-point difference, not a relative percentage improvement.

WebWalker leads overall accuracy within all six Table 3 backbones, but the authors' generalized Reflexion-over-ReAct ranking has an exception: Qwen2.5-32B ReAct scores 25.44% overall versus Reflexion's 23.26%.

Table 4 reports no-retrieval overall accuracies of 8.08% for Gemini-1.5-Pro and 9.85% for o1-preview, while Tongyi has the highest search-enhanced overall accuracy at 40.73%; these are factual QA conditions, not adversarial security comparisons.

The hybrid RAG configuration appends critic memory to relevant retrieved documents and reports improvement across difficulty levels, especially multi-source questions; exact hybrid accuracies are not printed in the supplied Figure 8.

The action-budget experiment varies K over 5, 10, 15, 20, and 25 using Qwen-Plus and reports better performance at larger budgets within the tested range; the plotted high-budget results visibly flatten and no cost-normalized or security result is provided.

The authors acknowledge a 680-pair verified benchmark, approximately 14k not-carefully-human-verified silver QA pairs, HTML-DOM-only interaction, prompt-driven agents without additional training, and supplied-root limitations in RAG integration.

Page 4 contains an unresolved domain-percentage discrepancy: prose assigns game questions 24.0%, while Figure 3's game-colored slice is labeled 21.9%; no exact domain counts are supplied to resolve it.

The reasoning case distinguishes locating the correct page from correctly processing its contents; the six-day lounge schedule supports the reported 66-hour answer, but no full failed agent calculation is supplied.

Analyst inference: the documented webpage-to-observation, observation-to-memory/action, and memory-to-RAG-generation flows identify candidate security boundaries for studying web-agent exposure; the paper does not test malicious content or establish exploitability.

The supplied paper does not directly compare adversarial vulnerability of web AI agents and standalone LLMs: its no-retrieval comparison concerns answer accuracy, and its error analysis concerns refusal/wrong location, reasoning errors, and action-budget exhaustion rather than attacks.

research.title: A Whole New World: Creating a Parallel-Poisoned Web Only AI-Agents Can See
research.research_question_relevance: ANALYST INFERENCE, MEDIUM confidence: The paper suggests that autonomous retrieval of attacker-controlled web content, recognizable agent fingerprints, and tools with access to sensitive resources create additional attack routes. research.attack_surface: Attacker-controlled website responses selected using browser, automation, behavioral, or network fingerprints; malicious content may contain indirect prompt injection or an explicit authentication prerequisite involving a secret.
research.method: Conceptual two-stage fingerprinting-and-cloaking attack, structured threat model, six-step illustrative execution flow, and one internal API documentation-site demonstration in Cursor with Claude 4 Sonnet, GPT-5 Fast, and Gemini 2.5 Pro. Figure 1 depicts distinct human and agent paths.
research.limitations: Success is reported qualitatively without trial counts, detector metrics, detailed traces, exact permissions, or a standalone-model baseline. The experiment uses one described internal site and one agent application. Broad attack consequences and defensive proposals are not all experimentally tested. Text coverage spans pages 1–10; visual coverage is limited to pages 1, 5, 6, and 7.

claims.statement: The paper describes agentic LLMs as tool-augmented systems that interact with the external world through a sense-plan-act loop.
The central thesis is that malicious websites can distinguish AI agents from human visitors and selectively serve malicious payloads; the paper does not quantify detection reliability.
The threat model grants the adversary control of a web server and server-side logic for analyzing requests and selecting responses.
The proposed benign default includes human visitors, known security crawlers, and otherwise unidentifiable visitors; strongly identified agents receive the cloaked response.
The malicious response may be a completely different page, so the attack family is not limited to hidden instructions on a visually identical page.
The experiment used an internal API documentation website whose agent-facing response requested authentication using a specific environment variable.
The author reports success for the listed Cursor configurations powered by Claude 4 Sonnet, GPT-5 Fast, and Gemini 2.5 Pro; this qualitative statement has no reported trial denominator.

The experimental list contains three powering-model configurations: one Claude 4 Sonnet entry plus one GPT-5 Fast entry plus one Gemini 2.5 Pro entry equals three; this is not a count of independent trials.
Figure 1 visually distinguishes a green benign documentation route from a red agent route that passes through a private-key authentication request before reaching documentation.

The paper proposes planner-executor isolation in which a sandboxed low-privilege executor handles untrusted content and returns structured data to a privileged planner; it does not report testing this defense.

The supplied experimental account does not specify repetitions, a numerical success rate, confidence intervals, detector accuracy, or a standalone-LLM baseline; its success statement cannot establish comparative vulnerability quantitatively.

For the user's research question, the paper suggests that untrusted web exposure combined with tool-mediated access to sensitive resources creates additional attack routes; this is analyst inference rather than a direct agent-versus-standalone experiment.
The author identifies standardized robustness benchmarks for cloaking and indirect prompt injection as future work, rather than supplying such a benchmark in this study.
The author explicitly acknowledges that broader network and server-side defensive contributions are harder to implement universally.

research.title: AdvAgent: Controllable Blackbox Red-teaming on Web Agents
research.research_question_relevance: MEDIUM confidence, analyst inference: the paper shows how attacker-controlled, visually hidden HTML can influence a web agent's executable action arguments. Its relevance to why agents may face greater security exposure concerns environmental inputs, HTML grounding, and consequential action execution. It does not conduct a matched comparison against standalone LLMs and cannot establish a comparative vulnerability rate.
research.attack_surface: Webpage HTML accessible to SeeAct during action grounding, primarily non-rendered aria-label attributes near the expected target element; an id-field variation is also evaluated. The attacker controls HTML and obtains black-box feedback but lacks agent-framework, model-weight, logit, and gradient access. The formal objective changes the action argument while preserving operation and target element.
research.method: GPT-4 generates candidate adversarial prompts with replaceable target placeholders. Victim-agent responses label candidates as successful or failed. A Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.2 prompter receives positive-only supervised fine-tuning and then direct preference optimization using positive and negative prompts with a fixed SFT reference. Evaluation uses SeeAct with gpt-4-vision-preview and gemini-1.5-flash on a four-domain Mind2Web subset of 440 tasks split into 240 training and 200 testing tasks, with exact action-triplet step ASR.
research.limitations: Author-stated limitations are offline victim-feedback optimization and step-based evaluation that does not fully capture complete-task risks. Analyst observations include one evaluated agent framework, two backend identifiers, four selected domains, conditional reuse experiments, incomplete denominators and reproduction details, no matched standalone-LLM comparison, no measured completed financial harm, and no review of the linked code or absent supplements.

claims.statement: AdvAgent operates without access to agent weights or logits and uses victim feedback to optimize generated adversarial prompts.
The formal targeted attack preserves the operation and target HTML element while maliciously replacing the operation argument.
The attack design places prompts in non-rendered HTML attributes such as aria-label to preserve webpage appearance, and uses placeholders to enable target substitution.
The prompter is trained with SFT on successful adversarial prompts, followed by DPO using successful and unsuccessful prompts and a fixed SFT reference policy.
The selected Mind2Web corpus contains 440 tasks across four domains, divided into 240 training tasks and 200 testing tasks; this does not mean 440 held-out test tasks.
Table 1 reports AdvAgent mean step-based ASR of 97.5 ± 2.0% for GPT-4V SeeAct and 99.8 ± 0.3% for Gemini 1.5 SeeAct; the error terms describe variation across domains.
The reported training ablation improves mean ASR by 28.0 percentage points when adding DPO: 97.5% minus 69.5%. This is an absolute difference, not a relative percent improvement.
Table 2 shows conditional reuse ASR of 97.0 ± 1.7% after changing the HTML field, but 71.0 ± 26.1% after changing injection position; finance position success is only 26.0%.

Retargeting previously successful adversarial prompts produces mean ASR of 98.5% on GPT-4V and 100.0% on Gemini; these are conditional controllability results rather than universal fresh-attack success rates.

Transferring 25 successful GPT-4V attacks per domain to Gemini yields mean ASR of 18.0%, compared with 99.8% for reported direct attacks; the direct row is not explicitly shown to use the identical selected sample.
Against Gemini SeeAct, sequence enclosure, instruction defense, and sandwich defense leave mean ASR of 89.8%, 88.8%, and 89.8%, respectively; housing and cooking remain at 100.0% under each defense.
The authors acknowledge that victim feedback for attack-string optimization must be obtained offline; online feedback-based real-time optimization is proposed as future work.
The authors acknowledge that individual-step ASR does not fully capture risk across complete user requests and call for end-to-end interactive evaluation.

Analyst inference: combining screenshot-based action descriptions with HTML grounding creates a route for visually hidden environmental content to influence executable actions, making this paper relevant to added web-agent exposure. It does not directly compare vulnerability with standalone LLMs.
Figure 5 visibly demonstrates typing NVIDIA rather than Microsoft and searching for Aspirin rather than Tylenol; its displayed actions do not by themselves establish completion of a stock purchase.

quality.limitations: Quotation presence and page bounds do not prove claim entailment or full coverage.

research.title: AgentVigil: Generic Black-Box Red-teaming for Indirect Prompt Injection against LLM Agents
research.research_question_relevance: Analyst inference, MEDIUM confidence: the paper explains an agent-specific attack pathway in which third-party web content enters an LLM planner and redirects tool-mediated actions. This is relevant to understanding additional exposure and consequences in web agents. The paper does not directly compare standalone LLMs with agents, so it cannot establish a comparative vulnerability rate or prove the research question's premise.
research.attack_surface: Attacker-controlled external data read during legitimate agent execution, including environment-state placeholders, text triggers in web tasks, and customer reviews in a local shopping site. The attacker lacks internal model and agent access, can test similar tasks, and receives binary attack feedback. Image-trigger optimization and direct infrastructure compromise are outside the reported evaluation scope.
research.method: Black-box adaptive fuzzing using collected prompt templates, GPT-4o-mini-assisted Shorten, Expand, Rephrase, Crossover, and GenerateSimilar mutations, attack-success plus intended new-task-coverage scoring, and MCTS-inspired UCB1 seed selection. Evaluation covers AgentDojo and VWA-adv, held-out tasks, other model backbones, selected defenses, two ablation conditions, a local shopping-site case, extra models, additional baselines, and scenario breakdowns.
research.limitations: No standalone-LLM control, uncertainty intervals, repeated-run variability, complete corpus, exact split memberships, numerical scoring weights, complete query costs, or measured scalability results are supplied. Transfer gains are not universal, especially for Claude. Scoring and selection are ablated jointly. VWA headline/table results, defense prose/table interpretations, and Appendix B.1/Table 4 values have unresolved inconsistencies. The practical example is locally deployed, and web attacks focus on text triggers.

claims.statement: The paper describes indirect prompt injection as malicious instructions placed in external data sources that an agent encounters, potentially redirecting it from the user's task.
The threat model restricts attackers to manipulating external sources and observing binary success/failure feedback for individual tasks, without internal model or agent access.
AgentVigil combines initial attack templates, five randomly selected LLM-assisted mutation methods, attack-success and coverage scoring, and MCTS-inspired UCB1 seed selection.
AgentDojo evaluation uses 142 fuzzing scenarios and 173 test scenarios, an o3-mini fuzzing backbone, GPT-4o-mini mutation, and ten iterations with three mutated prompts per iteration.
For AgentDojo o3-mini fuzzing, the paper reports 38% handcrafted-baseline ASR, 63% initial-corpus ASR, and 71% final AgentVigil ASR; Table 1 agrees with the 38% and 71% values.

The VWA-adv evaluation focuses on text-trigger attacks in a multimodal web environment, with 99 fuzzing tasks, 100 test tasks, GPT-4o as the fuzzing backbone, and ten mutations per iteration for ten iterations.

Section 5.2 reports a 70% final VWA-adv fuzzing result, whereas Tables 1 and 3 show 0.60 for GPT-4o selected-prompt fuzzing/no-defense ASR. The supplied paper does not resolve the aggregation difference.

Table 1 supports conditional transfer: AgentVigil achieves test ASR 0.65 on AgentDojo o3-mini and 0.67 on VWA-adv Gemini, but is below the handcrafted baseline on Claude in every displayed benchmark/split comparison.

Tested defenses reduce AgentVigil ASR while leaving nonzero residual attacks: AgentDojo values are 0.25, 0.12, and 0.49; VWA-adv values are 0.29, 0.33, and 0.27. Superiority over baseline is not consistent under defenses.

The AgentDojo ablation replaces the initial corpus in one condition and jointly replaces adaptive scoring and MCTS selection with random selection in another; it does not separately isolate scoring and selection.

The shopping-site case uses a local WebArena deployment and a normal customer account to inject a malicious review; it demonstrates redirected behavior rather than reporting a deployment-wide attack frequency.
Table 4 reports AgentVigil fuzzing/test ASR 0.73/0.76 on o3-mini-2025-01-31 and 0.72/0.74 on QwQ-32B, exceeding all three displayed baselines; nearby Appendix B.1 prose contains inconsistent values.

Algorithm 1 intends a reward for newly successful combinations, but its displayed coverage-bonus condition only tests injection success; the explicit novelty predicate and the numerical coverage weight are not supplied.

Analyst inference: the paper is relevant to agent-specific vulnerability because external web content can influence an LLM planner with action-capable tools. It does not directly compare agent vulnerability with standalone-LLM vulnerability.

Analyst-derived: AgentDojo o3-mini fuzzing improves by 33 percentage points, calculated as 71% minus 38%; relative improvement is approximately 86.8%, calculated as (71 minus 38) divided by 38 times 100.

quality.limitations: Quotation presence and page bounds do not prove claim entailment or full coverage.

research.title: AGENTVIGIL: Automatic Black-Box Red-teaming for Indirect Prompt Injection against LLM Agents

The paper explains how external content consumed during multi-step agent execution can influence the planning LLM and trigger tool-mediated unauthorized actions. This is relevant to why web-agent interfaces may expose additional attack pathways. It does not directly compare matched standalone LLMs with web agents or establish a numerical increase in vulnerability due to agentization.
research.attack_surface: Attacker-controlled external data encountered by benign-user agents: environmental placeholders, shopping reviews, email/calendar-style content, and VWA-adv text triggers. Image-trigger attack generation, direct harmful-user misuse, and infrastructure attacks are outside the evaluated scope.

claims.statement: The threat model restricts the attacker to manipulating external data sources and observing individual-task binary success/failure, without access to model or agent internals.
AgentVigil combines initial templates, five helper-LLM mutation operations, ASR-plus-new-coverage scoring, and confidence-bound seed selection to iteratively optimize injections.
AgentDojo optimization against o3-mini reports 71% ASR, compared with 38% handcrafted baseline and 63% initial-corpus ASR, using 142 fuzzing tasks and 10 iterations.

VWA-adv optimization against GPT-4o uses text-trigger tasks and reports 70% final success versus 36% baseline; Tables 1 and 3 instead report 60% selected-prompt fuzzing ASR, an incompletely explained distinction.

Table 1 reports held-out-task ASRs of 0.65 for AgentDojo/o3-mini, 0.59 for VWA-adv/GPT-4o, and 0.67 for VWA-adv/Gemini; Claude transfer underperforms the handcrafted baseline in all displayed conditions.

Table 2 contradicts the prose's universal defense-superiority wording: fixed selected AgentVigil attacks obtain 0.12 ASR under repeat versus 0.21 for handcrafted attacks. Separate adaptive optimization against repeat reports 74% versus 21%.

The ablation supports the curated corpus and combined scoring/selection mechanism, but cannot isolate scoring and selection individually because they are replaced together by uniform random selection.

The deployment-style shopping case uses a local WebArena/Magento2 copy and a regular account's malicious review; it demonstrates author-reported unwanted URL navigation without supplying a quantitative trial denominator.
The authors acknowledge high optimization cost and relatively poor performance against models such as Claude, limiting scalability and cross-model generalization.

Appendix B.1 and Table 4 disagree about updated o3-mini: prose reports AgentVigil 72%/74% and baseline 50%/53%, whereas the table lists 0.73/0.76 and 0.47/0.49. The correct representation cannot be determined from the supplied work.
Table 5 favors AgentVigil in every listed scenario/model/split comparison, but outcomes vary substantially; GPT-4o test ASR is 0.76 for illusioning and 0.42 for goal misdirection.
The AgentDojo optimization gain is 71−38=33 percentage points, or (71−38)/38×100≈86.8% relative improvement; these differ from a 33% relative improvement.

This supports an analyst explanation of agent exposure, but the paper does not establish greater vulnerability than matched standalone LLMs through a controlled comparison.

Algorithm 1 combines ASR with normalized coverage bonus, and Algorithm 2 adds a visit-dependent exploration term; numerical coefficients and epsilon are not specified, and the novelty check is expressed in a comment rather than the visible conditional.
