research.title: Attacking Vision-Language Computer Agents via Pop-ups
research.research_question_relevance: Analyst inference, MEDIUM confidence: the paper identifies mechanisms relevant to why web and computer agents may acquire additional vulnerabilities—untrusted environmental instructions, combined visual/accessibility exposure, executable actions, and repeated opportunities for malicious clicks. It does not directly compare agents with standalone LLMs, so any claim that agents are more vulnerable in magnitude is UNKNOWN from this study.
research.attack_surface: Author-reported, HIGH confidence: attacker-controlled pop-up pixels and associated accessibility-tree content, including ALT descriptors and clickable-element roles. The default attacker knows the user query, pop-up position, and agent framework; reduced-information variants are evaluated.
research.method: Author-reported, HIGH confidence: a four-component pop-up attack evaluated with five closed-source VLM backbones on 50 selected easy OSWorld tasks and 72 selected easy VisualWebArena tasks, with model comparisons, component ablations, prompt defenses, task-level attack metrics, generated-thought analysis, accessibility-template comparisons, and delayed attack onset.
research.limitations: Author-reported and analyst-observed: closed-source-only evaluation; no advanced optimized or persuasive jailbreak construction; idealized default attacker knowledge; selected task subsets; ignored malicious clicks without actual redirection; no matched standalone-LLM or human control; no reported confidence intervals or repeated-run counts; causal explanations partly hypothetical; code and separate supplements not inspected.

claims.statement: The threat model targets agent clicks by manipulating observations related to an adversarial pop-up, including screenshots and accessibility-tree content.
The attack uses four components: an attention hook, a clicking instruction, an information banner, and an ALT descriptor when the agent consumes accessibility text.
The evaluation uses 50 selected easy OSWorld tasks with a 15-step limit and 72 selected easy VisualWebArena tasks with a 30-step limit; VisualWebArena tests only SoM agents.

Table 1 reports default ASR above 60% for every tested model/setting: 80.0–100.0% for OSWorld-Screen, 88.7–95.3% for OSWorld-SoM, and 62.1–78.4% for VisualWebArena-SoM. ASR measures pop-up clicks among injected steps.
Malicious pop-up clicks are ignored during execution and do not trigger redirection, so reported task success does not measure actual malware or deceptive-site consequences.

Using speculated rather than known user-query hooks yields ASR 53.9% for GPT-4-Turbo OSWorld-Screen, 34.4% for GPT-4-Turbo OSWorld-SoM, and 8.0% for GPT-4o VisualWebArena-SoM, compared with default 93.3%, 91.8%, and 62.1%.
Replacing OK with ADVERTISEMENT reduces ASR but leaves it at 66.5%, 77.9%, and 56.7% in the Screen, OSWorld-SoM, and VisualWebArena-SoM ablation settings, respectively.
Empty ALT text lowers ASR from 91.8% to 68.1% in OSWorld-SoM and from 62.1% to 42.9% in VisualWebArena-SoM, while the visible attack remains.
For GPT-4-Turbo OSWorld-Screen, step-wise defense gives ASR 5.9%, TASR 32.0%, and SR 8.0%; removing Please click from the attack changes these to 10.4%, 44.0%, and 10.0%. OSR is 18.0%.
TASR counts a task as attacked if the agent ever clicks a pop-up during its trajectory, distinguishing task-level exposure from ASR's step-level rate.

The paper supplies a successful-attack example in which generated thoughts describe the intended action correctly but executable click coordinates are influenced by the pop-up; the prevalence of this pattern is not quantified.
The authors acknowledge closed-source-only evaluation and not exploring advanced jailbreak-string optimization or stronger persuasion, limiting mechanistic understanding and attack coverage.

When attacks begin after the seventh step, reported OSWorld ASR remains 80.4% for screenshot agents and 88.1% for SoM agents; the authors' clean-history explanation is a hypothesis rather than an isolated causal finding.

The specific system-prompt defense reduces OSWorld-Screen ASR from 93.3% to 52.0%, a 41.3-percentage-point decrease and approximately 44.3% relative reduction: (93.3−52.0)/93.3×100. Thus, the introductory 25%-relative statement cannot be a bound applying to every defense condition.

Analyst inference: the paper is relevant to agent vulnerability because untrusted visual and accessibility content can steer executable actions repeatedly during a task. It does not directly compare agents with standalone LLMs, so relative vulnerability between those system classes remains unmeasured.

quality.limitations: Quotation presence and page bounds do not prove claim entailment or full coverage.

research.title: Commercial LLM Agents Are Already Vulnerable to Simple Yet Dangerous Attacks
research.research_question_relevance: Analyst inference, MEDIUM confidence: the paper explains mechanisms relevant to why web AI agents may be more vulnerable than standalone LLMs, including attacker-controlled environmental inputs, memory and retrieval dependencies, accessible sensitive information, delegated tool authority, and context-dependent safety. The authors explicitly argue that agent components make attacks easier, but do not report a matched quantitative standalone-versus-agent experiment.
research.attack_surface: External web posts and destination sites, search-mediated discovery, sensitive memory and system-prompt information, download/execution tools, authenticated email access, scientific retrieval databases, and chemical-name safeguards. Memory poisoning, API compromise, and multimodal manipulation are also taxonomic surfaces, but are not all separately evaluated.
research.method: Taxonomy plus handcrafted illustrative attacks. A four-stage web pipeline is evaluated through trusted-platform exposure, destination redirection, and harmful action, with a direct-link comparison and qualitative post-feature ablation. Scientific tests insert one malicious document into a synthetic database of over 10,000 documents and examine PaperQA retrieval and ChemCrow obfuscation-related outputs.
research.limitations: Small and narrow web trial sets; conditional exposure rather than natural encounter rates; unspecified trial independence and configurations; proprietary internals unknown; MultiOn unavailable for extensive systematic evaluation; privacy counts not product-disaggregated; qualitative ablation without numeric details; synthetic scientific database; unquantified ChemCrow bypass trials; redacted screenshot; no matched standalone baseline or evaluated defense; behavioral proxies rather than demonstrated downstream physical or financial harm.

claims.statement: The authors argue that agent components introduce additional vulnerabilities compared with isolated LLMs; the supplied paper does not quantify this with a matched standalone-model experiment.
The primary threat model emphasizes external attackers who manipulate dependencies outside the legitimate user–agent interaction.
All web attacks use a four-step pipeline involving trusted-platform access, attacker-post exposure, redirection, and harmful instructions at a malicious destination.
The authors do not deploy the large-scale posting scenario; numerical stage evaluations begin with exposure to adversarial content rather than measuring natural encounter probability.
Sensitive information is disclosed in 10 out of 10 trials after trusted-platform redirection; the paragraph does not disaggregate that count by product.
Direct provision of the malicious website URL fails in all ten reported trials, contrasting with the trusted-platform condition.
Computer Use downloads and executes the test file in 10 out of 10 trials conditional on landing on the attacker's Reddit posts; this does not establish actual malware damage.
The Computer Use phishing experiment assumes user credentials in the system prompt and reports two message conditions tested five times each, with all ten attempts successful.
The scientific retrieval experiment uses a controlled synthetic database with over 10,000 chemical-recipe documents and a single malicious inserted document.
PaperQA retrieves the fabricated malicious document in 100 out of 100 trials specifically requesting the best synthesis route; retrieval is the counted endpoint.
The authors report that ChemCrow's safeguards fail to recognize an IUPAC name as referring to a controlled substance; no quantified bypass denominator is supplied.
MultiOn is disabled before systematic success-rate recording, limiting the extent of its quantitative evaluation.
The authors argue that output-only defenses can fail because identical output may be safe or harmful depending on the interaction context; this is not a measured defense evaluation.

Analyst inference: the paper is relevant to explaining increased web-agent vulnerability through extra inputs, accessible private assets, and authority to execute external actions, but it does not supply a matched quantitative comparison with standalone LLMs.

quality.limitations: Quotation presence and page bounds do not prove claim entailment or full coverage.

research.title: Dissecting Adversarial Robustness of Multimodal LM Agents
research.research_question_relevance: ANALYST INFERENCE, MEDIUM confidence: The paper explains how environmental inputs, image-to-text preprocessing, evaluators, and value functions distribute an agent's attack surface and propagate attacker influence into actions. Clean added components can improve robustness, while attacked components can worsen it. This supports a mechanism-based security analysis of web agents, but does not establish that agents are quantitatively more vulnerable than standalone LLMs under matched experimental conditions.
research.attack_surface: Attacker-owned listing or post content: one injected text fragment or one image perturbed within an infinity-norm bound of 16/256. The image occupies less than 5% of webpage pixels in the described setting. Downstream recipients include captioners, policies, trajectory evaluators, and value functions; direct modification of the legitimate user goal or agent is excluded.
research.method: Closed-document analysis of the supplied 22-page text and 18 rendered page images. The paper constructs 200 VWA-Adv tasks with targeted execution-based evaluation and ensured trigger exposure, models component information flow with ARE, and evaluates prompt injection, white-box captioner optimization, CLIP surrogate transfer, reflexion, shallow tree search, defenses, and transfer ablations.
research.limitations: Fixed web environments and selected agent/model snapshots; attacks establish lower-bound risk rather than maximum possible risk; two-attempt reflexion and branching-three/depth-one search; curated solvable tasks and guaranteed trigger exposure; no matched standalone-LLM comparison; incomplete uncertainty and optimization reporting; unresolved relative-percentage discrepancies. Pages 11–13 and 22 were reviewed as text only, and external repository/supplementary contents were not inspected.

claims.statement: The authors create VWA-Adv with 200 adversarial tasks, each including an original VWA task, a trigger, a distinct adversarial goal with evaluation script, and an initial state.
The threat model excludes direct modification of the user goal or agent and limits the attacker to an untrusted portion of the environment.
ARE defines intermediate adversarial influence as a worst-case upper bound with no further downstream attack, and edge weight as its expectation over upstream-generated outputs.
Image access is restricted to one trigger image with an infinity-norm perturbation bound of 16/256; the described setting leaves approximately 95% of screenshot pixels unchanged.
For the GPT-4o policy evaluation, text injection achieves 40% final ASR; the white-box captioner attack produces 92% adversarial-caption influence and 31% final ASR.
The CLIP attack yields 19% final ASR through self-captioning and 10% through the base agent's screenshot without captions; these are distinct transfer conditions.
In the two-attempt GPT-4o-plus-captioner reflexion experiment, a clean evaluator reduces ASR from 31% to 25%, while jointly attacking policy and evaluator gives 36%.
Attacking only the evaluator achieves 8% final ASR through adversarial feedback, despite clean direct policy inputs.
With tree-search branching factor three and depth one, a clean value function gives 26% ASR versus the 31% baseline, joint policy/value attack gives 38%, and value-only attack gives 8%.

For GPT-4o plus a white-box captioner under captioner attack, paraphrasing lowers ASR from 31% to 27.5%; separate-image consistency reduces that fixed attack to near zero but adds API calls and remains susceptible to attacks on self-captioning.

Table 7 reports 71% target-equivalent caption success for the full CLIP objective, 46% without negative text, and 9%, 23%, 20%, and 31% for individual surrogate encoders; these are not final web-task ASRs.
The authors limit generalization because evaluated attacks are lower-bound risk demonstrations, environments are fixed, and emerging agent algorithms are outside the tested set.

The displayed evaluator ASRs of 31% and 25% imply a 6-percentage-point reduction and approximately 19.35% relative reduction, calculated as (31−25)/31×100; this does not reproduce the introduction's 23% relative-reduction statement.

For the research question, the paper supports distributed attack surfaces and attack propagation through action-producing components as mechanisms of agent vulnerability. It does not establish a matched empirical ranking against standalone LLMs.
Agents start at the selected trigger state to ensure exposure, so reported attack effectiveness should be interpreted under that controlled encounter condition.

quality.limitations: Quotation presence and page bounds do not prove claim entailment or full coverage.

research.title: EIA: Environmental Injection Attack on Generalist Web Agents for Privacy Leakage
research.research_question_relevance: MEDIUM confidence, analyst inference: the paper explains mechanisms relevant to why web agents may add security exposure—attacker-controlled HTML and screenshots are processed alongside private task context and converted into executable browser actions, permitting disclosure with continued task progress. It does not directly compare web agents with standalone LLMs and cannot establish a general comparative vulnerability rate.
research.attack_surface: Compromised webpage HTML elements, text and aria-label attributes, DOM-relative placement, CSS-controlled visibility, and automatic transmission from injected fields. Invisible content targets grounding; faintly visible content can also target screenshot-based generation.
research.method: Offline SeeAct evaluation with GPT-4V, Llava-1.6-Mistral-7B, and Llava-1.6-Qwen-72B on 177 curated Mind2Web action steps. Specific-PII experiments compare FI text, FI aria, and Mirror Injection across eight placements at opacity zero. Full-request experiments introduce FI text at opacity 0.2. Additional analyses examine tool detection, next-action continuation, three defensive prompts, five adapted webpages, subgroup results, and element selection versus content leakage.
research.limitations: Offline step-level evaluation rather than real-time end-to-end tasks; one framework; sparse subgroup counts; no standalone-LLM baseline; no controlled human-detection study; narrow defense family; incomplete reported reproduction settings and absent implementation artifacts; unlabeled curve values and Table 1 variance/aggregation inconsistencies. Broader relevance is analyst inference, not an author-tested comparison.

claims.statement: The threat model assumes no prior attacker knowledge of the user task or previous actions, while allowing website-based attacks adapted to available functionality.
SeeAct's default generation stage uses only the screenshot, whereas grounding maps textual action descriptions to executable events using screenshot and HTML information.
The evaluation contains 177 manually verified and filtered PII-related action steps adapted from Mind2Web snapshots, rather than 177 end-to-end live tasks.
EIA includes Form Injection and Mirror Injection; its automatic submission mechanism waits one second after typing stops, transmits the entered information, and removes the injected elements.
The maximum specific-PII ASR is 70% with GPT-4V, Mirror Injection, and P+1 placement under invisible EIA; this is a condition-specific action-step result.
Invisible EIA yields zero full-request ASR across all tested positions and three backbones, even though agents can select the injected element.
Relaxed-EIA uses FI text at opacity 0.2 and reaches a maximum 16% full-request ASR with GPT-4V at P−3; the two tested Llava backbones remain at zero.
The authors report that VirusTotal did not flag any tested attacked webpages as malicious or suspicious; detailed detection receipts and configurations are not supplied.
The tested attacks show ASRpt close to ASR, supporting limited disruption of measured subsequent actions rather than establishing complete end-to-end task integrity.
Three similar defensive system prompts emphasizing ordinary website elements and screenshot-visible content do not materially reduce the reported EIA or Relaxed-EIA ASRs.
Five carefully adapted webpage examples achieve 4/5 specific-PII attack success, but the demonstration does not include a controlled human-detection study.
The authors explicitly limit their evaluation to offline action steps and identify real-time end-to-end evaluation, multiple injection points, and multi-turn compositional attacks as remaining work.

Analyst inference: user task context, attacker-controlled environmental inputs, and executable browser actions explain added agent attack surfaces relevant to comparison with standalone LLMs; this paper does not directly measure that comparison.
Table 1 shows GPT-4V FI text has a higher displayed mean ASR, 0.45, than MI, 0.38, despite MI producing the highest individual ASR; the accompanying prose also qualifies MI's average performance.

quality.limitations: Quotation presence and page bounds do not prove claim entailment or full coverage.

research.title: How Much Can We Trust LLM Search Agents? Measuring Endorsement Vulnerability to Web Content Manipulation
research.research_question_relevance: MEDIUM confidence; ANALYST INFERENCE. The paper demonstrates how web retrieval exposes agents to publisher-controlled metadata, page content, fabricated authority, apparent consensus, and citation dependencies that can become recommendations. This provides a mechanism relevant to why web agents may face additional vulnerability. It does not directly compare matched standalone LLMs with web agents, establish universal greater vulnerability, or estimate the comparative gap.
research.attack_surface: HIGH confidence; author-reported. Structured web-search results comprising URL, title, snippet, optional extracted text, and multi-result relationships. The user is benign; attacker placement is assumed within query clusters. Attackers cannot access system prompts, internal reasoning, memory, or tool configurations, and do not control real high-authority domains.
research.method: HIGH confidence; author-reported. SearchGEO combines a cached/live hybrid search proxy, embedding-based query routing, controlled result replacement, 44 tasks across four domains, 13 main backends, five conceptual modes implemented as six attack conditions, paired clean controls, and LLM-judged ASR, baseline-adjusted OSS, and blind SS. Additional experiments examine source count/rank, prompt and adapted OpenClaw defenses, skill recommendations, generator control, and bounded judge coupling.
research.limitations: HIGH confidence for stated boundaries. Static proxy and assumed exposure omit live ranking dynamics; approximately 30% of cached results are snippet-only; skill probes are small and mechanism-level; GPT-mini is both subject and judge; bounded validation sample sizes are unspecified and full cross-family judging is absent. Analyst observations include no standalone comparator, limited uncertainty reporting, unequal source counts across modes, adapted rather than untouched OpenClaw conditions, no command execution demonstration, and unavailable raw artifacts.

claims.statement: SearchGEO measures endorsement corruption rather than merely retrieval visibility or instruction-following success; the studied failure is transforming manipulated retrieved content into a user-facing claim, recommendation, or action.
The main matrix evaluates 13 backends on 44 queries under one clean baseline and six attack conditions, totaling 308 cases per backend and 4,004 cases including clean controls.

Attacker placement success is assumed for eligible query clusters, while the attacker has no access to the agent's system prompt, internal reasoning, memory, or tool configurations; this measures vulnerability conditional on exposure.
Table 1 reports attack-only ASR from 0.0% for Claude-Sonnet-4.6 to 31.4% for Gemini-3-Flash; clean cases are excluded, leaving 264 attacks per backend.

Trust-signal and compound attacks drive most observed endorsement vulnerability; on Gemini-3-Flash, factual hidden payloads achieve 18.2% ASR versus 2.3% for imperative payloads using the same carriers.

Mode 3 produces 54 silent shifts among 359 non-endorsement cases, reported as 15.0%, where baseline-adjusted OSS is at least 0.3; failed explicit endorsement therefore does not imply no measured influence.

On 189 successful Consumer IT attacks, self-SS is 0.609 versus external SS 0.297, a reported +0.312 credibility-score gap; the auditor metric measures apparent credibility rather than factual correctness.

The Gemini-3-Flash sensitivity probe finds increasing ASR with distinct-source count in consensus and citation-chain modes, while repeating one source is approximately flat; rank tests at N=3 report p=.27 and p=.89, which do not establish equivalence.

Adapted OpenClaw condition C raises Gemini-3-Flash Mode 2A ASR from 27.3% to 59.1%, a +31.8 percentage-point change, while reducing that mode on DeepSeek-V4-Flash and MiniMax-M2.7; the responsible component is not isolated.

In ten paired OpenClaw skill scenarios, Claude falsely rejects legitimate guidance in 8/10 clean cases and denies useful answers in 10/10; GPT-mini accepts fabricated skills and emits install commands in all ten attacked cases.

The matched 18-case cross-ecosystem Mode 2B skill slice reports fabricated-skill acceptance of 0/18 for Claude, 17/18 for GPT-5.4-mini, and 16/18 for GPT-5.5; these are mechanism-level small-sample results.
The hybrid proxy omits live ranking dynamics, freshness, and competitive SEO, so reported rates are controlled-environment estimates rather than direct predictions of real-world attack rates.
A bounded cross-family judge check reports κ=1.0, but its sample size is unspecified and a full re-evaluation of all 308 GPT-mini cases has not been run.

Research relevance: web retrieval adds publisher-controlled evidence surfaces that can influence a benign agent without control of its system prompt. This is an analyst inference about an additional attack channel; the paper does not directly compare matched standalone LLMs and web agents or quantify their vulnerability difference.
Main attack-only observations total 3,432: 13 backends multiplied by 44 tasks multiplied by six attack conditions. The remaining 572 of 4,004 main cases are clean controls.

quality.limitations: Quotation presence and page bounds do not prove claim entailment or full coverage.

research.title: Identifying AI Web Scrapers Using Canary Tokens
research.research_question_relevance: ANALYST INFERENCE, MEDIUM confidence: The paper provides evidence that web-enabled chatbot outputs incorporate website-controlled values through diverse scraper and intermediary paths, and that previously acquired information can persist after origin access changes. This informs analysis of provenance, external-input exposure, and downstream control boundaries. It does not directly compare web AI agents with standalone LLMs, establish that web agents are more vulnerable, or measure prompt injection or harmful tool actions.
research.attack_surface: ANALYST INFERENCE: Relevant information-entry and retention surfaces are dynamic webpages, scraper requests identified by User-Agent and ASN, search-engine indexes, retained content, and retrieved material incorporated into chatbot answers. The study uses benign fictional tokens as a measurement instrument, not adversarial instructions or an implemented exploit.
research.method: AUTHOR-REPORTED: Deploy 20 dynamic fictional websites with ten canary placeholders each; assign stable content versions to UA–ASN pairs; promote indexing; query 22 production chatbots using two tailored prompts; extract and filter matching values; infer associations; compare a two-month accessible baseline with ten offline sites and ten robots.txt-restricted sites at one- and two-week intervals, then repeat after restoration. Attribution is obtained for 18 systems. The printed threshold rule is internally inconsistent.
research.limitations: AUTHOR-REPORTED: Twenty websites, one U.S. university-network vantage point, finite observation window, prompt-dependent visibility, insufficient output evidence, and scaling/adversarial-token challenges. ANALYST OBSERVATIONS: Undefined F notation and contradictory acceptance logic; incomplete detailed temporal coverage; unspecified service versions and randomization; no controlled accuracy estimates; cache ownership unresolved; no standalone comparison or demonstrated attack; external code/data artifacts were not reviewed.

claims.statement: The method serves scraper-specific canary values and uses their appearance in chatbot answers as an attribution side channel linking content versions to scrapers.
A scraper identity is operationally defined by the combination of User-Agent and ASN, with repeated visits receiving a stable token-specific website view.

The experimental sample comprises 20 websites with 10 token placeholders each and 22 production chatbot services; usable User-Agent attribution is reported for 18 services, while four lack elicited site information.

After a two-month accessible baseline, ten sites are taken offline and ten are restricted through robots.txt, with queries one and two weeks after restriction and again one and two weeks after restoration.

Generic-browser-associated website content is observed for six of the 18 attributable systems; this supports difficulty identifying all AI-related traffic through declared bot names but does not establish evasion intent.

Content associated with Googlebot, Bingbot, or Bravebot appears in ten of the 18 analyzed systems; this broad search-agent count includes relationships classified as first-party for some chatbot providers.

In the specific search-crawler offline analysis, seven of eight chatbots continue returning associated content after the origin sites have been offline for one week; the retained copy's exact storage location is not established.
Twelve of the 18 attributable chatbots continue returning associated content in both offline and robots.txt-restricted conditions, specifically in a scenario where content had already been scraped.
Duck.ai is the only measured chatbot reported to stop returning associated content in both restriction conditions; this observation is confined to the study's sites, prompts, and time window.
More observed User-Agent associations under robots.txt do not establish that a particular scraper violated the policy; the authors explicitly identify confounding explanations.
The authors limit generalization because the study uses 20 websites, a single U.S. university-network vantage point, and prompts and observation windows that affect scraper visibility.

Equation (1) uses an undefined F where the preceding definition introduces W; provisionally treating F as W makes the printed OR rule at t=2 and w=1 accept a one-token/one-interaction case that the prose says is ignored. The actual implemented rule remains unresolved.
Token quality control excludes ambiguous shared values, subset matches, and numerical matches; Table 7 reports 2325 baseline detections and 928 baseline exclusions.
Table 7 implies 1397 retained baseline detections by subtraction, 2325 found minus 928 discarded; this is not a count of unique scrapers or independently verified facts.

For the user's security question, the observed propagation of externally served values through multiple scrapers and retained information paths supports analyzing additional provenance and control boundaries in web-enabled systems. It does not establish greater vulnerability than standalone LLMs or demonstrate malicious-instruction execution.

quality.limitations: Quotation presence and page bounds do not prove claim entailment or full coverage.

research.title: Not What You’ve Signed Up For: Compromising Real-World LLM-Integrated Applications with Indirect Prompt Injection
research.research_question_relevance: ANALYST INFERENCE — MEDIUM confidence: The paper helps explain why web-connected AI agents can acquire additional security exposure relative to a model receiving only authorized direct instructions. Third-party retrieval supplies attacker-influenced input, tool interfaces turn altered model decisions into application actions, persistent memory can reintroduce injections, and subsequent searches can reinforce manipulated narratives. These mechanisms are supported by the supplied taxonomy and demonstrations. The paper does not directly compare standalone LLMs and web agents under matched conditions and does not quantify their relative vulnerability.
research.attack_surface: AUTHOR-REPORTED: Inference-time third-party content including retrieved websites, the current page read through the Bing/Edge sidebar, incoming email, imported package comments and documentation, personal or documentation files, and persistent memory. Delivery families are passive, active, user-driven, and hidden. Consequences depend on available tools such as search, URL retrieval, email, address-book access, and memory. Public-web discovery, image-hidden payloads, and some other proposed delivery routes are discussed without corresponding live deployment measurements.
research.method: AUTHOR-REPORTED: Threat-based cybersecurity taxonomy plus manually constructed qualitative proof-of-concept attacks. Synthetic applications use OpenAI API models, selected described tools, prepared interface responses, and sampling temperature 0. text-davinci-003 uses LangChain/ReAct; GPT-4 uses chat-format tool descriptions and direct instructions. Real-system tests use Bing Chat through local Edge HTML and GitHub Copilot through injected package context. Outcomes are reported as triggered behaviors rather than statistical benchmark results.
research.limitations: AUTHOR-REPORTED: Local HTML replaces public injection, some applications were inaccessible, systematic success-rate and user-persuasion measurement is deferred, Copilot attacks are context-sensitive, and black-box dynamism limits exact reproducibility. ANALYST OBSERVATIONS: Missing total trial counts and full supplied artifacts constrain reliability estimates and reconstruction; prepared synthetic tools do not establish real-network harm; researcher interactions do not measure victim conversion; no matched standalone-versus-agent comparison or evaluated robust defense is supplied.

claims.statement: Indirect prompt injection can remotely affect another user's LLM-integrated system by placing instructions in data retrieved at inference time; the attacker need not use the victim's direct conversation interface.
The threat model assumes attacker control of potential inference-time inputs rather than control of the target model, white-box knowledge, or a surrogate model.
The taxonomy is organized around security threats rather than techniques to support generalization as attack methods and models evolve.
Synthetic demonstration interfaces return prepared content and cannot contact real websites or systems; their sampling temperature is 0, a generation configuration rather than a success statistic.
Unauthorized third-party instructions need not be harmful or misaligned in isolation: even normal assistant functionality can be an attack when third-party data supplies an unauthorized command.

The authors report that the selected threat demonstrations triggered their intended behavior. They do not supply the total number of trials, so this statement is not an overall attack-success percentage.
In the information-gathering example, the model can supply context-sensitive persuasion details even though the injected prompt provides only a high-level goal.
A synthetic email-capable application demonstrates propagation of an injection to messages that other models may later read; real-network propagation scale is not measured.
The GPT-4 synthetic memory demonstration stores injection content, resets the agent, and reinfects it when a user request causes contaminated memory to be read.
Code-completion injection is possible in the reported Copilot examples but is very sensitive to context, with significantly reduced efficacy in larger packages or projects.
Injected instructions can affect subsequent search/API calls so that later retrieved material reinforces the injected narrative; the observation is qualitative and tied to selected sessions.
The Bing capability-inhibition scenario often prevents an API call but does not do so consistently; no numerical frequency is supplied.
The multi-stage demonstration uses synthetic search rather than a public indexed Bing injection; the authors explicitly avoided the latter deployment.

The Base64 demonstration succeeds after an explicit decoding instruction without an additional explicit natural-language request to treat the decoded string as a new prompt; spontaneous decoding is not demonstrated.
The study leaves systematic success-rate evaluation across dynamic conversations, repeated generations, and prompt/topic variations to future work.

Microsoft 365 Copilot and ChatGPT plugins are not directly tested in this study because the authors lack access; follow-up exploits mentioned by the authors are not substitute experiments reviewed here.
Exact reproducibility of the real-world black-box results is difficult because generation parameters and the dynamic environment are not controlled.

Research relevance, analyst inference: retrieval and API integration create additional entry routes and action consequences for unauthorized instructions, helping explain web-agent risk. The paper does not provide a matched numerical comparison with standalone LLMs.

The supplied Appendix A contains a conversation snippet in which work-related questioning progresses to asking whether the user writes under a pen name or real name, illustrating contextual information elicitation rather than a measured user study.
Proposed defenses are not established as robust by this study; the authors explicitly say their efficacy against obfuscation and evasion needs further investigation.

quality.limitations: Quotation presence and page bounds do not prove claim entailment or full coverage.

research.title: One Polluted Page Is Enough: Evaluating Web Content Pollution in Generative Recommenders
research.research_question_relevance: ANALYST INFERENCE, MEDIUM confidence: The paper helps explain how web-connected recommendation systems acquire an additional attacker-influenced evidence channel, and how plausible polluted content can become an on-task false recommendation with invented justification. It does not directly establish that web AI agents are more vulnerable than standalone LLMs: there is no matched standalone attack comparison, and evidence-free controls measure spontaneous fake-prefix emission rather than equivalent adversarial exposure.
research.attack_surface: Open-web content consumed through search-result evidence bundles. The live threat assumes fake-page publication and indirect SEO visibility; the actual experiments locally manipulate selected documents after retrieval. Default entity replacement preserves original URLs, ordering, and surrounding context. The evaluated asset is recommendation integrity, not credentials, tool execution, purchases, or multi-step agent control.
research.method: FORGE freezes ten accepted search documents for each of 225 Chinese product queries across fifteen categories and five scenarios. A three-stage LLM/rule/human pipeline selects brand anchors. Twelve models receive top-three entity replacement at temperature zero; secondary experiments vary rank, count, attack style, language, and reasoning. Audits assess false positives and endorsement; analyses connect evidence-free brand agreement and trace characteristics to vulnerability; defenses are measured alongside legitimate-recommendation removal.
research.limitations: Local placement bypasses upstream indexing/ranking costs; several experiments cover only open-weights models or Digital Products; English replication uses three fresh categories and changed geography; evidence is a single April 2026 snapshot; attacks are unoptimized; richer attack styles change multiple dimensions. Raw artifacts were not supplied. Important unresolved issues include reasoning-baseline mismatch, Rec/mention scope, and prose claims contradicted by the English and defense tables.

claims.statement: FORGE locally rewrites selected retrieved documents in a frozen evidence bundle rather than polluting the live web, preserving rank and surrounding context in its default entity-replacement condition.
The main benchmark includes 225 product queries across five scenarios and fifteen categories; each query receives a frozen bundle of ten accepted retrieved documents.

Across the twelve evaluated models, fooled rates under top-three entity replacement range from 13.3% to 73.8%, with 225 query responses per model; this is conditional downstream evidence-consumption vulnerability.

A single rank-one polluted document produces up to 27% fooled rate in the six-open-weights-model Digital Products experiment, with 45 queries per model/condition; this result does not cover all models or categories.

Category-level agreement between six models' evidence-free brand recommendations is negatively associated with fooled rate, Pearson r = −0.65 and p < 0.01; this is observational evidence for the authors' brand-prior explanation.

In 225 matched queries per condition, disabling reasoning reduces fooled rate from 56.9% to 38.7% for Qwen3.5-9B and from 80.4% to 71.6% for GLM-4.6V-Flash; the ON rates differ from the main cross-section without an explicit explanation.

On a matched five-product-per-category subset, full synthesis averages 78% fooled rate versus 38% for entity replacement and 25% for passage injection, and is strongest on eleven of twelve models; these styles change several dimensions simultaneously.

The specific D1 skepticism instruction increases pooled fooled rate by 10.5 percentage points across 2,700 cells; reported subgroup changes are +24 points for six closed-source models and −3 points for six open-weights models.

D2 removes about 95% of fake-brand recommendations in its six-open-weights panel but loses a mean 68% of legitimate baseline recommendations; D3 at threshold four catches about 90% across twelve models while losing a mean 63%.

Table 12 supports the aggregate English ordering of smartphones below skincare below restaurants, but contradicts the prose assertion that this ordering holds on every model: Gemini 3 Flash has English rates 70%, 70%, and 40%.

The false-positive audit reports five triggers among 1,680 no-evidence cells, 0.30%, and zero among 275 clean-bundle cells; these assess spontaneous prefix matches rather than a matched standalone-model attack.

Authors acknowledge that attacks are unoptimized, several subexperiments cover only open-weights models or Digital Products, and evidence is frozen at one April 2026 snapshot; full multilingual and multiregion evaluation remains future work.

For the research question about web agents versus standalone LLMs, the paper provides evidence of an external-evidence attack surface and downstream amplification into plausible recommendations. It does not establish a quantitative comparative vulnerability increase because it lacks a matched standalone attack condition.
Equation (4)'s broad target-occurrence rule and Appendix O's group with Rec=0 despite a fake-brand occurrence require a scope qualification that the supplied text does not clearly resolve.

The authors report that fooled responses use social-proof markers 1.5–11 times more often than resisted responses and provide fake-Langyu recommendation examples; absence of those phrases from the original polluted documents cannot be independently checked from the supplied artifacts.

Table 17's rejected-mention group has about 5.87 times the median reasoning characters of the fooled group, calculated as 7,983 divided by 1,360; this is a descriptive association, not an isolated causal effect of trace length.

quality.limitations: Quotation presence and page bounds do not prove claim entailment or full coverage.

research.title: Overcoming the Retrieval Barrier: Indirect Prompt Injection in the Wild for LLM Systems
research.research_question_relevance: ANALYST INFERENCE — MEDIUM confidence. The paper supports mechanisms by which retrieval-enabled agents gain additional exposure: attacker-controlled external content can enter context, tools can convert redirected instructions into harmful actions, and agent delegation can amplify code-execution risk. It compares two controlled email-agent configurations for GPT-4o code execution, with adapted payloads and workflows that prevent isolating agent count as the causal factor. It does not directly compare web AI agents with matched standalone LLMs, and its agent experiments concern email workflows rather than web browsing.
research.attack_surface: Author-reported external-corpus poisoning under embedding-based top-five retrieval.
