Across 300 randomly selected P1 websites, operationally defined prompt extraction succeeded in 1% through the ordinary user request, 56% through forged system messages, and 55% through forged assistant messages; 219 sites, or 73%, succeeded in at least one condition, without access to ground-truth live prompts.

The controlled simulation used 35 product pages, 600-token chunks with 300-token overlaps, 11 commercial models, and 10 trials per supported configuration at temperature 0.5; unsupported separate-system conditions were omitted for Anthropic and Gemini.

Table 3 reports overall task-hijacking means of 9.8, 5.9, and 1.0 successes per 10 trials under insecure system, assistant, and user injection conditions; hardened-specific means are 2.4, 1.5, and 0. System means cover five OpenAI models, while assistant and user means cover eleven models.

General system-prompt hardening did not reliably prevent Notification-tool hijacking in the controlled experiments; success required a tool call using both the attacker-selected #general channel and www.abcxyz.com topic.

The indirect experiment varied wrapping, three system-prompt designs, and content insertion modes; success required a Search-tool call with query Hydro Flask and inclusion of returned URLs. Tool-role insertion was generally robust in aggregate, but Table 4 contains exceptions to literal dominance across every condition.

UGCBuster was manually evaluated on 10 sites with three pages each, with one reported false positive and about $0.05 average cost per page; separately, tool-instruction hardening reduced attack success by a reported 40–75%, without a complete disaggregated result table.
The supplied meta-review states that security of the proposed defenses against strong adaptive attacks remains unclear; the prototype results therefore do not establish adaptive-attack robustness.

For the research question, the paper supports an integration-layer explanation: web plugins can expose privileged message roles, ingest attacker-authored content, and connect external tools, increasing attack opportunities beyond ordinary user-role text interaction. This is analyst inference, not a direct broad comparison of standalone LLMs and web agents.

After disclosure, P1 moved message handling server-side and adopted hardened prompts by December 2024, while P2 remained vulnerable but added warnings; these are historical author-reported remediation outcomes, not current verification.

Marker-bearing deployments increased by 7,057 sites, approximately 67.7%, from August 2024 to April 2025: 17,474 minus 10,417 equals 7,057, and 7,057 divided by 10,417 times 100 is approximately 67.7%. This interval differs from the paper's claim about growth during 2025 alone.

quality.limitations: Quotation presence and page bounds do not prove claim entailment or full coverage.

research.title: AgentLAB: Benchmarking LLM Agents against Long-Horizon Attacks
research.research_question_relevance: MEDIUM confidence; analyst inference. The paper provides mechanisms relevant to why web AI agents may face additional security exposure: repeated contact with attacker-controlled environmental text, tool-mediated actions, harmful composition across steps, gradual goal changes, and persistent poisoned memory. It empirically compares attack strategies on agents, not matched standalone LLMs against web agents, so it does not establish the magnitude or universal existence of that comparative vulnerability gap.
research.attack_surface: User instruction interfaces; webpage and search-result text; product descriptions and reviews; email and document content; repository comments; API/tool outputs; automatically extracted persistent preferences; and, in the task-injection implementation, attacker-visible tool trajectories and intermediate reasoning.
research.method: A modular benchmark with agent, environment, task, and attack components; 28 environments and 644 malicious tasks; five attack families; coordinated planner, attacker, judge, and optional verifier; adaptive task injection with bridge actions and exemplar retrieval; two-phase memory poisoning; six target model families; ASR and success-conditional T2S; one-shot comparison, turn/optimization ablations, and baseline defense evaluation.
research.limitations: Preliminary evaluation without a matched standalone baseline, reported uncertainty intervals, repeated-run counts, exact per-condition allocations, complete prompts, or full target version identifiers. The supplied material contains unresolved category-count, aggregation, and Llama-result discrepancies. Some attacks assume privileged reasoning access, memory settings differ from defaults, frugality is undefined, and separate artifacts were not reviewed.

claims.statement: AgentLAB currently contains 28 agentic environments and 644 malicious tasks spanning five long-horizon attack types; the statistics section specifies nine risk categories, although the introduction specifies ten.
The threat model includes attacks replacing user instructions and attacks replacing environmental observations, with the objective of inducing a malicious action sequence.
The attack framework coordinates a planner, attacker, and judge, with an optional verifier that validates generated tool calls through environment execution.
Table 2 reports unprotected tool-chaining ASR of 96.3% for Qwen-3, 90.4% for Llama-3.1, 94.1% for GPT-4o, 94.6% for GPT-5.1, 95.9% for Gemini-3, and 73.3% for Claude-4.5.

Against the important-message one-shot injection baseline, GPT-4o ASR rises from 62.5% to 79.9% under long-horizon injection; Claude-4.5 remains at 0.0% in both conditions. This compares attacks on agents, not agents against standalone LLMs.
Turn to Success averages turns over successful attacks. The authors report Qwen-3 averages of 4.6 turns for intent hijacking and 8.5 for tool chaining; these are conditional on success.
The turn-budget ablation reports GPT-4o task-injection ASR increasing from 0% at zero allowed turns to about 80% at five; the supplied figure displays two attack families and two target models.
With Self-Reminder, Claude-4.5 intent-hijacking ASR is 6.9%, but its tool-chaining ASR remains 57.9%; defense effectiveness is attack-specific rather than uniformly protective.

Appendix A.4 implements adaptive task injection with access to the complete tool trajectory and intermediate reasoning, uses GPT-5.1 for generation and rewriting, and reports ne=2, Ni=5, Nr=1. This privileged condition limits direct generalization to attackers lacking such access.
Memory poisoning does not require direct memory-system access: attacker-controlled content can be extracted as user preferences and later retrieved to influence unsafe behavior.

GPT-5.1's Table 2 family scores yield the unweighted mean (59.8+94.6+73.7+21.5+51.3)/5=60.18%, whereas the table reports overall 69.9%. The supplied work does not explain an aggregation resolving this discrepancy.

The evaluation is explicitly preliminary. The supplied pages do not report confidence intervals, repeated-run counts, random seeds, a matched standalone-LLM baseline, or exact per-condition sample counts.

Analyst inference: repeated environmental observations, tool execution, compositional action sequences, and persistent memory provide mechanisms explaining additional web-agent security exposure. The paper does not directly measure a standalone-versus-web-agent vulnerability difference.

In the single shopping demonstration, the reported baseline price is $13.71 and attacked price is $49.99, a derived increase of $36.28 and approximately 3.65 times the baseline price. The reported frugality scores are 1.0 and 0.22, but their formula is unspecified.

quality.limitations: Quotation presence and page bounds do not prove claim entailment or full coverage.

research.title: AI Agent Traps
research.research_question_relevance: ANALYST INFERENCE, MEDIUM confidence: The taxonomy explains additional attack paths when web agents ingest externally controlled content, use privileged tools, preserve memory, adapt from context, delegate, interact collectively, or influence human approval. It does not directly compare matched standalone LLMs and web agents or quantify a comparative vulnerability increase.
research.attack_surface: AUTHOR-REPORTED: Webpages and other digital resources; hidden HTML/CSS/metadata; dynamically cloaked responses; media and formatting syntax; retrieved corpora; persistent memory; demonstrations and feedback; emails, pop-ups, and API/tool responses; delegated control flow; shared environmental signals; counterfeit agent identities; human-facing outputs.
research.method: Conceptual functional-architecture taxonomy and narrative literature synthesis. Six overlapping families target perception, reasoning, memory/learning, action, multi-agent dynamics, and human oversight. Mechanisms are illustrated using prior studies and scenarios; mitigation pathways and evaluation priorities are proposed. No reproducible systematic-search protocol or original controlled experiment is reported.
research.limitations: Uneven research maturity; some systemic and human-targeted mechanisms remain theoretical or preliminary; compositional fragment traps are explicitly more hypothetical; delegation mechanisms need further work; suggested defences are not evaluated. Secondary empirical outcomes use different tasks, privileges, metrics, and conditions and cannot be pooled. Direct visual review covers five supplied pages, while all 25 pages were reviewed as text.

claims.statement: The paper defines AI Agent Traps as adversarial content designed to manipulate, deceive, or exploit visiting agents, with the information environment functioning as the attack surface.
The methodology categorizes traps by the component of the agent's functional architecture they target and allows attacks to overlap across categories.
Evidence maturity is uneven: systemic and human-in-the-loop traps are described as comparatively theoretical surfaces anticipated as agent economies scale.

A cited study of 280 static webpages reports altered summaries in 15–29% of cases after hidden HTML-element injections; the range depends on the tested model and is not a general agent compromise rate.
The cited WASP benchmark reports partial agent commandeering in up to 86% of scenarios, while full attacker-goal completion is substantially lower and not numerically specified here.
A cited trigger-based memory-poisoning study reports success exceeding 80% with less than 0.1% data poisoning, while benign behavior remains largely unaffected; these are study-specific conditions.

A separate cited contextual-backdoor study reports 95% average attack success across model scales when demonstrations or contextual prompts are poisoned; this is not the same experiment as persistent memory poisoning.
The described exfiltration threat requires attacker-controlled untrusted input together with an agent's privileged read access to sensitive data and write access to tools or communication channels.

The paper reports cited task-aligned exfiltration success exceeding 80% across five web-use agents with browser and operating-system privileges; this cannot be generalized to agents without those capabilities.
Early cited evidence reports multi-agent control-flow hijacking success of 58–90% depending on the orchestrator, but the authors say further work is needed on the underlying mechanisms.

Compositional Fragment Traps are described as more hypothetical; related composite and distributed backdoor results support potential viability rather than universal validation of multi-agent fragment attacks.

The paper's primary contribution is identification and classification; mitigation pathways are preliminary, and comprehensive evaluation frameworks, standardized benchmarks, and robust defences remain future work.

For the user's research question, externally controlled inference-time sources, tools, persistent state, and delegation offer mechanisms for additional web-agent exposure; the paper does not directly measure comparative vulnerability against standalone LLMs.
The visually inspected Table 1 distinguishes six functional targets and lists mechanism rows for the first five families, while the human-in-the-loop family has only a category-level description.

quality.limitations: Quotation presence and page bounds do not prove claim entailment or full coverage.

research.title: Breaking Agents: Compromising Autonomous LLM Agents Through Malfunction Amplification
research.research_question_relevance: Analyst inference, MEDIUM confidence: the paper explains mechanisms relevant to why web-connected AI agents can have greater exposure and more consequential failures than text-only LLM use: extra component-mediated entry points, autonomous tool execution, iterative planning, and downstream agent communication. It does not experimentally compare matched standalone LLMs and agents or establish universal greater vulnerability.
research.attack_surface: Author-reported: direct user instructions, intermediate tool outputs such as received email and CSV content, and agent memory. Advanced scenarios transmit attack-bearing outputs from an attacker-controlled upstream agent to downstream agents. Susceptibility is conditional: Gmail external content is effective in tested cases, CSV external content and listed memory attacks are not.
research.method: Empirical security and robustness study using an LLM-emulated sandbox with 144 test cases, a reported 36 toolkits and more than 300 tools, plus implemented LangChain Gmail and CSV agents. Compares infinite-loop and incorrect-function goals; prompt injection, SCPN/VIPER/GCG perturbations, and adversarial demonstrations; three core LLMs; tool properties; entry surfaces; two multi-agent workflows; and policy versus malfunction self-examination. ASR is failed-task percentage assessed through agent self-reflection.
research.limitations: Author-stated limitations include two implemented agents, three core model variants, restricted agent categories, potential self-reflection errors, and emulator uncertainty for actual tool reactions. Analyst observations include missing matched standalone baselines, per-cell denominators, uncertainty statistics, model snapshots and runtime details, unequal toolkit representation, limited memory-dependent testing, no measured resource or propagation scaling, and no end-to-end protected-task evaluation. Text-only coverage applies to six pages; plot estimates and several text–table inconsistencies remain disclosed.

claims.statement: The authors argue that additional agent components introduce attack surfaces beyond those of original LLMs; this is an architectural argument rather than a matched experimental comparison with standalone models.
The ordinary threat model treats the target agent's core LLM as black-box and assumes knowledge of some available functions, while direct memory access is an expanded evaluation condition.

The emulator evaluation reports 144 test cases covering 36 toolkits and more than 300 tools, with GPT-3.5-Turbo-16k as the sandbox and GPT-3.5-Turbo as the default agent core; plotted toolkit-label reconciliation remains unresolved.

Attack success rate is operationalized as task failure under attack, with completion assessed using agent self-reflection; the authors acknowledge possible incorrect judgments and report random human inspection without its sample size.
Table 1 reports emulator failure of 15.3% without attack, 59.4% for infinite-loop prompt injection, and 26.4% for incorrect-function prompt injection.
For emulator infinite-loop prompt injection, Table 2 gives 59.4% failure with GPT-3.5-Turbo, 32.1% with GPT-4, and 88.1% with Claude-2; their respective clean failures are 15.3%, 9.1%, and 10.5%.

The default emulator loop condition increases failure by 44.1 percentage points, calculated as 59.4 minus 15.3, and yields approximately 3.88 times baseline failure, calculated as 59.4 divided by 15.3.

In Table 4, user-input prompt injection yields Gmail loop/incorrect-function ASR of 90.0%/75.0% and CSV ASR of 85.0%/90.0%; external-input injection yields Gmail 20.0%/60.0% and CSV 0.0%/0.0%. These are separate surface conditions.

The reported memory attacks do not succeed in the tested implemented-agent conditions, and ten normal instructions after prior successful attacks exhibit no residual malfunction; this does not establish robustness for all memory-dependent tasks.

The authors report no strong relationship between tool or toolkit count and attack success; Table 3's injection rates are 60.0%, 60.0%, and 50.0% for one, two, and three toolkits, so the two-toolkit condition ties rather than uniquely leads.
Table 5 reports loop/incorrect-function ASR of 30.0%/50.0% in same-type Gmail scenarios and 80.0%/75.0% in different-type CSV-to-Gmail scenarios, assuming attacker control of the upstream agent.

Policy self-examination detects 0.0% of listed loop and incorrect-function attacks, whereas malfunction-oriented inspection detects 20.0% of complete loop prompts and 30.0% of complete GCG prompts but 0.0% of incorrect-function prompts. Detection is not an end-to-end mitigation rate.
The authors explicitly limit implementation coverage to two agents and model coverage to three LLM variants, proposing broader agent categories and more models as future work.

Analyst inference: the paper is relevant to web-agent security because external content, executable tools, and inter-agent communication can expand exposure and amplify consequences. It does not provide a matched empirical demonstration that agents are universally more vulnerable than standalone LLMs.

quality.limitations: Quotation presence and page bounds do not prove claim entailment or full coverage.

research.title: Context manipulation attacks : Web agents are susceptible to corrupted memory
research.research_question_relevance: MEDIUM confidence, ANALYST INFERENCE: The paper supplies a mechanism relevant to 'Why Are Web AI Agents More Vulnerable Than Standalone LLMs? A Security Analysis': multi-step agents depend on mutable application-managed context, and corrupted plans/history can lead to unauthorized browser actions despite tested retrieved-content prompt defenses. It does not directly compare a standalone-LLM baseline with web agents. The similarly titled Chiang et al. work is only a cited reference, not the supplied target paper.
research.attack_surface: Stored execution context and high-level task plans, alongside a general taxonomy covering user prompts, retrieved external data, and interaction history. The restricted context attacker cannot alter the original user instruction, browser observations, system prompts, or code. Acquiring storage write access is assumed or motivated through possible deployment scenarios, not experimentally quantified.
research.method: Empirical evaluation of Agent-E and Browser-use using a four-category Plan Injection Benchmark with 15 samples per category and five executions per sample, plus 45 WebVoyager-Privacy scenarios across nine domains. Compares non-contextual, task-aligned, and context-chained attacks; weak/strong retrieved-content prompt attacks; and Undefended, SECURE, and SECURE+SANDWICH configurations. Uses GPT-4o controller/planner components, GPT-4o-mini browser navigation as described, headless execution, and attack success rate with partial/full privacy outcomes.
research.limitations: No direct standalone-model comparison, controlled architecture ablation, confidence intervals, or reported statistical tests. Privacy-suite repetitions, exact prompts, model snapshots, grading implementation, and injection interfaces are unspecified. Linked benchmark artifacts are unavailable. Figure 5 conflicts with the blanket undefended greater-than-80-percent statement for weak-prompt bars. Headline percentages do not consistently identify partial versus full success. The similarity analysis is descriptive and subset-based; proposed stronger-model and memory-integrity defenses are not comprehensively evaluated.

claims.statement: Plan injection directly modifies the high-level task plan included in the planner's context, rather than only modifying external retrieved data.

The restricted evaluation attacker cannot modify the original user instruction, browser observations, system prompts, or agent code, and is permitted to inject stored context; the implementation relationship between history and a separately represented plan is not fully specified.
The Plan Injection Benchmark has four categories with 15 samples each, and each sample is executed five times; samples are generated semi-automatically with a standardized template and GPT-4o.

WebVoyager-Privacy contains 45 evaluation scenarios sampled as five tasks from each of nine domains, with a consistent goal of exfiltrating name, date of birth, and address; injections are crafted adaptively from the current trajectory.
On Agent-E's Plan Injection Benchmark, task-aligned opinion steering has 94.7% ASR and direct insertion 70.7%; factual manipulation has 18.7% and 0%, respectively.

For Agent-E privacy tasks in the Plan Injection Benchmark, context chaining increases reported ASR from 35.6% to 53.3%, an analyst-derived increase of 17.7 percentage points, or approximately 49.7% relative to 35.6%.

SECURE system-prompt guidelines and SANDWICH retrieved-content delimiters reduce prompt-injection vulnerability, but the reported privacy context attacks remain effective, including 46% ASR for Agent-E and up to 63% for Browser-use.

On WebVoyager-Privacy, Browser-use is reported at 19% ASR for no-context attacks, 31% for task-aligned attacks, and 63% for context-chained attacks; Agent-E is reported at 20.6% for task-aligned and 46% for context-chained attacks. These are system comparisons, not an isolated causal test of hierarchy.

The plotted privacy evaluation distinguishes partial success, defined as attacker tool access, from full success, defined as complete private-data exfiltration; these outcomes must not be treated as interchangeable.

Figure 5's undefended weak-prompt-injection bars are visibly below 0.8, approximately around 0.6, qualifying page 7's blanket claim that both agents exceed 80% for prompt and plan attacks; exact bar values and agent allocation are not supplied.

The authors acknowledge that comprehensive evaluation of stronger reasoning models remains future work; the supplied document does not provide detailed model-comparison results establishing such a defense.

Analyst inference: mutable multi-step execution context provides an additional mechanism relevant to why web agents may be vulnerable compared with standalone LLM applications. The paper evaluates agents and does not experimentally establish a standalone-LLM versus web-agent vulnerability difference.

The experiment uses GPT-4o for Browser-use's controller and Agent-E's planner, GPT-4o-mini for browser navigation as described, and headless execution; exact model snapshots and decoding settings are not reported.

Figure 4 compares task-aligned and context-chained injections using user-task and attacker-instruction embedding similarity. Context-chained points generally have higher attacker-instruction similarity, but the plot does not encode individual attack success or visibly include non-contextual points.

quality.limitations: Quotation presence and page bounds do not prove claim entailment or full coverage.

research.title: Hidden in Memory: Sleeper Memory Poisoning in LLM Agents
research.research_question_relevance: ANALYST INFERENCE — MEDIUM confidence: The paper explains a specific route through which externally exposed, memory-enabled, tool-using agents can incur additional risk: untrusted content becomes durable user state, later retrieval gives that state renewed influence, and tool access translates contextual assimilation into operational pursuit. This supports mechanisms relevant to 'Why Are Web AI Agents More Vulnerable Than Standalone LLMs? A Security Analysis.' It does not directly compare matched standalone LLMs and web agents or establish a general vulnerability ratio.
research.attack_surface: Author-reported external contexts include webpages, uploaded/shared documents, emails, repositories, transcripts, and workspace files. The targeted asset is the integrity of persistent user memory and later behavior. The attacker lacks direct memory-store access and is absent from future sessions. External writing can additionally launder adversarial claims through the target assistant's completion into a separate extractor.
research.method: Reusable actor–critic payload optimization; constrained embedding-oriented goal rewriting; 700 injection pairs; 400 standardized downstream samples; two writing regimes; full-context, LLM-managed, and top-k semantic retrieval; six principal target models; conditional IR/RR/AUR and five-model coupled end-to-end compositions; four prompt defenses, scanners, benign-save checks, activation probes, attention analyses, wording/position/language ablations, selected production transfer, and provider/manager swaps.
research.limitations: Author limitations include judge disagreement, reconstructed provider pipelines, single-document scope, and omitted deletion/correction/review/provenance defenses. Analyst observations include standardized-memory fallback, broad action-uptake scoring, selected production validation, bundled setup effects, incompletely specified probe grouping and operational detector costs, estimated semantic end-to-end rates, unresolved text/table/figure discrepancies, and absent supplementary artifacts. All supplied text was inspected; visual inspection was limited to the 56 supplied rendered pages.

claims.statement: The threat model is an external-content adversary without direct read/write access to the memory bank and without presence in future sessions; it seeks injection, retrieval, and adversarial usage.

Universal payload search uses an actor–critic loop on a disjoint development set of 125 document–goal pairs, with Kimi-K2.5 as actor/critic and GLM-4.7-Flash as shadow target, followed by held-out-model filtering.
The injection benchmark contains 700 document–goal pairs, divided into 500 behavior and 200 agent-action samples; later evaluations remove the original adversarial document.

Table 1 reports no-defense tool-based actor–critic behavior IR of 99.8±0.3% for GPT-5.5 and agent-action IR of 6.5±3.5% for Claude-Sonnet-4.6; the uncertainty is reported as 95% bootstrap confidence intervals.

Standardized downstream evaluations use directly saved paraphrased goals and substitute another model's paraphrase when the target refuses, so their AUR measures susceptibility given an available memory rather than indirect-injection end-to-end success.
Table 34 reports standardized agent AUR of 60–89% for goal-adjacent tasks and 6–17% for distant tasks, with 100 traces per split per model; these rates concern uptake of an available poisoned memory.

Semantic-retrieval end-to-end rates are approximate compositions that borrow usage from the external retrieval-manager setting, whereas external-manager rates compose measured injection, retrieval, and usage components.

Tables 3 and 20 show model-dependent adaptive defense failure: under GEPA, Kimi behavior IR increases from 6.2% for AC to 64.6% for AC+; DeepSeek's table value is 25.2%, conflicting with 21.8% in main prose.

The provider-setup swap changes the entire configuration rather than only prompt wording; GPT-5.5 overall IR is 97%, 3%, and 1% under GPT-, Claude-, and Gemini-style setups on the same 100-sample subset.
Activation-probe transfer results apply to the evaluated open-weight models and may not extend to proprietary models; integrating probes into memory-write governance remains future work.

The authors identify judge disagreement, partially observable provider pipelines, a single-adversarial-document scope, and omitted memory deletion/correction/review/provenance-aware defenses as limitations.

For the research question about web agents versus standalone LLMs, the paper supports persistence and tool-enabled action as plausible amplification mechanisms, but does not provide a matched standalone-versus-web-agent vulnerability comparison.

The agent-action judge accepts claims, attempts, requests for missing details, and movement toward the goal as YES, so AUR must not be interpreted solely as completed malicious execution; its audit reported 2 false positives in 80 predictions.
Production validation demonstrates transfer of previously successful attacks, not unbiased production prevalence: the authors explicitly select successful attacks and evaluate 25 examples per system.

GPT-5.5 tool-based behavior injection exceeds User Review by 95.6 percentage points, calculated as 99.8% minus 4.2%; this is an absolute percentage-point difference, not a relative percentage improvement.

quality.limitations: Quotation presence and page bounds do not prove claim entailment or full coverage.

research.title: Honeyval: A Comprehensive Evaluation Framework for LLM-powered HTTP Honeypots
research.research_question_relevance: ANALYST INFERENCE, MEDIUM confidence: Honeyval is relevant to how tool-using agents repeatedly consume potentially deceptive external service responses, make stopping decisions, and balance detection with legitimate capability. Its controls are useful for distinguishing sustained engagement, false alarms, simulation fidelity, and successful manipulation. It does not directly compare agents with standalone LLMs, isolate tool access as a cause of vulnerability, or establish a general successful prompt-injection rate.
research.attack_surface: Author-described surface: HTTP REST API responses generated by an LLM-powered honeypot and consumed by hacking agents through curl, Python, or coding-agent tooling. Appendix F.15 attempts to use response content and formatting to influence the attacker into disclosing provider, instructions, tools, and organization. Both sides know the API specification; the honeypot is assumed to lack actual system-resource access.
research.method: Benchmark and empirical systems evaluation using 16 BaxBench-derived backend applications, four exploit-goal families, a direct agent–honeypot task, an agent control on real secure/insecure implementations, and a honeypot control using functional tests. Four agent configurations face five LLM honeypots and simple rule-based mocks. Each experiment has five independent repetitions. Outcomes include HTTP request count, detection TPR/FPR, API-running cost ratio, latency, generated tokens, functional fidelity, and real-application exploit success under prompt variations.
research.limitations: Author-stated limitations include a naive full-context architecture, latency and token overhead, only 16 HTTP applications, often unsuccessful injection attempts, and omitted long-context pricing thresholds. Additional analyst observations include missing formal uncertainty definitions and complete executable artifacts in the supplied material, reliance on request count as an intelligence proxy, heterogeneous effects hidden by averages, and absence of a standalone-LLM comparator or dedicated successful-injection disclosure metric.

claims.statement: Honeyval grounds honeypot evaluation in 16 backend applications and uses two control tasks to monitor agent and honeypot capabilities.
The modeled honeypots have no system-resource access, so actual exploit success is unavailable in direct interaction with them; real-application controls assess attacker capability.
Both agent and honeypot receive the complete API specification; the threat scenario does not rely on hidden specification details.

The paper reports overall mean interaction lengths of 82.6 requests for LLM honeypots versus 30.6 for rule-based mocks; request count measures engagement rather than directly measured intelligence yield.
Each experiment uses five independent repetitions, with four agent configurations and five LLM honeypot models described in the setup.
Agents have a $10 per-run budget; ReActAgent additionally has a 50-iteration cap, while Claude Code and Gemini CLI have a one-hour cap.
Detection performance requires false-positive controls: Gemini CLI's comparatively high honeypot detection is accompanied by a similarly high false-positive rate.
Table 2 reports median latency from 3.3 seconds for Gemini 3 Flash to 13.7 seconds for Claude Haiku 4.5; the fastest measured backend still takes more than three seconds.

Across all agents and honeypots in Table 3, Convince raises mean interaction length from 82.6 to 102.6 requests and detection TPR from 0.24 to 0.45; Careful PI reduces functional pass fraction from 0.84 to 0.62.

The authors observe prompt-injection attempts that are often unsuccessful and instead lead to honeypot detection; the paper does not provide a dedicated quantitative rate of successful instruction disclosure.
Relative cost advantage divides agent running cost by honeypot running cost; most tested pairings favor the honeypot, with configuration-specific exceptions.
Generalization is limited by the naive full-context honeypot architecture and the framework's scope of 16 HTTP backend applications.
Cost estimation omits pricing thresholds for very large input-token counts, slightly underestimating very long interactions according to the authors.

For web-agent security research, Appendix F.15 identifies an external-response influence surface: the honeypot tries to manipulate an AI attacker through service outputs. This supports relevance to agent exposure, but not a causal or quantitative comparison with standalone LLMs.
Using the reported aggregate request means, LLM honeypots produce 52.0 more requests and approximately 2.70 times as many requests as rule-based mocks: 82.6 − 30.6 = 52.0; 82.6 / 30.6 ≈ 2.70.
Agent-prompt effects are heterogeneous: adding detection changes vulnerable-application success from 60.8% to 58.8% for Gemini ReActAgent but from 55.0% to 67.5% for Claude ReActAgent.

quality.limitations: Quotation presence and page bounds do not prove claim entailment or full coverage.

research.title: How Adversarial Environments Mislead Agentic AI?
research.research_question_relevance: Analyst inference, MEDIUM confidence: the paper explains additional vulnerabilities introduced when agents trust external observations and repeatedly navigate tool-provided structures. This is relevant to 'Why Are Web AI Agents More Vulnerable Than Standalone LLMs? A Security Analysis,' but the work does not directly compare matched standalone LLMs with web agents, and empirical validation on general web-search agents remains future work.
research.attack_surface: Compromised runtime tool outputs: poisoned search snippets and retrieved evidence for breadth attacks; fabricated paper metadata, entry points, and directed reference connections for depth attacks. The stated attacker cannot access model weights, system prompts, or internal state.
research.method: POTEMKIN intercepts tool responses using an MCP-compatible server or Python integration, serves frozen snapshots, and applies seeded transformations. Five original agents are evaluated across contamination, linguistic style, matched hedge/booster framing, cycle length, plausibility, and clean baselines; analyses include engagement conditioning, Llama-3 Reflexion, SHAP, cross-dimension logistic-regression transfer, five-model frontier validation, and exploratory defenses.
research.limitations: Citation-graph domain, no standalone-model comparator, restricted independent-verification assumption, heterogeneous agent interfaces and scaffolds, API exclusions, incomplete condition-level and statistical documentation, absent release artifacts, and unresolved figure/table/prose inconsistencies. Figures A1–A2 were text-only in the supplied material; all other identified figures had supplied images. Supplemental analyst review visually confirmed Figure A2/Table A5 inconsistencies on physical pages15–16; no reconciliation is inferred.

claims.statement: The paper defines environmental deception through compromised runtime tool outputs as Adversarial Environmental Injection, separating poisoned evidence from structural navigation traps.
POTEMKIN intercepts the tool response channel and transforms results before returning them; frozen snapshots and seeded perturbations support controlled evaluation.
The attacker may modify returned tool content but is excluded from access to the agent's internal state, system prompt, and weights.
The original victim agents use temperature 0.0 and a maximum of ten tool calls per task; open-source agents use a standardized ReAct harness.
Overall breadth Drift Rate is reported as 40.2%, 55.8%, and 57.9% at 10%, 30%, and 50% contamination respectively, where contamination replaces one, three, or five of ten retrieved passages.
Table 3 gives the highest aggregate style drift to neutral Wire content, 54.8%, compared with 42.4% Professor and 36.9% Rumor; these are style conditions rather than clean baseline errors.
The minimal-pair framing experiment reports true-claim errors of 14.5% under hedging versus 6.8% under boosting, approximately 2.1 times as high; the effect is heterogeneous across individual models.

The principal depth analysis reports 94.6% GPT-4o and 96.1% Qwen2.5 entry, while several engaged agents waste roughly 44–73% of counted retrieval effort after entering traps; Llama is an engagement-related exception.

In the principal engagement analysis, only eight of 450 Llama-3 runs meet the depth-engagement criterion and seven of those eight enter traps, so low unconditional entry cannot be interpreted as demonstrated robustness.

Cross-dimension classifier transfer is reported as AUC 0.55 with 95% CI [0.47, 0.67] from breadth to depth and 0.58 with [0.53, 0.62] in reverse; the reverse interval excludes chance 0.5, qualifying the authors' stronger independence language.
The newer five-model validation reports mean Drift Rate 42.5% at 50% contamination and mean Entry Rate 72.7% for three-hop cycles, using valid runs after API-timeout exclusions.

Table A5 reports clean utility falling from 83% without defense to 48%, 54%, and 58% with perplexity filtering, spotlighting, and both, while all three defenses show 0.0% depth ASR in that exploratory setup.

The paper explicitly leaves empirical validation on web-search agents, code tools, and database-backed assistants to future work; its general threat-model claim is broader than its principal citation-graph evidence.

Analyst inference: tool-mediated evidence and reference-following introduce additional attack paths relevant to why web agents may be vulnerable, but this paper does not measure a matched agent-versus-standalone-LLM vulnerability difference.

LER measures entry into the forged login path and does not itself establish leakage; ASR requires entry followed by sensitive-information input into the controlled form.

research.title: LoopTrap: Termination Poisoning Attacks on LLM Agents
research.research_question_relevance: ANALYST INFERENCE — MEDIUM confidence: The paper identifies an additional agent-level vulnerability pathway: external observations influence both task reasoning and the decision to continue a repeated tool-use loop. research.attack_surface: Indirect prompt injection through retrieved web pages, documents, third-party API responses, shared files, and published skills/plugins that contaminate progress assessment. Adaptive evaluation allows 20 episodes per agent–task pair and ten independent runs, reporting ASR, SAF, TAF, and EFS.
research.limitations: No direct standalone-LLM comparator; simulated rather than live external tools; no inspected repository or raw data; no reported held-out task/model transfer protocol; unvalidated proposed defenses; incomplete configuration and feedback-access details; finite bounded runs do not establish literal nontermination. Material contradictions affect profiles, model rankings, category counts, aggregates, ablations, strategy distributions, and metric labels. Figure 11 changes the final answer between conditions.

claims.statement: Termination poisoning targets the progress signals that govern an agent's stopping decision, with continued resource consumption as the attacker objective.

The initial study uses 60 selected GAIA tasks, ten strategies, and five executions per task–strategy pair, reporting 3,000 runs per model across eight target models.

LoopTrap's fingerprinting stage uses four clean and four injected executions, then caches the resulting profile for reuse.
LoopTrap evaluates candidates using profile alignment, contextual plausibility, and predicted trap potency, and refines failed attempts using execution-trace feedback.

Adaptive evaluation allocates 20 episodes per agent–task pair, up to three refinement attempts per episode, three generated candidates per attempt, and ten independent runs; evaluation sets the success threshold to 2×.
The published aggregate comparison reports LoopTrap ASR of 86.3% and SAF of 3.57×, versus Static-Best at 71.7% and 2.61×, corresponding to 14.6 percentage points and 0.96× differences.
Table 4 contradicts universal per-agent ASR superiority: on GLM-5, NoProfile reports 77.0% versus LoopTrap's 71.8%, although LoopTrap leads every displayed per-agent SAF column.
The authors report 79% cumulative attack success within five episodes and final 86.3% by episode sixteen.
Table 6 reports aggregate token amplification of 3.93× for LoopTrap over ten runs.

The authors explicitly limit their behavioral schema to dimensions derived from ten strategies and eight models and state that proposed defenses have not been empirically validated against adaptive adversaries.
Figure 11 shows different static and adaptive final answers, Bravo and Hercules, so that case does not demonstrate preservation of the original answer while increasing execution length.

For the comparative research question, the paper suggests an additional web-agent risk mechanism because untrusted observations influence a repeated execution loop and its stopping decision. It does not directly measure greater vulnerability than matched standalone LLMs.

Finite amplification under bounded experimental budgets supports prolonged execution, but does not establish literal nontermination; the ethical appendix reports a per-trial step ceiling without supplying its numerical value.

research.title: The Compliance Trap: Diagnosing How AI Agents Consume Conflicting Memory
research.research_question_relevance: MEDIUM confidence, analyst inference: the paper explains a mechanism relevant to why web agents may face additional security risk—misleading contextual memory can redirect a multi-step action trajectory, repeated exposure can amplify influence, and behavioral correction may fail to reverse prior outcome damage. It does not directly compare web agents with standalone LLMs, so it cannot establish that web agents are generally more vulnerable or quantify a relative vulnerability gap.
research.attack_surface: Controlled external textual memory inserted into agent context, primarily through system-prompt placement and an observation-footer ablation. Conflicting guidance is plausible but task-wrong and often references executable interface elements. Real-world memory poisoning, retrieval compromise, arbitrary website injection, and attacker access costs are not evaluated.
research.method: Entry–Propagation–Recovery framework; paired no-memory and memory-conditioned browser trajectories; early, persistent, and late exposure; recommendation-compliance judging and conditional Damage Per Compliance; WebArena full-distribution and selected-subset analyses; 231-task main MemTrapBench plus a 16-task pilot; factorial entry/grounding probes; channel, model-family, horizon, and retry ablations.
research.limitations: Long-horizon evidence is limited to browser agents with AXTree observations; no standalone LLM baseline or deployed defense. WebArena diagnostic selection can inflate effects. Constructed traps support mechanism analysis rather than attack-prevalence estimates. Several source inconsistencies remain unresolved, and referenced implementation and trace artifacts were not supplied.

claims.statement: The study isolates memory consumption by holding a memory passage fixed while varying its availability across early, persistent, and late schedules, using paired no-memory trajectories.

On the selected WebArena diagnostic pool, persistent conflicting memory reduces Qwen3.5-27B success by 20.8 percentage points; persistent versus early conflict is reported as significant at p=0.013. This is not a full-distribution effect estimate.

Under persistent conflicting memory on WebArena, judged recommendation compliance ranges from 63% to 72% across five models; conditional DPC ranges from 2.1 to 25.5 percentage points, with intervals excluding zero only for Gemini-3-Flash and Qwen3.5-27B.

On 231 main MemTrapBench tasks, persistent helpful memory yields gains of 25.5–30.7 percentage points and persistent conflicting memory yields losses of 9.5–26.0 percentage points across four reported models. Table 3 DPC uses an action-divergence subset, not necessarily the judged-compliance subset of Table 2.

Trajectory-level recovery and final task recovery are distinct: Table 22 reports persistent-conflict recovery of 45.0–61.0% but only 1.3% final success for the three displayed main MemTrapBench models.

In a persistent-conflict DECOY factorial with 32 tasks per cell per model, grounding main effects are −29.7 percentage points for Qwen3.5-27B and −23.4 for Gemma-4-26B-A4B, with both reported confidence intervals excluding zero.

For three open-weight models on MemTrapBench, moving the same persistent memory from system prompt to observation footer changes conflicting-memory damage by at most 0.5 percentage points, while helpful gain attenuates by 4.4–16.0 percentage points.

The compliance trap does not strongly replicate in the reported short-horizon MiniWoB++ control: persistent-conflict changes are 0.0, −2.9, and +3.9 percentage points for Qwen9B, Qwen27B, and Gemma26B respectively. The source inconsistently reports median horizon as 2 or 3 steps.

Table 29 reports retry-helpful versus retry-no-memory success gaps of 17.7, 28.6, and 28.4 percentage points for Qwen9B, Qwen27B, and Gemma26B. These comparisons use a first-failure signal and an additional attempt; caption ranges conflict with some row values.
The authors restrict their long-horizon evidence to web-browsing agents and do not establish transfer to terminal-use or embodied agents or deliver a newly trained memory-management intervention.
The authors acknowledge that outcome-based selection of the 77-task WebArena diagnostic subset can inflate effect sizes relative to the full distribution.

Analyst inference: the results identify a security-relevant mechanism in which misleading memory influences consequential multi-step browser actions, but the paper does not directly compare web agents against matched standalone LLMs and cannot establish their relative vulnerability.

quality.limitations: Quotation presence and page bounds do not prove claim entailment or full coverage.

research.title: Autonomy Comes with Costs: Detecting Denial-of-Service Vulnerabilities Caused by Resource Abusing in LLM-based Agents

research.attack_surface: Ordinary remote prompt interfaces to benign, uncompromised agent applications; user-influenced download, parsing, container-growth, tool-output, logging, and disk-write operations. Exhaustion may occur within one request, across turns in one session, or across sessions depending on cleanup timing. Detector source access is distinct from attacker capabilities.
research.method: Directed grey-box fuzzing: static source analysis identifies memory/disk sinks, classifies resource lifecycles, and filters candidates by input influence and size constraints. Runtime system-prompt capture informs LLM seed generation. CFG proximity, semantic scores, resource consumption, and selection frequency guide scheduling; Explorer and Exploiter mutations refine tool reachability and resource intensity. Lifecycle-aware dispatch and an availability oracle produce reports, followed by manual confirmation.
research.limitations: Source access is required; black-box adaptation is proposed rather than evaluated. The corpus contains 20 selected open-source web agents using GPT-4.1 and minimum/fallback Docker resources. Recall is based on 38 constructed verified cases, with sampled false-negative review, a 20-minute per-site cap, and early-stop heuristics. Missing reproduction details and source inconsistencies are disclosed. Referenced artifacts and external citations were not reviewed.

claims.statement: The authors classify agent resources by release timing into short-lived, long-lived, and full-lifecycle categories, requiring respectively single-interaction, same-session, or cross-session exhaustion strategies.
AgentDoS combines static operator/lifecycle modeling with dynamic LLM-generated prompt fuzzing, guided by execution and resource-consumption feedback.

Evaluation uses 20 selected open-source web-service agents, GPT-4.1 for tester and targets, temperature 0, and minimum specified Docker resources; the fallback is 4 GB RAM, 10 GB disk, and a 64-core Intel CPU.

Operator modeling identifies 2,025 potential sites and achieves reported lifecycle identification accuracy of 95.2% through sampled manual dynamic verification, rather than exhaustive proof of every site.
AgentDoS reports 36 manually confirmed zero-day vulnerabilities with 100% observed precision, affecting 16 applications; 15 CVE identifiers were assigned at reporting time.
On a constructed benchmark of 38 verified vulnerabilities, Table 3 reports AgentDoS TP/FP/FN of 36/0/2 and recall 94.7%, versus adapted AgentFuzz 3/0/35 and recall 7.9%; both have 100% precision.
Testing is capped at 20 minutes per sink, with three-minute trigger/resource-growth early-stop rules using a 20 MB threshold; these conditions can limit detection of slow accumulation.
The reported fuzzing total is 119.08 CPU hours across 20 applications; average model usage is 9.32 million tokens per agent, with an associated estimated $44.3 cost based on August 2025 pricing.

Table 4 reports 31, 25, and 16 true positives without generation, scheduling, and mutation, versus 36 for the full system. The scheduling prose reports nine misses while the table reports thirteen false negatives, an unresolved discrepancy.
AgentDoS requires source access and cannot directly be applied to black-box commercial agents; latency or other side-channel feedback is suggested as a possible adaptation, not demonstrated here.

For the supplied research question, the paper supports a mechanism-based inference that tool execution and retained application resources add availability attack surfaces beyond model inference. It does not directly compare standalone LLMs with web agents or establish a universal vulnerability ranking.

The authors report an AutoGPT mitigation combining a 100 MB per-download limit, a 1 GB per-execution-directory limit, and automatic directory deletion after task completion; no separate controlled defense benchmark is supplied.
