Analyst observations include missing implementation/statistical settings, ambiguous ASB correction comparisons, unexplained InjecAgent averages, unsupported probability independence, inconsistent example details, and no direct standalone-LLM comparison. No absent supplement or release code was reviewed.

claims.statement: The paper identifies indirect prompt injection as malicious instructions embedded in external content or tool outputs that can cause tool-calling agents to perform unintended or harmful behavior.

The method places a Tool-Input Firewall, called the Minimizer, and a Tool-Output Firewall, called the Sanitizer, at the agent–tool boundary; it is proposed as a modular defense requiring no agent retraining.
The formal threat model restricts the attacker to content returned by tools, excluding modification of the tools themselves, the user's prompt, and the agent's system prompt.

Fixed AgentDojo Table 5 reports GPT-4o overall tool_knowledge ASR of 34.32±2.49 without defense, 0.01±0.03 with Sanitizer, and 0.00±0.00 with both firewalls. Small nonzero Sanitizer results for other models and suites qualify the main text's all-zero claim.
The Minimizer can remove task-important arguments through aggressive redaction, reducing legitimate task utility even while reducing attack success.

Utility effects depend on model and condition: fixed AgentDojo Table 6 reports Llama overall UA of 57.92±2.04 without defense versus 48.67±2.03 with Sanitizer, while Qwen3 32b rises from 47.60±1.56 to 62.98±1.02. These values do not establish a uniform absence of utility cost.
The authors identify forced insertion of attacker tools into ASB plans as a source of inflated attack success because the benchmark changes execution independently of the agent selecting those tools.

Fixed ASB combined-attack Table 15 reports Sanitizer ASR of 2.58±1.26 for GPT-4o, 7.25±0.35 for Llama, and 3.00±0.66 for Qwen3 8B. These are the lowest displayed ASRs within their model blocks, but remain nonzero and use a benchmark whose utility semantics the authors criticize.
AgentDojo injection placements can replace information necessary for legitimate task completion, confounding utility losses caused by missing data with losses caused by successful prompt injection.

For GPT-4o AgentDojo tool_knowledge utility, Table 3's original 60.87±2.59 and fixed 72.19±2.79 means imply an increase of 11.32 percentage points and approximately 18.60% relative: 72.19−60.87=11.32; 11.32/60.87×100≈18.60. This does not isolate placement fixes from scoring fixes or establish statistical significance.

InjecAgent lacks utility metrics, so the supplied evaluation cannot determine benign utility, utility under attack, or whether attack reduction is obtained at the expense of legitimate task performance.

InjecAgent Table 16 reports Sanitizer base/enhanced averages of 0.3±0.0/0.0±0.0 for GPT-4o, 3.0±0.1/1.1±0.1 for Llama, 0.5±0.1/0.1±0.1 for Qwen3 32B, and 0.3±0.1/0.3±0.2 for Qwen3 8B. Attack suppression is strong but not universally zero or uniquely best against every comparator.

The Tau-Bench evaluation adds data-stealing attacks through DoomArena to a benchmark originally designed for agent utility; the reported security results therefore concern an augmented evaluation rather than unmodified Tau-Bench.
The authors acknowledge that rigid, context-agnostic attacks and fixed trigger phrases limit current benchmarks' ability to evaluate adaptive or real-world threats.

Analyst inference: the paper is relevant to why web AI agents can face additional security risks because they read attacker-controlled external content and can convert it into information disclosure or tool actions. It does not directly compare standalone LLMs with web agents or establish a comparative vulnerability rate.

Analyst observation: the paper's assertion that user-task and attacker-task success are probabilistically independent is not established by the fact that both, neither, or either task can succeed; no proof or dependence analysis is supplied.

quality.limitations: Quotation presence and page bounds do not prove claim entailment or full coverage.

research.title: SafeArena: Evaluating the Safety of Autonomous Web Agents
research.research_question_relevance: ANALYST INFERENCE — MEDIUM confidence: The paper informs 'Why Are Web AI Agents More Vulnerable Than Standalone LLMs?' through evidence of harmful browser execution, poor reported alignment transfer, and selected decomposition and priming bypasses. Browser access expands consequences, and sequential or state-dependent interactions can undermine refusal. However, there is no matched standalone-LLM baseline, so the paper does not directly establish or quantify greater relative vulnerability.
research.attack_surface: Malicious user instructions executed through authorized browser functions in four controlled website simulations: forum posts/comments, repository operations, shopping functions, and retail administration. Tested manipulations are direct harmful prompting, manual sequential task decomposition, and rule-based changes to starting URLs and remaining-task wording. Indirect prompt injection, privilege escalation, and production-system compromise are contextual concerns rather than demonstrated primary experiments.
research.method: A 500-task benchmark pairs 250 harmful tasks with 250 safe counterparts across five harm categories. Human-designed and GPT-4o-Mini-assisted tasks undergo author review. Five vision-capable instruction-tuned model backbones operate through BrowserGym. Evaluation combines functional binary reference checks, normalized safety score, GPT-4o ARIA judging, a separate refusal detector, and human trajectory annotation for Claude and Qwen. Additional analyses examine priming, selected manual decomposition, curation source, website/category variation, and completion divergence.
research.limitations: Explicit harmful intents; granted task permissions; simulated websites; brittle reference checks; no matched standalone-model control; selected manual decomposition cases; bundled priming changes; absent repeated-run uncertainty and several reproducibility details. Functional completion and judge-based results differ. Table 5 weighting, a 10.10% HITL safe result, Figure 24's category caption, and Table 10's first explanation remain unresolved. External artifacts and raw trajectories were not supplied or reviewed. Additional analyst check: reported NSS cannot be reconstructed from the Figure 3 functional totals under the stated same-pair binary-outcome assumption; reward/subset aggregation remains unresolved.

claims.statement: SafeArena contains 500 tasks, comprising 250 harmful tasks and 250 corresponding safe tasks, across four simulated website environments.
The experiment assumes agents receive the permissions required for each task; it evaluates misuse of available functionality rather than demonstrating access-control compromise.
Benchmark curation begins with 30 manually designed harmful tasks per harm category, totaling 150, and uses GPT-4o-Mini to assist with 200 additional safe and harmful tasks combined.
ARIA separates immediate refusal, delayed refusal, attempted but failed execution, and successful completion, allowing attempted harmful compliance to be distinguished from refusal.

Under direct prompting, functional harmful completion rates are GPT-4o 22.8%, Claude-3.5-Sonnet 7.6%, GPT-4o-Mini 14.0%, Llama-3.2-90B 11.2%, and Qwen-2-VL-72B 26.0%; corresponding safe rates are 34.4%, 21.2%, 18.4%, 8.4%, and 24.4%.
Normalized safety score evaluates paired harmful completion only among safe tasks the agent successfully completes; Table 3 reports Claude at 55.0 and Qwen at 21.5 on the results' 0–100 presentation.
The LLM-based ARIA judge classifies Qwen as attempting and failing 72.0% of harmful tasks and completing 27.3%; these trajectory labels differ from its 26.0% functional task completion rate.
For 49 selected harmful tasks initially refused by Claude, a human was allowed three decomposition attempts per task; the authors report successful jailbreaks for all 49, averaging 1.26 attempts.

Priming increases aggregate functional harmful completion for all five models: GPT-4o 22.8% to 31.2%, Claude 7.6% to 14.8%, Mini 14.0% to 19.2%, Llama 11.2% to 22.8%, and Qwen 26.0% to 33.2%. Priming changes both starting URL and remaining-task wording.
Human annotation agreement is reported as Cohen's Kappa 0.96, while judge-human agreement is 0.82 only on the subset where both human annotators agreed.
The authors limit the benchmark to explicit harmful intents and acknowledge that brittle automatic reference checks may miss harmful message variants or harm occurring at other locations.

The reported configuration uses temperature 0, maximum generated tokens 1024, maximum prompt tokens 2048, and a 30-step limit; software versions, hardware details, and repeated-run uncertainty are not supplied.

The paper is relevant to why web agents may expose additional security risks because browser access converts outputs into actions and decomposition or priming can bypass refusal in tested settings. It does not provide a matched standalone-LLM control, so a causal or quantitative relative-vulnerability conclusion remains unsupported.
Figure 24's caption calls its primed example illegal activity, but the displayed task metadata labels the harm as Misinformation; the supplied work does not resolve the discrepancy.
Llama's functional harmful completion rises by 11.6 percentage points under priming, calculated as 22.8% minus 11.2%; this is the largest absolute rise among the five displayed model comparisons.

quality.limitations: Quotation presence and page bounds do not prove claim entailment or full coverage.

research.title: SecureWebArena: A Holistic Security Evaluation Benchmark for LVLM-based Web Agents
research.research_question_relevance: Analyst inference, MEDIUM confidence: the paper provides mechanisms relevant to why web agents may face additional vulnerability—untrusted visual and textual website observations influence multistep decisions that become consequential actions. It does not directly compare standalone LLMs with matched web-agent configurations and therefore cannot establish the comparative vulnerability magnitude or isolate the causal effect of agent deployment.
research.attack_surface: Author-reported: malicious user goals through direct prompt injection and jailbreak; untrusted webpage observations through pop-ups, visual distraction, deceptive advertisements, and indirect prompt injection. Environment attackers control website DOM, CSS, content, and injected scripts, but are excluded from browser chrome and the agent system prompt.
research.method: Six SoM-instrumented simulated applications, six attack families, 330 adversarial task-adversary combinations, nine LVLM agents, and 2,970 trajectories. RVR measures initial reasoning compliance using GPT-4o, BCR measures unsafe actions using expert annotation, and PDR measures final attacker-goal achievement using environment logs. Additional analyses examine stage changes, environment profiles, two qualitative failure pathways, and three agents on Amazon/Wikipedia under user-level attacks.
research.limitations: Authors acknowledge simulation-to-real gaps, evolving/composite threats, and agent-scope limits. Analyst observations include absent standalone baselines, limited live coverage, unclear live denominators, no reported uncertainty intervals or repeated-run variation, incomplete reproduction details, annotation error, and several text–table inconsistencies. Exact radar vertices and some fine visual content remain unreadable; no absent supplements were reviewed.

claims.statement: The threat model permits intervention in the user's goal or the webpage observation; environment attackers control website structure, styling, and content but cannot access browser chrome or the agent system prompt.

SecureWebArena contains 330 adversarial tasks across six environments and six attack vectors; nine agents executing those tasks produce 2,970 trajectories and 8,910 three-layer evaluation decisions. Jailbreak variants explain the expansion beyond five tasks per attack/environment.

The evaluation separately measures initial reasoning compliance through RVR, any unsafe executed behavior through BCR, and final attacker-objective completion through PDR; higher rates represent worse security.

BCR expert annotation achieved Cohen's kappa 0.88 on 10% dual-annotated samples; the GPT-4o reasoning judge agreed with human experts on 85.5% of 200 stratified traces. These are distinct agreement measures.
Table 2 reports pop-up PDR from 76.67% for Aguvis to 100.00% for Sonnet 3.7 across nine models, with each entry averaged across six simulated environments.

The p. 7 prose attributes 80.00% and 76.67% PDR to GUI-grounded AdInject failures, but Table 2 assigns those values to pop-ups and gives both GUI models AdInject PDR 3.33%; the source does not resolve this discrepancy.

GPT-5's reported jailbreak vulnerability decreases from 80% initial reasoning compliance to 40% final delivery, while its pop-up vulnerability stays at 96.67% across stages; these are different diagnostic rates, not a controlled defense improvement.

The small live evaluation tests GPT-5, GLM-4.5V, and UI-TARS-1.5 on Amazon and Wikipedia using only jailbreak and direct prompt injection. It does not test live environment-level attacks; Table 3 states 20 trials per setting without fully specifying allocation.
UI-TARS-1.5 has 0.00% direct-injection RVR, BCR, and PDR on both live sites, but 60.00% jailbreak PDR on each, demonstrating attack-dependent outcomes within this restricted evaluation.

The authors acknowledge a simulation-to-real gap, incomplete coverage of evolving or composite threats, and limited generalization from the evaluated agents to other architectures or proprietary models.

In the shopping credential case, the authors diagnose GPT-5 as rationalizing an unsafe password request and UI-TARS-1.5 as misinterpreting a visually prominent button. The scenario combines a pop-up advertisement with indirect prompt injection and is qualitative evidence.

Analyst inference: the paper helps explain web-agent security risk through untrusted website observations and their influence on executed actions, but it does not establish that agents are quantitatively more vulnerable than matched standalone LLMs because that comparison is absent.

quality.limitations: Quotation presence and page bounds do not prove claim entailment or full coverage.

research.title: Silent Failures in Agentic Security Evaluation: A Validated Harness for Tool-Call Mediation Under Indirect Prompt Injection
research.research_question_relevance: Analyst inference, HIGH confidence: the paper explains an agent-specific exposure-and-action pathway in which untrusted retrieved content enters the instruction-bearing context and can redirect privileged tool calls. It also shows why apparent vulnerability differences can be artifacts of exposure, scoring, capability, and environment failures. It does not directly compare standalone LLMs with web agents, evaluate a browser-specific agent, or quantify relative vulnerability.
research.attack_surface: Author-reported: attacker-controlled email bodies, files, attachments, and database cells encountered during trusted user tasks. Five tools support email, file, and SQL operations. Direct injection, multi-agent attacks, tool-description and supply-chain poisoning, persistent-memory attacks, and multimodal injection are outside scope.
research.method: Audit one benchmark and harness; classify four measurement defects; construct isolated scenario environments, structured payload locators, argument-level attacker predicates, preflight checks, and persistent traces; re-score recorded behavior and evaluate frontier and small models using security, utility, capability, disclosure, and judge-analysis measurements.
research.limitations: Static attacks; one domain and five tools; 43 attack scenarios; only 12 benign cases in the reduced suite; simulated environments; underpowered frontier comparisons and disclosure/calibration analyses; absent underlying artifacts; unresolved count, rounding, and FRR-attribution issues; no direct standalone-model comparator.

claims.statement: The paper attributes indirect prompt injection to instructions and retrieved data sharing model context, allowing adversarial tool-returned content to be treated as a directive.
The evaluated scope is single-agent, single-user episodes with five email, file, and SQL tools; multi-agent, cross-episode memory, and multimodal attacks are excluded.
Section IV reports that 39 of 43 attack payloads were never delivered in the audited suite despite being counted as trials; a later passage's reference to 38 undelivered payloads remains unexplained.
The corrected harness uses per-scenario environments, resolvable injection locators, argument-level attacker predicates, feasibility checks, and persistent self-describing traces.
Re-scoring 258 attack runs changes ASR from 21.7% under tool-name scoring to 1.2% under argument-level scoring, a reported 20.5-percentage-point distortion involving 53 misclassified runs.
Table I reports D3 FRR values of 10.3% and 6.7% and an error of +3.5 percentage points; the displayed rounded endpoints instead subtract to 3.6 points.

On the frontier model's 43 attack scenarios, observed ASR is 2.3% without a defense and 0% with CapabilityRouter, but corrected defense comparisons have p=1.0 and do not establish a significant defense advantage.
Three models produce valid calls on all ten capability-probe tasks, whereas qwen2.5-coder:7b produces none; the paper treats qwen's security as unmeasurable rather than secure.

The corrected llama3.1:8b evaluation records zero successes in 43 attacks, compared with a prior reported 62.8% ASR; actual injected-content exposure occurs in 41 of 43 attacks, so the result is not explained simply by complete failure to read payloads.
The single successful frontier attack is concealed from the user, who receives only a report of benign task success; the paper treats disclosure evidence as underpowered.
The frontier judge analysis covers 367 decisions, reports AUC 0.63 and blocking of 6% of legitimate calls, and is limited by having only one adversarial call.
The author explicitly limits the study to static attacks and says the zero-ASR small-model result must not be interpreted as a safety or robustness claim.

Analyst inference: the paper is relevant to agent-versus-standalone security because retrieved text can influence privileged actions, but it contains no direct standalone-LLM comparison and cannot establish a relative vulnerability rate.

Analyst observation: the formal UPR definition checks whether required tool names appear among executed calls, so it does not by itself establish correct task outcomes or prove that every benign failure was caused by a defense.

quality.limitations: Quotation presence and page bounds do not prove claim entailment or full coverage.

research.title: ST-WebAgentBench: A Benchmark for Evaluating Safety and Trustworthiness in Web Agents
research.research_question_relevance: ANALYST INFERENCE — MEDIUM confidence: The paper helps explain additional risk opportunities created by browser integration: partially trusted page content becomes model input, generated decisions become consequential actions, policies must persist across workflows, and consent or clarification can be skipped. It does not directly compare standalone LLMs with browser agents or establish a comparative vulnerability rate. Its statement about safe models not guaranteeing safe agents is partly motivated through cited prior work, which was not independently reviewed.
research.attack_surface: AUTHOR-REPORTED — HIGH confidence: Partially trusted DOM content, form fields, historical records, job-title/description strings, restricted values, conflicting instructions, incomplete forms, and disruptive pop-ups. In-scope risks include environmental prompt injection, fabricated inputs, incorrect policy priority, and irreversible or high-impact actions without confirmation. Network attacks, model-weight attacks, supply-chain compromise, and multi-agent collusion are excluded.
research.method: AUTHOR-REPORTED — HIGH confidence: A BrowserGym benchmark comprising 375 tasks and 3,057 policy instances across GitLab, ShoppingAdmin, and SuiteCRM; six stakeholder-informed safety/trustworthiness dimensions; ten reusable templates; deterministic evaluators with RapidFuzz message checks; injected policy hierarchy/context; simulated auto-approval; three public gpt-4o-backed agents; completion/compliance metrics, scoring-dimension removal, and policy-load grouping.
research.limitations: AUTHOR-REPORTED and ANALYST OBSERVATIONS — HIGH confidence for explicit scope, MEDIUM for methodological interpretation: Three open agents, shared backbone, English-only interaction, three applications, limited runs, one policy hierarchy, organizational-panel bias, and restricted adversarial coverage. No standalone-model control, raw artifacts, modality-specific results, controller evaluation, or adequate detail for independent statistical reconstruction. Several numerical, definition, and figure-reference discrepancies remain unresolved.

claims.statement: ST-WebAgentBench contains 375 tasks with 3,057 policy instances, organized around six safety and trustworthiness dimensions.
Completion under Policy gives credit only for full task completion satisfying every policy constraint; it therefore filters unsafe nominal successes.
The prose reports average raw completion of 24.3% and CuP of 15.0% across three agents, an approximately 38% relative drop; these averages differ slightly from arithmetic means of Figure 2's labels.
Figure 2 labels AWM CR/CuP as 33.8%/20%, WebVoyager as 12.8%/10.3%, and WorkArena as 26%/15%; the setup describes main metrics as pass@3.

In the policy-load analysis, CuP declines from 18.2% for exactly one policy to 7.1% for more than five; the reported correlation is −0.71 with p < 0.001. Existing tasks are grouped rather than subjected to a described controlled policy-addition intervention.
Consent and strict-execution dimensions account for a reported 70% of total violations; this is a violation-count share rather than a normalized attack-success probability.

The threat model assumes a benign operator but partially trusted page content; environmental prompt injection, hallucinated inputs, policy conflicts, and missing consent can lead to unsafe agent actions.
Evaluation is described as deterministic without an LLM judge; user-message checks use RapidFuzz similarity against policy templates, but exact thresholds are not supplied.
Only three open agents sharing a gpt-4o backbone are evaluated; the paper acknowledges limited applications, English-only interactions, and incomplete adversarial coverage.
The benchmark excludes network-level attacks, model-weight attacks, compromised dependencies, and multi-agent collusion, so it is not a comprehensive deployment security assessment.

For the research question, browser agents introduce additional risk opportunities through environmental instructions and consequential actions; the supplied paper does not directly compare standalone LLMs against browser agents under matched conditions.
The offscreen modality example permits a vision-only agent to scroll and re-observe, qualifying the broader claim that every modality task is absolutely unsolvable by the other modality.
Appendix I proposes a dedicated policy controller that filters candidate actions and triggers consent or escalation; the supplied paper does not report a controlled evaluation of this controller.
The policy-load endpoint decline is 11.1 percentage points, calculated as 18.2% − 7.1%, equivalent to approximately 61.0% relative decline using 11.1/18.2.

quality.limitations: Quotation presence and page bounds do not prove claim entailment or full coverage.

research.title: WASP: Benchmarking Web Agent Security Against Prompt Injection Attacks
research.research_question_relevance: MEDIUM confidence, explicitly analyst inference: WASP demonstrates how third-party webpage instructions, URL/state persistence, and browser actions create consequential attack surfaces for web AI agents. It supports a mechanism-based security analysis of the user's question, but does not directly compare matched standalone LLMs and web agents or establish a numerical vulnerability increase.
research.attack_surface: Attacker-created GitLab issues/comments and Reddit/Postmill posts/comments encountered by an authenticated web agent; task-related or task-agnostic instructions can induce navigation and subsequent unauthorized operations. URL fragments provide a persistence channel when the current URL remains in context. Attackers lack detailed agent implementation knowledge and cannot arbitrarily modify site layout, add form fields, or create pop-ups.
research.method: Empirical benchmark using two self-hosted VisualWebArena applications, 21 listed attacker goals, two benign objectives per environment, 42 reported scenarios, and two main injection templates yielding 84 reported attack tasks. Tests span VisualWebArena, Claude CURI, and a modified tool-calling loop. Goal-specific final-state rules measure end-to-end ASR, a GPT-4o judge measures intermediate compromise, and 37 separate legitimate tasks measure utility. Main comparisons, manual behavioral labeling, defense comparisons, template ablations, and task-knowledge ablations are distinct analyses.
research.limitations: Two environments and limited manually written prompt diversity; no direct standalone-LLM control; partial visual-page coverage; absent repository/supplementary implementation inspection; no reported statistical uncertainty; incomplete compute and inference details; judge validation not supplied; forced exposure does not measure live-web encounter prevalence; unresolved scenario wording and o1 developer aggregation discrepancy.

claims.statement: WASP restricts the attacker to an adversarial website user rather than someone controlling the entire site; the attacker cannot arbitrarily redesign website structure.
The benchmark uses GitLab and Reddit-like VisualWebArena environments and permits attacker-created issues, posts, and comments rather than layout modifications or pop-ups.

The reported attack evaluation comprises 84 tasks from 42 scenarios and two injection templates; the phrase 'in each web environment' on page 5 is inconsistent with the aggregate task construction and is not silently resolved.
ASR-end-to-end uses goal-specific rule-based final-state evaluation, whereas ASR-intermediate uses a GPT-4o judge examining reasoning traces and actions for diversion.
URL injections place malicious instructions after the anchor symbol so that the current URL can preserve the payload in agent context even when ordinary action history is limited.

For task-related prompts in Table 2, o1 tool calling with system-role capability instructions has intermediate ASR 0.857, end-to-end ASR 0.167, and utility 0.486; these are configuration-specific proportions, not standalone-model results.
Figure 2 illustrates a completed attack in which GPT-4o with VisualWebArena axtree plus SOM, without a defensive prompt, replaces the user's account email instead of upvoting the requested post.

The authors interpret the diversion/completion gap as partly caused by agents' limited ability to execute multi-step attacker goals; this is an explanatory interpretation rather than a controlled causal capability experiment.

For GPT-4o VisualWebArena axtree plus SOM, defensive prompting reduces intermediate ASR by 20.3 percentage points, from 0.429 to 0.226, while utility decreases by 16.3 percentage points, from 0.622 to 0.459.
In Table 4, task-agnostic injections reduce intermediate ASR for both defended agents, but GPT-4o's end-to-end ASR remains 0.012; Claude 3.7's end-to-end ASR changes from 0.036 to 0.000.

Under equal template-subset weighting, Table 3's o1 developer end-to-end values imply (0.095 + 0.294)/2 = 0.1945, which does not match Table 2's 0.155; the supplied paper does not explain the discrepancy.
The authors acknowledge that WASP currently supports only two environments and lacks a diverse set of injection prompts, proposing expansion to more websites and other agentic tasks.
The checklist explicitly reports no statistical-significance information and insufficient compute-resource detail; the supplied results contain point estimates without reported uncertainty measures.

Analyst inference: external website observations, persistent state, and action capability explain agent-specific attack surfaces relevant to the user's standalone-LLM comparison question; WASP does not directly test or quantify that comparison.
The utility metric uses a separate set of 37 tasks without attacks, combining attacker goals presented as legitimate requests with common website activities.
The intermediate-compromise judge excludes confusion without evidence of adversarial pursuit, and ordinary navigation to a site's homepage is not itself classified as compromise.

quality.limitations: Quotation presence and page bounds do not prove claim entailment or full coverage.

research.title: ACE: A Security Architecture for LLM-Integrated App Systems
research.research_question_relevance: ANALYST INFERENCE, MEDIUM confidence: The paper supports a mechanism-based explanation for additional vulnerability in application-connected agents: untrusted descriptions affect selection, outputs enter shared planning context, chained actions propagate influence, and applications receive sensitive data and execution capabilities. It mentions web search as an indirect-injection source but does not directly compare web agents with standalone LLMs or quantify their relative vulnerability.
research.attack_surface: AUTHOR-REPORTED: Installed application implementation, schema, name, natural-language description, and outputs under the strong threat model; planning integrity, execution integrity, execution availability, and execution privacy. Demonstrations target IsolateGPT's description-based planner and raw-output execution manager.
research.method: AUTHOR-REPORTED: Query-only trusted abstract app/program generation; embedding filtering and independent abstract/concrete matching with a compatibility layer; lattice-based static information-flow checks including implicit branch/loop dependencies; restricted Python execution through a privileged orchestrator and isolated Docker workers; three attack cases, adapted INJECAGENT and ASB, StruQ comparison, and LangChain Tool Usage evaluation.
research.limitations: Single-query and standalone-app scope; simulated injection benchmarks do not measure output correctness; no formal privacy-soundness guarantee for Python/runtime; acknowledged container-escape and crafted-message risks; incomplete experiment configuration and uncertainty reporting; detailed extended results absent; several caption, numerical, and language-example inconsistencies; no controlled standalone-LLM or web-agent comparison.

claims.statement: ACE separates processing into abstract plan generation, concrete plan instantiation, and isolated execution, using trusted query information for the initial plan.
The strong application attacker can control execution, schema, and metadata, extending the attack surface beyond malicious returned text.
IsolateGPT passes raw application outputs into its execution-manager LLM without prior verification, enabling the demonstrated cross-application influence channel.
ACE performs independent binary matching between each abstract/concrete application pair to limit unintended cross-app interactions.
ACE statically checks concrete implementations against lattice-based information-flow policies and rejects implementations violating the defined constraints.
Application outputs in ACE are typed data processed by a predefined program rather than inputs to an LLM controlling execution flow.
ACE reports 100% security across 1,054 adapted INJECAGENT cases irrespective of planner model selection; security is attacker-app noninvocation, not complete output correctness or universal safety.

In 2,000 ASB trials, three designated attacker apps were invoked; the authors attribute all three to legitimate task suitability rather than prompt injection and report at least 86% utility for GPT-4.1 and GPT-4o.

Table III reports relational-data overall accuracy of 81.0% for GPT-4o, 85.7% for GPT-4.1, and 66.7% for GPT-4o/o3-mini; the at-least-80% utility claim applies to the first two configurations' overall accuracy.
The authors report a 7% attack-success rate for fine-tuned Mistral-7B StruQ on their adapted INJECAGENT evaluation; the supplied Llama-7B StruQ model was unevaluable because of context-window limits.
The Python-based planning language and runtime lack a formal soundness guarantee for the stated data-privacy protections, qualifying the paper's stronger guarantee language.
ACE's supplied scope is standalone applications and single-query interaction; application suites and multi-query interactions are future work.
The injection benchmarks' utility metric is limited because their trivially simulated apps do not measure output correctness.

For the user's research question, the paper supports a mechanism-based inference that application-connected agents add exposure through untrusted metadata, outputs, chained actions, and permissions; it does not directly compare web agents against standalone LLMs.

The raw fraction of ASB trials invoking a designated attacker app is 0.15%, calculated as 3 / 2,000 × 100; this is not an injection attack-success rate because the authors classify those calls as legitimate matches.
Appendix B acknowledges that crafted worker messages or a container escape can enable external damage, and that the orchestrator cannot fully validate traces without explicit plan-worker state.
Concrete matching can require a query for each abstract/concrete app pair, creating a multiplicatively large query workload whose batching reduces runtime but still affects financial cost.

Figure 11 visibly retains both applications under description-based manipulation and displays ACE fares of 51.4 for MetroHail and 54.0 for QuickRide, whereas the IsolateGPT trace selects only QuickRide.

quality.limitations: Quotation presence and page bounds do not prove claim entailment or full coverage.

research.title: Attention is All You Need to Defend Against Indirect Prompt Injection Attacks in LLMs
research.research_question_relevance: ANALYST INFERENCE, MEDIUM confidence: The paper explains an architectural mechanism relevant to why web AI agents acquire additional vulnerability: legitimate instructions are concatenated with externally retrieved, potentially attacker-controlled data, and the model's response may lead to API actions. It does not directly compare standalone LLMs with matched web agents or quantify their relative vulnerability.
research.attack_surface: External textual data retrieved by an LLM-integrated application. The attacker is assumed to control external sources and may use response feedback or gradients. Evaluations primarily measure injected-task following and response outcomes, rather than complete browser-action or exfiltration workflows.
research.method: RENNERVATE collects target-model attention features for each external-data token, applies response-wise and head-wise attentive statistics pooling, predicts token classes, smooths outputs with a mean filter, aggregates consecutive injected predictions, and optionally removes flagged tokens. FIPI supplies fine-grained labels. Evaluation covers five target models, 15 distinct baselines with model-specific availability, unseen cross-task settings, gradient attacks, adaptive attacks, ablations, and hyperparameter sensitivity.
research.limitations: Requires internal attention access; shadow-model deployment is proposed but not separately validated end to end. Utility can degrade severely when injected-task-specific content remains. Transfer results are heterogeneous, including 23.90% residual ASR in one unseen setting. No matched standalone comparison, universal robustness proof, repeated-run uncertainty, or comprehensive autonomous-web-agent evaluation is supplied. Pages 11–15 and 18 have text-only coverage; underlying artifacts are absent.

claims.statement: The described agent combines a legitimate instruction with retrieved external data, creating an indirect-injection entry point; the paper does not quantify an agent-versus-standalone vulnerability difference.
RENNERVATE uses token-level attention features and two-step attentive pooling to support injection detection and sanitization.
The defender requires white-box target-model knowledge and attention access, while the stated threat model gives the attacker control over external sources.
FIPI contains 100,000 injected and 10,000 benign instances; its balanced detection test set reserves 5,000 from each class.
On the balanced FIPI detection test, reported RENNERVATE accuracy is 99.05%, 97.88%, 99.58%, 99.43%, and 99.37% for ChatGLM, Dolly, Falcon, LLaMA2, and LLaMA3 respectively.
For 1,000 selected FIPI injected examples, Tables II–III report total defended ASRs of 0.10%, 0.00%, 0.00%, 0.20%, and 0.20% across the five models; these are finite-sample results.
Sanitization can damage legitimate-task utility: Table IV includes win rates below 10%, and the authors attribute some failures to remaining injected-task-specific content.
Transfer to unseen cross-task data is heterogeneous: LLaMA3 on MRPC–SST2 has 80.20% detection accuracy and 23.90% post-sanitization attack success.

Unseen GCG and Neural Exec evaluation is restricted to LLaMA2, with 500 and 250 optimization iterations respectively; defended ASR ranges 0%–7% for GCG and is 0% for Neural Exec across Table VII's datasets.
Adaptive black-box experiments use 100 injected instances per attack and bounded query budgets; residual ASR reaches 19% for PAIR and 9% for TAP on LLaMA3.
Detection-aware adaptive GCG on LLaMA2 uses 500 optimization iterations and yields defended ASR of 3%, 2%, 2%, 0%, and 5% across five datasets.
Real-world deployment requires internal attention access; provider integration or a locally accessible shadow model is proposed for API-only users.
RENNERVATE's LLaMA3 accuracy advantage over TaskTracker is 4.30 percentage points, calculated as 99.37% minus 95.07%, rather than a 4.30% relative improvement.

The paper is relevant to why web agents acquire additional vulnerability because externally controlled text enters their prompt and model responses may drive API actions. This is an architectural inference; the work does not directly compare a matched standalone LLM with a web agent.

The false-negative example in Figure 7 contains an injected instruction but explicitly reports attack failure, demonstrating that injection presence and successful behavioral compromise are distinct outcomes.
The 0.5–0.8 million parameter figure describes the RENNERVATE detector, while multimodal protection remains future work rather than an evaluated capability.

quality.limitations: Quotation presence and page bounds do not prove claim entailment or full coverage.

research.title: BrowseSafe: Understanding and Detecting Prompt Injection Within AI Browser Agents
research.research_question_relevance: ANALYST INFERENCE; MEDIUM confidence. The paper explains mechanisms relevant to why browser agents may face greater exposure and consequences than standalone LLM interactions: repeated attacker-controlled tool observations, complex HTML, hidden and coherent visible instructions, provenance-obscuring transformations, and tool-mediated actions. It does not directly compare matched standalone LLMs and browser agents or quantify their relative compromise probability.
research.attack_surface: Untrusted textual web content entering browser-agent tool outputs, including HTML comments, data attributes, hidden text, form fields, semantic attributes, paragraphs, lists, footers, and table cells. Attackers may control an entire website or submit content on a legitimate site. Non-textual and vision-specific attacks are excluded.
research.method: Construct 14,719 synthesized benign/malicious HTML samples informed by 100,000 anonymized production tool outputs; split into 11,039 training and 3,680 test examples; evaluate detector families and content-difficulty factors; fine-tune Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct-2507 for one epoch; integrate raw-content scanning, tool trust flags, parallel chunk classification, logical OR aggregation, and replacement placeholders; assess same-data Qwen3-8B fine-tuning, latency, refusals, and held-out characteristic generalization.
research.limitations: Synthetic/template-based workload; most objectives are exfiltration-related; limited multilingual coverage; very small footer/table rewrite groups; no uncertainty estimates or detailed timing hardware; incomplete calibration, annotation, and reproducibility details; unresolved text–figure and counting inconsistencies; ambiguous refusal scoring; no direct standalone comparison; no benchmarked non-text attacks or comprehensive end-to-end agent security evaluation.

claims.statement: BrowseSafe-Bench contains 14,719 constructed samples split into 11,039 training and 3,680 test examples; it is a synthesized detector benchmark rather than a collection of observed successful live attacks.
The authors sampled 100,000 anonymized and redacted production browser-agent tool outputs to inform HTML scaffolds and benchmark variation.
Figure 3 reports average balanced accuracy of 90.5% with zero distractors and 81.3% with three distractors; these groups have n=44 and n=340, respectively, and no uncertainty intervals are shown.

Visible paragraph, footer, and table-cell rewrites have lower average balanced accuracy than several hidden strategies, but footer and table-cell groups contain only 15 and 2 examples; balanced accuracy differences do not directly establish a real-world attack-success ratio.
Average balanced accuracy declines from 84.6% for explicit attacks to 78.1% for indirect and 75.3% for stealth wording; these are constructed linguistic-style groups averaged across models.
Multilanguage attacks have the lowest average balanced accuracy among the eleven tested attack types, 76.0%; the paper also acknowledges limited multilingual training coverage.
BrowseSafe fine-tunes Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct-2507 for one epoch with learning rate 1e-5 and weight decay 0.1, then uses parallel chunk classification, OR aggregation, and tool-output replacement.

Table 2 reports BrowseSafe F1 0.904, precision 0.978, recall 0.841, balanced accuracy 0.912, and zero refusals. It leads tabulated F1 and balanced accuracy but does not have the highest recall or precision.

In the same-data Qwen3-8B comparison, fine-tuning raises F1 from 0.559 to 0.765 and recall from 0.392 to 0.626, evaluated on 3,680 examples with separately selected thresholds at 1% false-positive rate.

The authors report BrowseSafe latency below one second and Sonnet-family latency of 23–36 seconds; these deployment comparisons lack hardware, serving-load, and tail-latency details in the supplied paper.

Generalization F1 is 0.905 for the standard baseline, 0.935 for held-out URLs, 0.863 for held-out attack types, and 0.788 for held-out injection strategies; strategy novelty is the most difficult tested holdout regime.

For the research question about web agents versus standalone LLMs, repeated tool observations and action execution provide a plausible mechanism for greater exposure and consequences. This is analyst inference; the paper does not perform a matched standalone-versus-browser-agent comparison.
The defense and benchmark explicitly exclude attacks based on non-textual inputs, including malicious images and inputs specialized for vision-based models.

Despite eleven semantic attack categories, the authors state that nearly all attacks reduce to exfiltration or a similar attempt, limiting conclusions about the full range of agent-security objectives.

Sonnet 4.5 configurations fail or refuse to provide classifications on 419–669 of 3,680 examples; Appendix E raises operational reliability concerns, but its precise treatment of refusals in performance scoring is unclear.
The authors explicitly caution that footer and table-cell rewriting appear in only a few samples and their results are likely not significant; no formal significance test is reported.

quality.limitations: Quotation presence and page bounds do not prove claim entailment or full coverage.

research.title: CELLMATE: Sandboxing Browser AI Agents
research.research_question_relevance: ANALYST INFERENCE — MEDIUM confidence: the paper explains how browser agents combine inherited LLM prompt-injection susceptibility with authenticated-session authority, sensitive-resource access, external communication, untrusted web content, and ambiguous UI tools. These mechanisms can amplify harm and complicate enforcement. It does not directly compare standalone LLMs with browser agents or measure a relative vulnerability rate.
research.attack_surface: Attacker-controlled issue descriptions, product reviews, and separate websites encountered by an authenticated browser agent; low-level navigation/click/type tools; sensitive HTTP operations and external destinations. Trusted browser enforcement, policies, and sitemap sources are assumed. Misuse entirely within permitted actions remains outside the evaluated protection.
research.method: Agent-agnostic Chrome-extension sandbox mediating HTTP requests through developer-provided agent sitemaps and trusted policies. Separate LLM domain prediction and per-domain minimal policy selection instantiate permissions, which users confirm. Compiled authorization lookup, runtime conditions, DOM monitoring, caching, and optional request counters enforce decisions. Evaluation includes curated model-selection benchmarks, 12 scripted GitLab attacker goals across two user tasks, and latency/memory measurements.
research.limitations: Single-turn focus; trusted browser and non-interfering privileged components; agent confinement to webpage operations; dependence on correct maintained sitemaps and policies; no general control/data-flow integrity; no prevention of all allowed-action misuse; freshness challenges for DOM arguments; general WebSocket enforcement left for future work. Security evaluation is restricted to scripted forbidden GitLab goals. Domain counts and one overhead percentage are inconsistent. No direct standalone-LLM comparison or reviewed external supplementary artifacts.

claims.statement: Browser-using agents inherit prompt-injection vulnerability from their underlying LLMs and combine it with authenticated-session privileges and untrusted content; this is a mechanism description, not a controlled standalone-LLM comparison.
CELLMATE mediates HTTP requests rather than low-level UI actions to enforce semantically meaningful policies independently of the UI sequence that produced a request.
The agent sitemap maps HTTP requests to semantic actions; the experimental GitLab sitemap was manually constructed and contains 51 GitLab project APIs.
Policy selection uses trusted user prompts and predefined policies, requires explicit target domains, and requires user confirmation before instantiated permissions are applied.
All nine model/category policy-selection results in Table 2 exceed 94%, with the lowest being GPT-5.1 on 36 travel tasks at 94.44% (34/36); this does not describe joint argument accuracy.

Retail joint policy-selection and argument-extraction accuracy is 84.38% (27/32) for GPT-5.1, 81.25% (26/32) for Gemini 2.5 Pro, and 96.88% (31/32) for Claude Opus 4.5; these conditional-policy subsets differ from the 149-task retail selection denominator.

The GitLab case study reports blocking all 12 scripted attacker goals under policies for two WASP user tasks; the scripts emulate a fully compromised agent and test actions explicitly forbidden by the active policies.
CELLMATE cannot prevent misuse of intentionally permitted actions; the GitLab evaluation excludes attacks wholly within granted permissions, including harmful content in otherwise allowed comments.

For an 11-navigation GitLab workload measured across 30 reported trials, baseline latency is 13.93 s; extension means are 14.94, 15.35, and 16.02 s for 100, 200, and 300 sitemap entries, with reported overheads of 7.25%, 10.10%, and 15.0%; memory is about 25 MB.

Using the displayed rounded means, the 200-entry relative latency increase is (15.35−13.93)/13.93×100 ≈ 10.19%, differing from the reported 10.10%; the supplied paper does not resolve whether unreported precision explains this.
The domain-dataset prose reports 132 zero-domain tasks, whereas Table 1 uses 136 as the denominator for every zero-domain model result; the intended zero-domain sample size is unresolved.
The prototype assumes no concurrent privileged browser interference and excludes local-file access, browser-setting changes, and developer-tool use by the agent; current task support is single-turn.
Conditional policies may use stale DOM values; the authors identify application cooperation as necessary for general sequential-effect completion and provide throttling as an interim mitigation.
General WebSocket enforcement is left for future work because messages can encode application-specific deltas or operational transforms in proprietary or binary formats.

For the research question, the paper supports the inference that browser integration can amplify the consequences and enforcement difficulty of prompt injection by combining authenticated authority, untrusted content, external communication, and non-semantic tools; it does not directly compare standalone LLM vulnerability.

quality.limitations: Quotation presence and page bounds do not prove claim entailment or full coverage.

research.title: Defeating Prompt Injections by Design
research.research_question_relevance: ANALYST INFERENCE — MEDIUM confidence: The paper explains mechanisms by which tool-using web agents connect untrusted pages, messages, and tool outputs to privileged actions, sensitive data, and externally observable behavior. These mechanisms support an architectural explanation of increased attack exposure and potential harm. The experiments compare native tool-calling agents against CaMeL agents, not agents against standalone LLMs; no relative standalone-versus-web vulnerability rate is established.
research.attack_surface: AUTHOR-REPORTED: Untrusted tool outputs, web pages, emails, shared documents, spreadsheets, extracted tool arguments, data-driven dispatch branches, error feedback, and behavioral side channels. Main assumptions trust the user prompt and memory. Malicious tools and rogue users are discussed as stronger conceptual scenarios outside the explicit AgentDojo evaluation.
research.method: CaMeL separates a privileged code-generating planner from a tool-free quarantined parser, executes restricted Python through a custom interpreter, propagates provenance and permitted-reader capabilities, and checks policies before tool execution. NORMAL and STRICT dependency modes are evaluated alongside AgentDojo utility, attack counts, policy triggers, baseline defenses, failure examples, and token overhead.
research.limitations: No direct standalone comparison; text-only manipulation and phishing are non-goals; utility loss varies substantially by model/suite; policies and annotations require maintenance; user approval can cause fatigue; partial side effects lack rollback; side channels remain possible; interpreter formal verification is future work; several numbers and appendix labels conflict; uncertainty and repetition reporting is incomplete; source-code artifacts were not supplied or inspected.

claims.statement: Agentic interaction with untrusted tool outputs and web pages exposes LLM systems to prompt injections that can exfiltrate data or cause harmful actions.
Dual-model isolation protects planning but can leave tool arguments vulnerable to manipulation through the quarantined model's outputs.

CaMeL combines a privileged code-generating model, a tool-free quarantined parser, a provenance-tracking interpreter, per-value capabilities, and tool-time security policies without modifying the underlying LLM.
The main threat model assumes a trusted user prompt and uncompromised memory; text-only manipulation and phishing without protected-flow consequences are explicit non-goals.

Table 2 reports benign overall utility of 77.3% ± 8.3 for o3 High with CaMeL versus 84.5% ± 7.2 with native tool calling; the meaning of the uncertainty terms is not specified in the supplied methods.

In the Claude 3.5 Sonnet baseline comparison, Table 7 reports zero successful attacks for policy-enforced CaMeL, five for spotlighting, eight for tool filter, 24 for prompt sandwiching, and 44 for the undefended agent; these are benchmark counts, not standalone-LLM comparisons.

STRICT mode mitigates selected implicit-flow and Q-LLM exception channels by propagating dependencies, but CaMeL remains subject to possible side-channel leakage and does not establish universal confidentiality.
The supplied implementation is not formally verified; the authors identify proof of interpreter correctness and intended policy enforcement as future work.

For the research question, the paper supports a mechanism-based inference that web agents add dangerous pathways from untrusted content to privileged actions and observable external effects; it does not directly measure relative vulnerability against standalone LLMs.

Token overhead is reported inconsistently: the main text/Figure 13 state median input/output multipliers 2.82×/2.73×, while explicitly adversarial Table 13 gives 2.02×/2.64×; the supplied work does not resolve the discrepancy.
A fixed generated plan can still implement a dispatcher in which untrusted email data chooses actions, making isolation alone insufficient for such delegated workflows.
CaMeL does not fully solve prompt injection or AgentDojo; the authors retain policy-maintenance, human-approval, side-channel, and compositional limitations.

quality.limitations: Quotation presence and page bounds do not prove claim entailment or full coverage.

research.title: Defending Against Indirect Prompt Injection Attacks With Spotlighting
research.research_question_relevance: ANALYST INFERENCE — MEDIUM confidence: The paper provides a mechanism-level explanation relevant to why web AI agents may face additional risk: they ingest outside content that can contain unauthorized instructions, and their plugins, access patterns, and capabilities can increase the consequences of following those instructions. It does not directly compare standalone LLMs with web agents, quantify a relative vulnerability rate, or evaluate an end-to-end browser agent. Its direct experiments concern source transformations, synthetic keyword attacks, and language-task performance.
research.attack_surface: AUTHOR-REPORTED: Untrusted external text, including websites, emails, and text messages, processed alongside legitimate instructions. The attacker embeds instructions in that content and may know the system prompt. Evaluated attacks seek full task replacement with a special keyword; broader session hijacking and exfiltration are motivating discussion rather than measured outcomes.
research.method: AUTHOR-REPORTED: Spotlighting combines optional input transformation with explanatory system-prompt instructions. Variants are boundary delimiters, markers interleaved throughout text, and encoding. Evaluation uses 1000 synthetic attack documents, summarization and document Q&A, text-davinci-003 and June 2023 GPT-3.5-Turbo/GPT-4, and temperature 1.0. Separate benchmark accuracy experiments examine task preservation; an appendix examines few-shot defenses and strict ASR scoring.
research.limitations: AUTHOR-STATED: Delimiter imitation, whitespace-free attacks against simple marking, decoding-related utility loss, use-case dependence, imperfect shared-channel security, incomplete mechanism understanding, and few-shot example/test correlation. ANALYST OBSERVATIONS: Narrow keyword takeover metric; missing exact configurations, splits, repetitions, uncertainty estimates, data, and code; unexplained baseline shifts; a below-3% versus 3.10% discrepancy; no direct standalone-versus-web-agent comparison; and no quantitative evaluation of proposed dynamic marking against adaptive attackers.

claims.statement: The authors identify external sources such as websites as entry points for indirect prompt injection and argue that additional plugins and capabilities increase its dangers; this is threat framing rather than a measured agent-versus-standalone comparison.
Spotlighting combines optional preprocessing of outside text with system-prompt instructions explaining how the text should be treated, and includes delimiting, datamarking, and encoding.
The evaluation uses text-davinci-003, June 2023 GPT-3.5-Turbo, and June 2023 GPT-4, with temperature set to 1.0 in all experiments.

The attack corpus contains 1000 synthetic documents with variations of a payload that asks the model to abandon prior instructions and return only a special keyword; ASR is the fraction producing successful injection.
For the displayed GPT-3.5-Turbo delimiter experiment, the baseline ASR is around 60%, warning instructions have little effect, and adding delimiters reduces ASR by approximately half.
Figure 4's caption reports datamarking summarization ASR of 3.10% for GPT-3.5-Turbo and 0.00% for Text-003; the 3.10% value conflicts with the page 6 prose saying below 3%.
For datamarking in document Q&A, Figure 5 reports ASR of 8.0% for GPT-3.5-Turbo, 1.0% for GPT-4, and 0.00% for Text-003; datamarking therefore does not uniformly attain below 2% ASR.
Figure 6 reports encoding ASR of 0.0% for summarization and 1.8% for Q&A using GPT-3.5-Turbo; these are observed experimental rates, not guarantees of future security.

The authors report no detrimental datamarking effect on the four shown GPT-3.5-Turbo language benchmarks, while the visible Figure 7 bars include a small BoolQ decline whose significance cannot be assessed.

Encoding impairs GPT-3.5-Turbo's ordinary-task performance; the authors recommend using it only with high-capacity models and validating performance for the specific use case. Figure 8 qualifies GPT-4 preservation as applying to most tasks.

The authors identify known-delimiter imitation and whitespace-free attack text as weaknesses of simple delimiting and whitespace-only datamarking, and propose dynamic markers and insertion locations without reporting a quantitative adaptive-attack evaluation.

The paper's strict ASR counts attacks that fully overtake instructions; a valid summary that mentions an attack keyword is classified as unsuccessful. A broader influence metric is discussed separately.

Few-shot treatments produce low reported ASR for GPT-3.5-Turbo, but the authors caution that known-tactic coverage and correlation between examples and test attacks limit confidence and generalization.
The authors acknowledge that spotlighting's mechanism is not clearly understood and that separating representations within a shared channel is not perfectly secure against interference.

Analyst inference: the paper helps explain web-agent risk through exposure to attacker-controlled external content and the consequences of additional capabilities, but it does not directly compare standalone LLMs with web agents or quantify their relative vulnerability.

quality.limitations: Quotation presence and page bounds do not prove claim entailment or full coverage.

research.title: IsolateGPT: An Execution Isolation Architecture for LLM-Based Agentic Systems
research.research_question_relevance: ANALYST INFERENCE — HIGH confidence in the relevance boundary: the paper explains how third-party apps, untrusted emails/websites, shared context, persistent user data, online services, and executable API actions introduce opportunities for cross-app manipulation and data theft. These mechanisms help explain why web-connected agents can have additional exposure relative to text-only models. However, its empirical comparison is IsolateGPT versus VanillaGPT, both GPT-4-based agentic systems; it does not directly measure agents against standalone LLMs.
research.attack_surface: AUTHOR-REPORTED: malicious app descriptions, hostile content processed by benign apps, shared model execution/context, app and system memory, cross-app exchanges, online service APIs, and outbound information flows. Attacker goals include changing other apps or LLM behavior and stealing sensitive data. Ambiguous benign instructions can also cause unintended sharing or interference. Within-app attacks remain outside the defense scope.
research.method: A hub-and-spoke architecture with process-isolated apps, dedicated LLM instances and memory, deterministic non-LLM operators, hub-mediated ISC messages, structural validation, ephemeral identifiers, and configurable user permissions. Evaluation uses an enhanced 1,598-attack benchmark, four case studies, four LangChain functionality/performance workloads, and a 10% query cost sample. Both compared systems use GPT-4; artifact details identify version 0613.
research.limitations: Permission-mediated protection depends on user decisions; the artifact assumes rejection of warned requests for two cases. Warning rate is not directly comparable to baseline attack success. No human permission study, formal proof, standalone-LLM comparison, broad model comparison, or supplied repeated-run statistics appears. Benchmarks omit some complex real-world cases. Timings assume cold starts and automatically granted permissions. External artifacts were referenced but not reviewed.

claims.statement: The authors identify shared application execution as enabling apps to access data and influence other apps or the LLM, including risks without an adversary.
IsolateGPT isolates hub and spokes in separate processes and pairs each app with a dedicated LLM instance; hub-mediated communication restores collaboration.
The security evaluation extends an existing benchmark with 544 system-data-targeting attacks, producing 1,598 scenarios, and refreshes the system between scenarios.

Across the tested attacks, VanillaGPT has 20.2% reported overall attack success; IsolateGPT permission dialogs appear for 7.6% of attacks, with warnings in 100% of appearing dialogs. These are different outcome metrics, and isolated attack success can depend on permission grants.
Structured routing and format validation do not eliminate malicious-language screening: IsolateGPT requires users to screen exchanged messages where automatic validation is insufficient.
The artifact evaluation assumes users reject warned requests; reproducing the data-stealing and inadvertent-data-exposure defenses requires denying the permission requests.
Preventing attacks within a single app is outside scope; the defense targets propagation to other apps or the system.

Table II shows identical app-benchmark scores: both systems have 1.00 step/final correctness for single and multiple apps, and 0.76 step plus 0.95 final correctness for collaboration. This is tested-workload parity, not universal equivalence.
The authors report IsolateGPT overhead under 30% relative to VanillaGPT for 75.73% of tested queries; raw per-query overhead values are not supplied in this input.
Performance evaluation automatically grants permissions and assumes cold-start spokes without data; its timing does not measure realistic human permission-decision delay.
The authors acknowledge benchmark imperfections and that complex real-world use cases may fall outside the benchmark scope.

Analyst inference: web-connected agents gain attack surfaces through untrusted content, sensitive persistent context, service connections, and cross-app actions. The paper supports this mechanism but compares isolated and non-isolated agentic systems, not agents against standalone tool-free LLMs.

In Figure 5's example, the manipulated baseline books the $57.00 ride instead of the displayed available $51.80 ride, a derived $5.20 difference: $57.00 minus $51.80. This is one demonstration, not an average financial loss.

The implementation uses process separation, seccomp and setrlimit restrictions, resource limits, root-domain network restrictions, and permission-mediated data flow; exact numeric resource limits are not supplied.

quality.limitations: Quotation presence and page bounds do not prove claim entailment or full coverage.

research.title: MELON: Provable Defense Against Indirect Prompt Injection Attacks in AI Agents
research.research_question_relevance: ANALYST INFERENCE, MEDIUM confidence: the paper explains an additional risk path in tool-using and web-connected agents, where attacker-controlled retrieved content can redirect subsequent executable actions. Its state model and examples connect external information, persistent observations, and tool permissions. It does not directly compare standalone LLMs with web agents or quantify a comparative vulnerability increase.
research.attack_surface: AUTHOR-REPORTED: tool-retrieved websites, emails, files, and other external observations. Attackers manipulate this information to redirect legitimate user tasks; they do not control the model's internal input/output under the stated threat model.
research.method: Training-free masked re-execution preserves retrieved outputs while replacing user input and deleting generated-action history. A cache accumulates masked proposed tool calls, and embedding-based similarity detects matching original calls before execution. MELON-Aug adds Repeat Prompt. A distinct multi-prompt ensemble receives conditional theoretical error bounds.
research.limitations: Response-based harms evade call-only monitoring; redundant calls, state hallucination, and nonexistent-function calls cause mismatches. Benign delegated instructions can trigger detections. Model calls and API costs approximately double. Main evaluation uses AgentDojo, three models, four general text attacks, and no standalone control; VWA-Adv is excluded. The source contains unresolved numerical and notational inconsistencies, and exact reproduction settings are incomplete.

claims.statement: The threat model restricts attackers to manipulating external information retrieved through tools, such as websites, emails, or files; it assumes legitimate user tasks and defender access to agent state.

MELON compares calls from the original continuation with masked continuations that preserve retrieved outputs while replacing user input, using a historical call cache to accommodate timing differences.
The implementation uses embedding similarity with primary threshold 0.8 and selectively excludes some arguments, including email body and subject, from call comparison.
The main benchmark has 629 attack cases and uses GPT-4o, o3-mini, and Llama-3.3-70B with temperature 0; four general attack patterns and five baseline defenses are evaluated.
For GPT-4o averaged over four attack types, MELON-Aug reports 68.72% utility under attack and 0.32% attack success, compared with 69.08% and 16.06% without defense.
Augmentation does not improve every security metric: GPT-4o plain MELON has average ASR 0.24%, lower than MELON-Aug's 0.32%, while its average UA is lower at 58.78% versus 68.72%.

Under the evaluated termination policy, the LLM Detector reports zero utility under attack; MELON instead checks proposed actions before tool execution, aiming to stop only behavior influenced by the injection.
In the GPT-4o Important Messages ablation, original ASR is 0.95%; Basic, No Cache, and Full Comp. increase it to 2.70%, 1.75%, and 17.33%, respectively.
The authors analyze 66 Important Messages evasions across three models; response-based attacks account for 72.73%, exposing the limitation of monitoring tool calls alone.
Masked re-execution approximately doubles model calls and API costs relative to an undefended system; proposed latency optimizations are discussed without measured latency results.

The theoretical ensemble bounds are conditional on expected benign similarity falling below the threshold and expected malicious similarity above it; this ensemble differs from the main cached detector.

Substituting the paper's illustrative values into its displayed error-bound formula gives exp(-2 × 100 × 0.2²) = exp(-8), approximately 3.35 × 10^-4, rather than the reported approximately 1.8 × 10^-4.
MELON's GPT-4o false-positive rate is reported as 9.28%; the authors argue that authorized tasks asking the agent to follow external instructions can nevertheless pose security risks.
The false-positive account is internally inconsistent: section 4.4 reports nine detections, while Appendix E reports domain counts 3, 3, 0, and 2, which sum to eight.
VWA-Adv is excluded from the main evaluation because the authors report only 1% GPT-4o ASR for pure image-based goal-misdirection attacks; this limits multimodal conclusions.

For the research question, the paper supports an inferred retrieval-to-action risk mechanism: attacker-controlled external content can influence an agent that possesses executable tools. It does not directly compare vulnerability rates with standalone LLMs.

quality.limitations: Quotation presence and page bounds do not prove claim entailment or full coverage.

research.title: PlanGuard: Defending Agents against Indirect Prompt Injection via Planning-based Consistency Verification
research.research_question_relevance: ANALYST INFERENCE: The paper explains a mechanism relevant to why web-connected AI agents may face additional security exposure: attacker-controlled webpages, emails, or retrieved documents can enter the agent's context, and tool permissions can translate instruction confusion into unauthorized actions. It does not directly compare standalone LLMs with web agents or quantify a comparative vulnerability gap. Its empirical evidence compares three agent-defense configurations on InjecAgent under a compliance-inducing victim prompt.
research.attack_surface: AUTHOR-REPORTED: Malicious payloads embedded in untrusted external context or tool-return content, with the user instruction remaining trusted. Target outcomes are unauthorized tool selection and malicious arguments to an otherwise appropriate tool. Parameter-borne attacks against the intent verifier are discussed theoretically.
research.method: AUTHOR-REPORTED: Training-free isolated planning from the user instruction and tool definitions generates a reference action set. Execution-time verification passes exact matches, blocks non-reference tools, and sends permitted-tool parameter mismatches to an LLM intent verifier. Evaluation uses InjecAgent, DeepSeek-V3.2, Vanilla Agent, Stage-I Only, and full PlanGuard.
research.limitations: AUTHOR-STATED: Additional inference/token overhead and lack of ground truth for arguments that depend on external content. ANALYST OBSERVATIONS: One named backbone, modified victim prompt, unspecified benign/subset denominators and aggregation, no reported uncertainty or measured overhead, no dedicated adaptive-attack evaluation, and no direct standalone-versus-agent comparison. Referenced code and benchmark artifacts were not supplied or inspected.

claims.statement: The authors identify context mixing between trusted user instructions and untrusted external data as the source of indirect prompt-injection vulnerability in agents.
The paper restricts its scope to actionable indirect prompt injection that triggers unauthorized tool execution, rather than all harmful textual outputs.
The threat model assumes the attacker cannot modify the trusted user instruction and instead injects malicious content into external context.
PlanGuard's isolated planner generates its reference action set from the user instruction and tool definitions while excluding external retrieved information.
The hierarchical verifier passes exact reference matches, blocks tools absent from the reference, and uses an LLM intent verifier for permitted tools with mismatched parameters.
The reported InjecAgent dataset contains 1,054 test cases spanning 17 user tools and 62 attacker tools; per-subset and benign-case denominators are not supplied.
The evaluation uses DeepSeek-V3.2 for the victim and defense components and modifies the victim system prompt to encourage execution of commands in tool returns.

Under the compliance-inducing prompt, Vanilla Agent ASR is reported as 56.90% on Direct Harm and 88.67% on Data Stealing; these are subset-specific results rather than an agent-versus-standalone comparison.
Both Stage-I Only and full PlanGuard reportedly achieve 0.0% ASR in both DH and DS under the specified benchmark setup; this is not a universal security guarantee.
Adding Stage II reduces reported benign-scenario FPR from 27.00% to 0.97% on DH and from 38.01% to 3.28% on DS; the benign denominators are unspecified.
The absolute FPR reductions are 26.03 percentage points for DH, calculated as 27.00−0.97, and 34.73 percentage points for DS, calculated as 38.01−3.28.
The authors acknowledge additional computational overhead and token costs from planner and verifier inference, without reporting numerical latency or cost measurements.
The authors acknowledge that planner isolation leaves insufficient ground truth to verify context-dependent argument values, illustrated by paying a bill whose details are in an email.

Adaptive parameter injection is discussed theoretically through generation and schema-validation hurdles, but no separate adaptive-attack experiment, attack budget, or success rate is reported in the supplied paper.

For the user's research question, the paper supports the inference that retrieved attacker-controlled content adds an instruction-entry route and tool access makes resulting deviations consequential; it does not directly measure greater vulnerability than standalone LLMs.
Figure 1 visually depicts an injected $500 transfer instruction in product information and a transfer-tool candidate outside the trusted product-details reference.
The abstract reports aggregate FPR 1.49%, but the supplied main results do not state weights or denominators that reconcile it with DH 0.97% and DS 3.28%; their equal-weight mean is 2.125%.

quality.limitations: Quotation presence and page bounds do not prove claim entailment or full coverage.

research.title: Prismata: Confining Cross-Site Prompt Injection in Web Agents
research.research_question_relevance: ANALYST INFERENCE, MEDIUM confidence: the paper explains additional web-agent exposure through mixed-origin page content, ambiguous click/fill semantics, data-dependent workflows, and access to consequential site features. It does not directly compare web agents with standalone LLMs and cannot establish a numerical comparative vulnerability gap.
research.attack_surface: AUTHOR-REPORTED: text injected into user content, hosted-party content, or external content on benign websites can influence an agent and exploit legitimate browser/site features. Trusted-origin arbitrary JavaScript execution is outside scope. Within-task persuasion and non-textual attacks are not covered by the evaluated protection.
research.method: Task-only origin policy; per-element critical-path action gating; top-down Biba-inspired provenance and capability labeling; minimum-capability composition; deterministic observation filtering and identifier-based action checks. Evidence includes a 5,664-DOM structural corpus, WebArena attack/utility experiments, WASP/adaptive stress tests, expert agreement on 20 observations, and caching/overhead measurements.
research.limitations: Conditional structural guarantees; fallible labeling and incomplete structural cues; residual Case 3 exposure; textual modality; broad-permission tasks; captured/live DOM drift; small benign expert sample; limited adaptive protocol disclosure; model-roster inconsistencies; no direct standalone-LLM control or reported component ablation.

claims.statement: The web entanglement problem arises because the security meaning of a browser action depends on page structure and context, which can itself include untrusted content.
Prismata combines dynamic trust derivation with mechanical confinement to restrict both the agent's observations and task-dependent browser capabilities.

The action gate restricts each labeling input to the user task and target element's critical path; off-path injected content is therefore excluded from that input, without guaranteeing semantic label correctness.
Biba parsing locks resolved origin labels and prevents descendants from exceeding their parent's trust, using preceding structural cues to restrict untrusted subtrees before exposing their content.

Among 90,408 sampled untrusted path instances, 1,086 contain actionable descendants and 94 lack preceding cues; the residual becomes 15 cases, approximately 0.017%, only after excluding ordinary links under the stated web-best-practice and same-site assumptions.

Across the three main attack templates, the authors report average ASR decreasing from 85.5% to 0.7% and TSR increasing from 4.5% to 23.0% with Prismata; these are benchmark-condition averages rather than universal web-agent rates.
Under benign conditions, TSR decreases from 29.9% without Prismata to 26.6% with it, an author-reported difference of 3.3 percentage points.

Table 3 reports defended adaptive WA20 ASR of 0.0% for Shortcut, Completion, and Ignore, compared with undefended values of 100.0%, 65.0%, and 85.0%; the supplied protocol does not fully specify adaptive search strength.

The expert validation uses 20 benign WebArena observations from five domains; aggregate allowed-element F1 does not establish worst-case safety because a single critical mislabel may admit an attack-relevant element.
The evaluated defense targets attacks whose goals exceed task privileges and operates on textual input; in-scope manipulation and non-textual attacks remain outside its stated protection.
Matched 20-task runs have simulated cached costs of $1.105 without Prismata and $1.623 with it; the authors report $1.821 avoided through KV reuse and $1.102 through request-level reuse.

The paper informs the research question by showing how mixed-origin web content and context-dependent browser actions create additional exposure and consequential action paths. It does not directly compare web agents against standalone LLMs or quantify a comparative vulnerability gap.

The informal proof's statement that every action targets a DOM identifier is broader than the supplied action table, which includes navigation and control actions; the fully supported mediation description is clearest for element-targeting actions.
