research.attack_surface: Seven author-defined analytical layers: foundation, cognition, memory, tool execution, coordination, ecosystem, and governance. Web-specific exposure includes page-mediated indirect prompt injection, adversarial pixels, file and API returns, tool permissions, persistent writes, and MCP/tool-description initialization. Temporalities distinguish immediate, within-session, cross-session memory, and drift/dormant-trigger effects.
research.method: PRISMA-inspired systematic survey of 116 retained papers from 1,634 records across four databases and two search phases, with single-author layer/time coding into 144 reported assignments; conceptual architecture, conditional theorem sketch, defense/benchmark mapping, five-case taxonomy comparison, and four reported robustness protocols.
research.limitations: Single-coder classification; no inter-rater reliability; selective venue/citation/gap inclusion; excluded industry evidence; missing supplements; heterogeneous secondary metrics; unmeasured severity construct; claimed rather than validated defense coverage; internal numerical, coding, cutoff, and citation inconsistencies; no new controlled standalone-versus-agent security experiment.

claims.statement: The paper distinguishes agentic systems through cross-session planning, memory, external tools, and peer coordination; these are architectural claims rather than a new matched comparison experiment.
The PRISMA-inspired two-phase search retrieved 1,634 records and retained 116 papers after deduplication, title/abstract screening, and full-text assessment.
Table 5 places nine of 144 overlapping paper-cell assignments in L5–L7 × T3–T4, reported as 6.3%; this is literature coding volume, not attack incidence or a measured severity correlation.

The non-transferability theorem equates attack and no-attack alert probabilities only for a pure single-representation defense and an attack localized so other input distributions remain unchanged; the full supplementary proof is absent.

The author attributes L4 attacks to principal trust inversion: tool outputs enter planning context without trust marking despite the environment's low authority. The universal wording is a corpus synthesis, not independently verified for all agents.
Temporal escalation separates a malicious memory write from later-session exploitation, making cross-session correlation necessary to observe both events; the six-week refund example is illustrative.

The survey reports a cited ARE result of 67% attack success against visual web-browsing agents with perturbations affecting less than 5% of webpage pixels; this is condition-specific secondary evidence.
Figure 8 marks seven of 28 cells with zero claimed defense coverage; the source explicitly warns that nonzero coverage is not empirical effectiveness.
None of the ten benchmarks in Table 9 is assigned T3 or T4 coverage; this establishes absence within that inventory, not an externally verified universal absence.
One author performed the layer/time coding, formal inter-rater reliability was not measured, and the search excludes substantial industry evidence.

The four reported EF1 perturbation analyses show small selected-zone fractions, with displayed protocol bounds spanning 4.76% to 8.33%; the author states that these do not capture systematic coding bias.

For the user's web-agent question, the survey supports an architectural explanation: external observations repeatedly influence planning, tools create side effects, memory persists influence, and peers propagate it. It does not itself quantify a matched standalone-versus-web-agent vulnerability difference.
ABOM is proposed as a conceptual inventory extending software dependencies to behavioral components; the main text explicitly says it is not ratified and presents no tooling prototype there.
The reported 26 two-cell papers and two three-cell papers among 116 imply 88 + 52 + 6 = 146 assignments if all remaining papers occupy one cell, conflicting with the reported 144 total.
