research.title: SoK: Attack and Defense Landscape of Agentic AI Systems
research.research_question_relevance: ANALYST INFERENCE; MEDIUM confidence in the web-specific application. The paper directly discusses conceptual differences between agentic systems and standalone LLMs, including expanded interfaces and amplified consequences. Its framework helps explain conditional web-agent vulnerability through untrusted pages, dynamic tool use, memory, sensitive access, and action authority. It does not conduct a controlled comparison or establish that every web agent is more vulnerable than every standalone deployment.
research.attack_surface: AUTHOR-REPORTED: external pages and documents, third-party tool names/descriptions/implementations, direct user inputs, model components, memory and RAG stores, user interfaces, tool credentials, and external resources. Attack vectors V1–V6 are distinct from risks R1–R7.
research.method: Literature-based cybersecurity systematization of knowledge. The authors report a 2023–October 2025 review, four keyword dimensions, venue/source prioritization, manual exclusion of standalone-model work, and 128 papers including 51 attack methods and 60 defense methods. They synthesize design dimensions, threat models, interacting risks, defense mechanisms, and an Appendix A MITRE ATLAS crosswalk.
research.limitations: No original experiments, empirical effect sizes, shared benchmark comparison, or normalized defense performance. Search databases, full queries, screening flow, coding agreement, and evidence-quality ratings are not supplied. Internal inconsistencies include nine versus seven risks and an unexplained November-identified citation relative to the October search endpoint. Visual inspection covers 13 rendered pages; all remaining pages were text-only.

claims.statement: The study reviews academic literature and web documents from 2023 through October 2025 and reports 128 papers, including 51 attack methods and 60 defense methods; these are review counts rather than experimental performance results.
Seven design dimensions describe agent flexibility, and the three illustrated levels are representative positions on continua rather than measured vulnerability scores.
An external adversary can influence retrieved resources such as public pages or documents without directly interacting with the agent.

The paper explicitly argues that heterogeneous external-data, memory, and tool interfaces enlarge agents' attack surfaces compared with standalone LLMs; this is a conceptual comparison without a measured effect size.
Under the described unsafe-flow condition, automatically fetching URLs influenced by untrusted web content can enable private-data exfiltration; no attack-success percentage is reported.
The system-level synthesis describes risk cascades in which expanded entry points expose model weaknesses that amplify confidentiality, integrity, and availability consequences.
Contextual security concerns keeping agent contexts aligned with intended tasks, including admissibility and prioritization of context elements.
Input guardrails can produce false positives and false negatives, with ambiguous security boundaries and adaptive bypass limiting their effectiveness.
Information-flow defenses can impose substantial runtime overhead and suffer label creep; no normalized overhead measurement is supplied.
Privilege separation can reduce utility, and current research often addresses simplified environments rather than the full complexity of web, filesystem, and database risks.
The authors recommend complementary defenses guided by defense-in-depth, least privilege, and complete mediation rather than reliance on one mechanism.
The paper conducts no original experiments or empirical evaluations and therefore supplies no controlled numerical comparison of web agents with standalone LLMs.

For the user's web-agent question, the framework suggests that risk depends on combining untrusted retrieval, dynamic execution, sensitive access, and action authority; it does not establish a universal ranking of all web agents over all standalone deployments.
The introduction claims nine risk categories, while the detailed numbered taxonomy and figures expose R1–R7; the supplied work does not explicitly reconcile the count.

quality.limitations: Quotation presence and page bounds do not prove claim entailment or full coverage.

research.title: Talk is (Not) Cheap: A Taxonomy and Benchmark Coverage Audit for LLM Attacks
research.research_question_relevance: MEDIUM confidence, analyst inference: the paper helps explain additional web-agent failure channels through external-data instructions, tool-mediated side effects, exfiltration, and resource consumption. Its output-versus-execution distinction shows why harmful-text testing does not establish action security. It does not directly compare standalone LLMs with web agents, estimate a vulnerability multiplier, or causally isolate browsing and tool access.
research.attack_surface: Author-reported surfaces include direct prompts, web content, files, API responses, tool descriptions and returned content, agent-to-agent interactions, stateful or memory-related channels, multimodal inputs, and selected internal-generation or routing mechanisms. Attacker access varies; white-box internal mechanisms must be distinguished from externally supplied web content.
research.method: Literature-derived taxonomy and benchmark coverage audit: Gemini 3.1 Pro extracts 6,366 mentions from 932 arXiv papers; normalization yields 2,521 groups; direct, fuzzy, and semantic matching assign taxonomy leaves; authors construct a 507-leaf hierarchy and 4×6 operational matrix. Human, cross-model, recall, novelty, and provenance spot-checks qualify the dataset. Manual documentation mapping audits six benchmarks, and a worked specification proposes metrics for an uncovered disruption cell.
research.limitations: English arXiv corpus from one database with unpublished formal inclusion criteria; incomplete H1 2026 collection; shared-model extraction/classification dependence; limited and partly anchored recall evaluation; uncertain fine-grained boundaries; 106 unpopulated placeholders; approximate provenance; only six public benchmarks; no new attack execution or direct web-agent-versus-standalone experiment. Several prose claims conflict with tables or arithmetic, especially the assertion of zero overlap between all primary benchmarks.

claims.statement: The study uses a 932-paper arXiv corpus from the Promptfoo database, spanning H1 2023–H1 2026; this is a literature corpus rather than a direct agent-versus-standalone experiment.
Extraction yields 6,366 attack mentions across 863 attack-bearing papers, normalized into 2,521 unique attack groups; 69 corpus papers yield no inference-time attacks.
Of 507 taxonomy leaves, 401 are corpus-populated and 106 are author-created coverage placeholders; the latter are not observed corpus attack types.
Counting partial coverage, the benchmark mapping covers at most six of 24 cells, or 25%; this measures matrix occupancy rather than attack success or real-world risk coverage.

InjecAgent and AgentDojo share the Hijacking × Indirect Injection and Exfiltration × Indirect Injection cells, so the tables contradict a literal zero-overlap claim across all three primary benchmarks.

Human evaluation reports 92.0% accuracy on 200 stratified Tier 3 classifications, with Wilson 95% confidence interval 87.4–95.0%; this validates a sample of semantic matching rather than every dataset record.
The extraction spot-check reports 100% precision and 89.4% recall, based on 76 correct extractions and 85 eligible attacks across 13 reviewed papers; unfamiliar attacks are a recognized limitation.
The paper defines harmful output as Safety Bypass and successful action or side effects as System Hijacking, associating these outcomes with different defensive requirements.

For web agents, external web content, files, API responses, and tool descriptions create instruction-bearing channels beyond direct user prompts; combined with action capabilities, these suggest additional failure modes, but do not establish a measured vulnerability increase over standalone LLMs.
The paper assembles prior reports of up to 46× reasoning-token amplification across nine models with answer correctness maintained; it does not reproduce these attacks.
The Service Disruption × Instructional walkthrough is a benchmark specification assembled from published evidence, not a newly executed attack evaluation.
Several retained decoding-manipulation attacks require white-box access, creating an acknowledged tension with the nominal input-interface-only inference-time definition.
Original-source attribution is approximate: a 100-attribution spot-check reports 72% correct, 14% ambiguous, and 14% misattributed, limiting provenance-sensitive reuse.
Excluding two partial-coverage cells leaves 4/24 × 100 ≈ 16.7% cell coverage, rather than the maximum 25% obtained when partial cells count.

quality.limitations: Quotation presence and page bounds do not prove claim entailment or full coverage.

research.title: Toward Secure LLM Agents: Threat Surfaces, Attacks, Defenses, and Evaluation
research.research_question_relevance: MEDIUM confidence, explicitly ANALYST INFERENCE: the survey provides a mechanism-based explanation for additional web-agent exposure relative to text-only LLM applications. Untrusted page content can influence planning and action selection under delegated permissions; tool feedback, persistent memory, and coordination can extend effects when those capabilities exist. The paper directly discusses the architectural distinction but does not conduct a matched standalone-versus-web-agent experiment or establish a universal numerical vulnerability increase.
research.attack_surface: AUTHOR-REPORTED: user prompts, web content, tool outputs, retrieved content, files/code, planning loops, memory/scratchpads, and inter-agent channels. For web agents, the central path is low-authority external content entering reasoning and influencing privileged action. Memory and multi-agent propagation are conditional additional surfaces, not properties of every browser agent.
research.method: A lifecycle-based cybersecurity survey of 247 normalized papers, searched over a declared 1 January 2023–27 April 2026 window using six sources, GPT-5.4-assisted candidate expansion, and backward/forward snowballing. Screening starts from 275 records, removes 24, and reduces four through duplicate/version normalization. Three authors independently annotate the corpus, using single-label descriptive fields and multi-label technical fields; overall pre-harmonization Fleiss' kappa is reported as 0.86. Analyses are descriptive counts, co-occurrence matrices, and qualitative systems/engineering synthesis.
research.limitations: AUTHOR-REPORTED: overlapping categories, judgment-sensitive manual screening/annotation, search/publication bias, preprint instability, and retrieval-model bias. ANALYST OBSERVATIONS: no controlled standalone comparison, no pooled efficacy estimate, absent raw review artifacts, ambiguous Figure 5 denominator, unresolved publication-date markings, and an Appendix C.1 prose/matrix discrepancy. All 40 supplied text pages were read; 27 were visually inspected. No absent supplementary artifact or referenced paper was claimed as reviewed.

claims.statement: The paper frames agent security as extending from generated content to operational behavior because agents can invoke tools, change state, and produce external effects. This is an architectural argument, not a measured standalone-versus-agent vulnerability comparison.

The review retains 247 papers after screening a 275-record pool, excluding 24 records, and reducing the pool by four through duplicate/version normalization. Retrieval contributions are 209 database, 42 LLM-assisted, and 24 snowballing records.

Three authors independently annotated all 247 papers. The reported overall Fleiss' kappa is 0.86 before harmonization; technical dimensions are multi-label, whereas primary paper type and system setting are single-label.

The semi-formal agent model connects inbound information, planning, decisions, execution, memory, outputs, and coordination. The authors locate security problems in flows among these elements rather than in any element alone.

Prompt Injection and Indirect Prompt Injection occur in 142 and 86 papers in the threat-model field. These overlapping coded-paper counts describe research concentration, not attack success, incident frequency, or a severity ranking.

Within Web Browsing scenario annotations, Prompt Injection co-occurs 71 times and Indirect Prompt Injection 44 times. The paper explicitly cautions that this concentration is not a definitive ranking of deployment risks.

Memory Poisoning appears in 24 papers as a threat model, and Memory Safety in 32 as a research topic. Retained contamination can survive an interaction and influence later planning, so these numbers concern different annotation fields rather than contradictory estimates.

The authors argue that multi-agent security includes message integrity, role confusion, amplification, and topology-sensitive propagation, beyond repeating single-agent risks. Multi-agent Collaboration co-occurs with Memory Poisoning and Coordination Failures 14 times each.

The defense synthesis identifies differing trust assumptions and utility, latency, and engineering costs. It does not support a universal stack for every architecture, and memory and coordination remain less consistently protected.

Metric usage is concentrated on Attack Success Rate, reported in 129 papers, while Utility, Latency, and Cost appear in 22, 8, and 7 papers. These are usage counts, not measured metric values or pooled defensive effect sizes.

AgentDojo and InjecAgent have 30 and 11 reuse occurrences. Table 4 percentages use total benchmark annotations as their denominator, and Figure 7 represents corpus co-occurrences rather than intrinsic benchmark quality or guaranteed task coverage.

The authors acknowledge category overlap, manual judgment, search/publication bias, preprint instability, and LLM-assisted retrieval bias. The arXiv count of 169 out of 247 describes the normalized corpus and limits stability claims.
Table 11's browser, coding, memory, and multi-agent defense stacks are engineering interpretations of the corpus rather than a validated standard or a demonstrated sufficient-security guarantee.

Analyst inference: web agents can have additional exposure and consequences because untrusted web content can influence decisions made under delegated permissions, with optional memory and coordination extending persistence and propagation. The survey supports this mechanism but does not quantify a universal vulnerability increase over standalone LLMs.

Figure 6's Inter-agent Channels row has 21 for Inter-agent Comms and 16 for Coordination, whereas nearby prose says these channels align most strongly with Coordination. The visible matrix and prose are not silently reconciled.

quality.limitations: Quotation presence and page bounds do not prove claim entailment or full coverage.

research.title: AndroidWorld: A Dynamic Benchmarking Environment for Autonomous Agents
research.research_question_relevance: ANALYST INFERENCE, MEDIUM confidence: The paper helps identify how interactive agents consume task instructions, screenshots, and accessibility-derived UI content and turn decisions into device actions. Its ethics appendix explicitly mentions malicious alteration of prompts or screen outputs. It does not directly compare web-agent vulnerability with standalone LLM vulnerability, conduct adversarial attacks, or report attack-success rates. It is relevant as an architectural and evaluation-method source, not as direct evidence of the requested comparative security claim.
research.attack_surface: ANALYST INFERENCE, MEDIUM confidence: Candidate security-relevant interfaces include task prompts, screenshots, accessibility-element text and descriptions, stored app content, action-history/reflection content, and UI/API execution. The paper documents these system interfaces but does not establish attacker control over each one. Privileged adb state access belongs to the benchmark harness and must not automatically be attributed to all tested agents. Appendix B names altered prompts and screen outputs as possible malicious-use mechanisms.
research.method: A controlled Android benchmark with reported 116 tasks across 20 apps, seeded parameter generation, task-specific initialization and teardown, filesystem/database/system-state or UI validators, and composite partial rewards. M3A uses zero-shot action reasoning and post-action reflection; baselines include M3A-Simple and adapted SeeAct. The main evaluation uses seed 30 and temperature 0, with Gemini 1.5 Pro, GPT-4 Turbo, and Gemma 2 27B. MobileMiniWoB++ implements 92 tasks but evaluates 62. Additional analyses change seeds, repeat five selected tasks, inspect qualitative failures, and test Pixel 5/Android 12 alongside Pixel 6/Android 13.
research.limitations: Selected open-source and built-in apps, fixed emulator state, local storage, and no required authentication limit scope. Main results lack confidence intervals; repeated robustness trials cover five tasks, and statistical-test details are incomplete. Human performance uses two engineers. Table 4 task counts, app sourcing, MiniWoB++ porting counts, and several catalog rows contain unresolved inconsistencies. Only 17 pages were visually supplied; other pages were text-only. No implementation or supplement was reviewed. No standalone-LLM security baseline, adversarial condition, defense experiment, or comparative vulnerability result is present.

claims.statement: AndroidWorld is reported to provide reward signals for 116 programmatic tasks across 20 real-world Android apps; these are reported suite counts, with an unresolved discrepancy against the sum of Table 4 app counts.
Task parameters are generated using a controlled random seed and influence both initial state and reward outcomes, enabling different concrete instances of a task.

The benchmark harness uses adb to inspect filesystem, application database, and system-setting state, with UI-element validation when state inspection is impractical; this harness access should not be equated with every tested agent's capabilities.

The primary reproducible environment is a Pixel 6 emulator running Android 13, with app versions and task state controlled; selected apps do not require login/authentication and can store data locally.
M3A is a zero-shot Android agent combining ReAct-style action reasoning and Reflexion-style reflection; it uses observations to act and updates subsequent decisions from action outcomes.
The main evaluation uses seed 30 and temperature 0; MobileMiniWoB++ results cover 62 tasks rather than all 92 implemented tasks.

The best reported AndroidWorld configuration is M3A with GPT-4 Turbo and accessibility-tree input at 30.6% success, compared with 80.0% human success. These measure task completion, not attack susceptibility.

With GPT-4 Turbo on AndroidWorld, full accessibility-input M3A scores 30.6%, while M3A-Simple scores 19.8%; the comparison changes guidance and reflection together and does not isolate either component.
M3A using GPT-4 Turbo and accessibility trees scores 27.6%, 26.3%, and 33.2% across three seeds, with a reported mean of 29.0%; these results are separate from the single-seed Table 3 result.

The repeated-trial robustness analysis uses 20 trials per selected task and reports significant fixed-versus-varying-parameter differences for add-expense and edit-note tasks; Figure 3 uses 95% Wilson intervals and p < 0.05 markers without specifying the exact statistical test.
An alternate Pixel 5/Android 12 setup yields 28.4% success. The experiment changes device and OS together and does not establish broad device-independent performance.

MobileMiniWoB++ implements 92 tasks and excludes twelve named tasks for interaction, rendering, or timing problems; the 114-template comparison-table count does not by itself explain the porting pool.

Appendix A acknowledges current coverage of open-source Android apps and built-in system apps, with trending-app testing desirable and less optimized UIs sometimes requiring more complex interactions.
The ethics appendix warns that malicious actors could alter prompts or screen outputs to pursue harmful objectives; this is a risk statement, not a measured prompt-injection or attack-success result.

For the research question about web agents versus standalone LLMs, AndroidWorld is indirectly relevant because environment observations inform executable device actions. The supplied paper does not directly compare their security vulnerability or quantify an attack-surface advantage.

The best-agent human gap is 49.4 percentage points, calculated as 80.0% human success minus 30.6% M3A success; it is an absolute completion-rate difference, not a relative improvement or vulnerability difference.

Expense-task parameters can require initially hidden categories accessible through horizontal scrolling, and the authors report consistent failure for such categories in their qualitative analysis; no category-specific numerical success rates are supplied.

Human performance was evaluated using two software engineers, with one attempt per task for each participant as described; this small human sample qualifies interpretation of the reported human benchmark.

quality.limitations: Quotation presence and page bounds do not prove claim entailment or full coverage.

research.title: AWE: Adaptive Agents for Dynamic Web Penetration Testing
research.research_question_relevance: ANALYST INFERENCE — Indirect relevance only. The paper shows how HTTP interaction, browser verification, authentication state, memory, specialized procedures, and execution flexibility shape agents' web-exploitation capabilities. It does not measure attacks against AI agents, include a standalone-LLM vulnerability control, or establish that web AI agents are more vulnerable than standalone LLMs. Confidence: HIGH for this scope distinction.
research.attack_surface: AUTHOR-REPORTED — The attacked surface is the target web application's HTTP endpoints and attacker-controlled parameters, headers, cookies, request bodies, and dynamic client-side content. Included families are XSS, SQL injection, SSTI, command injection, file inclusion/path traversal, XXE, SSRF, and authenticated unauthorized object access. The security attack surface of AWE itself is not evaluated.
research.method: AUTHOR-REPORTED — Three-layer memory-augmented architecture with LLM orchestration, eight vulnerability-specific agents, reconnaissance, structured context/filter probing, constrained payload mutation, and browser-backed verification. Model selection uses DVWA; system comparison uses 104 XBOW challenges against published MAPTA results. Correct flag retrieval is required for a counted XBOW success.
research.limitations: AUTHOR-REPORTED — Injection-centric scope, limited multi-step planning, heuristic context/filter abstractions, and model sensitivity. ANALYST OBSERVATIONS — Different models and historical baseline measurements confound architectural attribution; small category samples, missing uncertainty estimates, no component ablations, unexplained DVWA percentages, a cost-per-solve inconsistency, and Figure 4 caption–visual misalignment limit inference. No direct evidence addresses comparative vulnerability of web agents and standalone LLMs.

claims.statement: AWE uses three architectural layers separating global orchestration, specialized exploitation agents, and shared foundation services.
The XSS procedure conditions candidate generation on reflection context and filtering behavior and requires concrete JavaScript-execution evidence.
An XBOW challenge counts as solved only when AWE retrieves the correct flag through a verified exploit; detection without exploit completion is excluded.
On all 104 XBOW challenges, AWE with Claude Sonnet 4 solves 54 (51.9%), while MAPTA with GPT-5 solves 80 (76.9%); this is a comparison of different complete systems and models.
AWE solves 20 of 23 XSS challenges versus MAPTA's 13; Table III also reports two versus one blind-SQL-injection solves out of only three challenges.
Table III qualifies broad injection-superiority language: AWE loses on SSTI (7/13 versus 11/13) and command injection (5/11 versus 9/11), while tying SQLi, XXE, and SSRF.
The full-benchmark comparison reports 1.12M versus approximately 54.9M tokens, and median solve times of 35.7 versus 156.2 seconds, favoring AWE on these resource summaries.
AWE's printed $0.113 cost per solve conflicts with total cost divided by its reported successes: $7.73/54 is approximately $0.1431. The supplied paper does not explain the discrepancy.
The evaluation resets memory between challenges and uses consistent headless Chromium verification, so the benchmark does not by itself establish gains from accumulated cross-target learning.
The authors acknowledge that largely independent specialist pipelines do not coordinate general multi-stage exploitation sequences.

Relevance to why web AI agents might be more vulnerable than standalone LLMs is indirect: the described system interacts with web applications and maintains state, but the study measures exploitation of web targets rather than compromise of AI agents.
The reported model comparison is conducted within AWE; it is not a direct comparison between web agents and standalone LLMs.
DVWA trial accounting is uncertain: the stated n=10 trials per vulnerability type does not directly explain reported binary success percentages of 67% and 55%. No reconciliation is supplied.
Figure 4's caption describes three-model iteration efficiency, but its four visible panels distinguish DVWA difficulty levels and XSSy rather than plotting separate model distributions.
MAPTA comparisons use publicly reported per-challenge results, limiting how strongly the supplied paper can establish a freshly controlled comparison.
Aggregate counts imply 45 challenges solved by both systems, nine by AWE alone, and 35 by MAPTA alone: union=104−15=89; intersection=54+80−89=45.

quality.limitations: Quotation presence and page bounds do not prove claim entailment or full coverage.

research.title: BackdoorAgent: A Unified Framework for Backdoor Attacks on LLM-based Agents
research.research_question_relevance: HIGH confidence analyst inference: the paper explains mechanisms relevant to why Web AI agents could acquire additional security risks through persistent intermediate artifacts, planning/memory/tool interfaces, and recurrent feedback. Its Web evaluation demonstrates heterogeneous backdoor susceptibility across four multimodal backbones. It does not directly compare matched standalone LLMs with Web agents, so it cannot establish a quantitative increase in vulnerability caused by agency.
research.attack_surface: Author-reported: planning artifacts, external memory or retrieval content, and tool/environment feedback. Attacks modify one component or its outputs, which may influence later context and state. Agent Web includes multimodal perception and action, with interface misdirection such as incorrect purchases described as a harm example.
research.method: A modular stage-aware runtime with injection hooks, component-local attack wrappers, configurable agent execution, and structured trajectory logging; benchmark evaluations across QA, Code, Web, and Drive; seven named attacks; clean task accuracy, attack success rate, and attacked task accuracy; family aggregation, poisoning-ratio and token-overhead analyses, and exploratory probability-based detection.
research.limitations: Controlled benchmark coverage is acknowledged as incomplete. No direct standalone baseline, concrete logged trajectory, named dataset sizes, numerical step budgets, run counts, uncertainty intervals, or full attack/detection configurations are supplied. Web results vary sharply across model and attack. Abstract persistence terminology differs from Table 6 ASR labeling; selected prose examples conflict with tables. The linked implementation and data were not reviewed.

claims.statement: BackdoorAgent organizes agent backdoor injection around planning, memory, and tool interfaces, allowing one component to be attacked while the other components remain unchanged.
The framework records structured trajectories to diagnose injection, activation, and downstream influence; no concrete execution log was supplied for independent inspection.
The benchmark includes QA, Code, Web, and Drive workflows; Web is evaluated separately and only on multimodal-capable backbones.
Code/GPT-4o-mini under AgentPoison has 98.01% ASR and 56.74% attacked ACC versus 58.95% clean ACC, illustrating high malicious success with task accuracy near its clean value in this condition.
Web attack success is heterogeneous: Claude's BadChain ASR is 97.39% while its other five reported ASRs are 0%; Gemini's BadChain ASR is 98.74%, whereas GPT-4o-mini and Qwen3-VL have 0% BadChain ASR.

BadChain exceeds 90% ASR for all five open-source Drive backbones in Table 4; this is consistent with the authors' sequential-amplification account, but no architecture-only causal ablation is supplied.
Table 6 reports GPT-family planning, memory, and tools ASR as 43.58%, 77.97%, and 60.28%. Memory is highest in four of five families; DeepSeek's tools ASR of 42.20% exceeds its memory ASR of 38.91%.

Increasing memory poisoning ratio from 0.1 to 0.2 to 0.5 monotonically increases reported memory ASR in all four Table 7 families; GPT-family values are 53.06%, 77.97%, and 97.72%. Corpus sizes, selection details, and uncertainty are unspecified.

The GPT-4o token-overhead plot shows memory attacks increasing token consumption more than tool-use and planning attacks as trigger strength rises; exact strength units and normalization are not specified.

The probability-based defense investigation is preliminary and proposes no new defense mechanism; Figure 5 visibly labels AUROC 0.7681, while the authors interpret transferability and separability as limited.
The authors acknowledge incomplete coverage of real-world architectures, environments, and threat models and identify adaptive adversaries and complex deployments as future work.

Research relevance is an analyst inference: persistent context, additional interfaces, and feedback provide mechanisms relevant to Web-agent security, but the paper does not directly measure whether Web agents are more vulnerable than matched standalone LLMs.

The GPT-family values called trigger persistence in the abstract are labeled module-wise ASR in Table 6; the supplied work gives no separate persistence-rate definition resolving this terminology discrepancy.

The Code/Qwen2.5/AgentPoison example decreases accuracy by 2.56 percentage points: 75.89% attacked ACC minus 78.45% clean ACC. Its placement among examples described as matching or exceeding clean accuracy is inconsistent with those operands.

quality.limitations: Quotation presence and page bounds do not prove claim entailment or full coverage.

research.title: Don’t Click That: Teaching Web Agents to Resist Deceptive Interfaces
research.research_question_relevance: ANALYST INFERENCE, MEDIUM confidence: the paper illustrates how untrusted visual interfaces can redirect task-driven agents from perception into harmful or intention-misaligned clicks. Its evaluator gate addresses this environment-to-action boundary. It does not directly compare agents with standalone LLMs, so it cannot establish the size or existence of a matched agent-versus-standalone vulnerability difference.
research.attack_surface: Visible webpage interfaces: deceptive pop-ups, fake download or continuation buttons, misleading visual hierarchy, preselected subscription controls, overlays, urgency cues, and commercial prompts misaligned with the user's task. Purely backend exploits without visible manifestations are outside the defense's stated scope.
research.method: DUDE evaluates screenshot, task, and candidate click using a ternary label and confidence; Stage 1 uses asymmetric hybrid-reward learning, Stage 2 summarizes persistent failures with successful anchors into contextual guidance, and inference gates execution with rejection/rethinking. RUC supplies 1,407 annotated examples; general reported evaluation uses 200 tasks across four domains, with Stage-1 training assessed separately through ablation.
research.limitations: Static screenshots; no asynchronous live-environment validation; English-focused data; ecological rather than maximal adversariality; visual-only coverage; evaluator-dependent task regressions; single-stage DFR increases; no matched standalone-LLM baseline; missing uncertainty estimates; unresolved step accounting, table averages, test-suite relationships, transfer denominator, confidence thresholds, and confidence-adjustment formula/rationale.

claims.statement: DUDE evaluates a screenshot, task specification, and proposed click, producing a correct/ineffective/deceptive judgment and confidence.
The hybrid reward assigns severity weight 10 to approving a deceptive click as benign, emphasizing that error over ordinary conservatism.
Stage 2 turns collected failures into transferable contextual experience without additional parameter updates.
RUC contains 1,407 samples: 910 normal and 497 deceptive, with the deceptive subset divided into 200 manual and 297 automatic examples.

On the reported Table 2 aggregate comparison, GLM-4.6V-Flash with the UI-TARS evaluator improves SR from 9.50% to 60.50% and reduces DFR from 4.00% to 1.50%; these are episode outcomes, not standalone-LLM comparisons.
Benefits are not uniform: Table 2 reports UI-TARS-1.5-7B success falling from 43.50% vanilla to 35.50% with the Qwen-2B evaluator, despite DFR falling to zero.
In the Qwen3-VL-4B stage ablation, Stage 1 alone and Stage 2 alone increase DFR from 2.00% to 5.50% and 4.50%, respectively, whereas their combination reports DFR 0% and SR 33.50%.
Removing severity weighting increases evaluator fatal-error rate from 9.75% to 27.53%; this metric concerns deceptive clicks classified as correct, rather than directly measuring episode-level DFR.
The closed-source transfer table reports SR 54.12% to 62.50% and DFR 25.00% to 19.38% after applying the Stage-2 prompt, but exact task denominator and agent/evaluator roles remain unclear.
Evaluation relies on static screenshots and has not validated DUDE in fully interactive environments with asynchronous feedback.
RUC's episode-level DFR can be suppressed because agents may complete the task before encountering a deceptive trigger; it should not be equated with forced-exposure deception rates.
The paper's reported Steps values cannot be reconciled from the supplied definitions: a three-step cap and deceptive-termination count of 10 coexist with Table 2 values as high as 31.00.

For the requested research question, the paper supports an inference that visible environmental content can redirect a web agent's actions through misleading interface affordances; it does not directly measure greater vulnerability than standalone LLMs.
DUDE's visual defense does not cover purely backend-based exploits without visible GUI manifestations.

quality.limitations: Quotation presence and page bounds do not prove claim entailment or full coverage.

research.title: DoomArena: A Framework for Testing AI Agents Against Evolving Security Threats
research.research_question_relevance: MEDIUM confidence, analyst inference: DoomArena provides evidence about mechanisms relevant to why web agents may be vulnerable, including attacker-controlled webpage content, hidden accessibility representations, repeated observation/action loops, and tools that enact malicious requests. Its own experiments do not directly compare standalone LLMs with matched agent implementations. Statements about such a comparative gap on page 2 summarize cited prior work, not DoomArena experiments.
research.attack_surface: Malicious user conversations; queried product catalogs and databases; webpage banners using accessibility attributes; pop-ups with hidden accessibility-tree-like instructions; screenshot overlays in desktop environments. Attacker control and success criteria differ across these surfaces.
research.method: A modular security-testing layer uses attack configurations, reusable attack implementations, environment-specific gateways, success filters, and optional aborting defenses. Evaluations use 50 airline tasks, 115 retail tasks, 114 Reddit tasks, 192 Shopping tasks, and a stated 39-task OSWorld subset. Metrics are attack success, legitimate task success with and without attacks, and joint-success stealth.
research.limitations: No matched standalone-model control; text-only browser evaluation; restricted LlamaGuard category selection; abort-based judge defense can eliminate attacked-task utility; conditional combined-attack denominators; unclear browser/desktop uncertainty procedures; incomplete exact execution configuration; unresolved main/appendix numerical discrepancies; Figure 3 raw trend data and Figure 5 exact category data unavailable. No absent supplement or external source was reviewed.

claims.statement: DoomArena is a configurable security-evaluation framework that supplies components for constructing benchmarks rather than being a benchmark itself.
Attack configurations specify the attackable component, chosen attack, and success filter; environment-specific gateways route the attack into the user-agent-environment loop.

In the 50-task airline malicious-user condition without defense, Table 2 reports ASR of 29.3 ±1.5% for GPT-4o and 2.7 ±0.2% for Claude-3.5-Sonnet; these are three-trial summaries, not a standalone-model comparison.
Browser experiments evaluate text-based agents receiving accessibility trees on 114 Reddit tasks and 192 Shopping tasks; multimodal web-agent evaluation is future work.
Undefended Claude-3.5-Sonnet pop-up ASR is 88.5 ±3.0% on Reddit and 42.7 ±3.6% on Shopping, demonstrating a descriptive domain difference under the supplied browser setup.

Every GPT-4o Judge attack row in the full Reddit and Shopping tables has 0% ASR and 0% task success under attack; the defense aborts on detection, so these results do not show preserved attacked-task utility.
The reported LlamaGuard evaluation flags only Code Interpreter Abuse, so its weak detection results concern that restricted configuration rather than all possible category settings.

For GPT-4o retail attacks in Table 8, catalog ASR increases from 34.8% alone to 70.5% combined, while malicious-user ASR decreases from 12.8% alone to 2.7% combined; combination has asymmetric component effects.
Combined-attack metrics exclude trials where the conditions for triggering both attacks were not met; these conditional results should not be treated as unconditional rates over every task.
On the stated 39-task OSWorld subset without defense, pop-up-inpainting ASR is 78.6% for GPT-4o and 22.9% for Claude-3.7-Sonnet; stealth rates are 2.9% and 5.7%, respectively.

For the requested research question, DoomArena supports the inference that attacker-controlled environment representations can redirect action-capable agents; it does not itself estimate a matched standalone-LLM versus agent vulnerability gap.
DoomArena does not enforce data minimization or anonymization; the authors warn that poorly handled sensitive test data could be exposed to external systems and actors.

Using the reported rounded means, Claude-3.5-Sonnet's undefended pop-up ASR is 45.8 percentage points lower on Shopping than Reddit: 88.5% minus 42.7%; this is approximately a 51.8% relative reduction.

The supplied work does not establish that the illustrated URL success filter verifies actual confidential-data theft; it checks redirection, and the caption describes theft at the target server as theoretical.

quality.limitations: Quotation presence and page bounds do not prove claim entailment or full coverage.

research.title: EvoCrawl: Exploring Web Application Code and State using Evolutionary Search
research.research_question_relevance: ANALYST INFERENCE, MEDIUM confidence: the paper shows that browser interaction sequences reach persistent application states, executable inputs, and authorization-sensitive resources. These are relevant environmental pathways for web AI agents. It does not directly compare agents with standalone LLMs, measure prompt injection, or establish a comparative vulnerability rate.
research.attack_surface: Author-studied surfaces are HTML inputs, JavaScript-triggered controls, hidden forms and links, stored/reflected XSS injection points, and directly requested resources with differing user privileges. Some reported findings require trusted administrator/editor privileges, and some are outside developer threat models.
research.method: A rapid Page Collection Module exchanges URLs with an Evolutionary Search Module. The latter searches element–interaction sequences using crossover, dependency-aware mutation, gene elimination, and weighted browser/database feedback. Modular XSS tracing and sitemap/replay/three-user IDOR analysis evaluate security consequences. Evaluation includes ten applications, 24-hour crawling, baseline comparisons, dependency ablation, selected known XSS, and new-finding reports.
research.limitations: Indirect relevance to AI-agent security; no standalone-LLM comparison. Required-field formats, cross-user workflows, inferred privacy, URL redundancy, token handling, instrumentation access, limited statistical specification, benchmark-version differences, and unresolved table/prose inconsistencies constrain conclusions. Referenced software artifacts were not inspected.

claims.statement: The authors argue that vulnerability triggering depends on executing vulnerable code while the application is in the required state.
EvoCrawl combines evolutionary sequence search with dependency tracking to prioritize successful submissions and newly revealed elements.
The fitness mechanism uses browser and server-side database feedback; successful submission is inferred from uniquely marked input reaching the database.
The authors report an average 59% coverage increase and fivefold more frequent HTML form submission; the latter is not reproduced by summing Table IV's distinct-form counts.
The evaluation uses 24-hour sessions, reset application instances, four-CPU virtual machines with 6 GB memory, and matched two-process coverage configurations.
Summing Table IV yields 265 distinct successful forms for EvoCrawl and 112 for BlackWidow: EvoCrawl-only 210 plus common 55 versus BlackWidow-only 57 plus common 55, a ratio of approximately 2.37.
On the selected known-XSS sample, Table V totals are 6/8 detections for EvoCrawl and 2/8 for BlackWidow; both detect 0/1 in Humhub.
EvoCrawl cannot submit forms whose required fields have input constraints its heuristics cannot infer.
The IDOR detector's interface-reachability policy can misclassify public resources as private, contributing substantially to reported false positives.
The authors report eight new findings, six acknowledged and confirmed by developers; acceptance and exploitation conditions differ across findings.
Table VIII qualifies the prose's universal ablation claim: Dokuwiki has 91 tracking-only versus 112 no-tracking-only lines, so tracking's total is 21 lines lower, 16722 versus 16743.
The authors identify manual fitness-parameter adjustment and redundant URL-based seed selection as limitations and propose automatic tuning and DOM-based page comparison.

For the user's research question, the paper indirectly illustrates security-sensitive browser interactions involving application state and authorization, but does not establish that web AI agents are more vulnerable than standalone LLMs.
The artifact's eight-hour demonstrations only partially reproduce the research results; full reproduction requires 24-hour experiments on each benchmark.

quality.limitations: Quotation presence and page bounds do not prove claim entailment or full coverage.

research.title: Gorilla: Large Language Model Connected with Massive APIs
research.research_question_relevance: Analyst inference, MEDIUM confidence: the paper identifies retrieval-conditioned API generation and a gap between API correctness and complete-program execution. These components are relevant to investigating how external information can influence an agent's actions. It does not establish that web AI agents are more vulnerable than standalone LLMs and contains no direct adversarial comparison.
research.attack_surface: Analyst inference: candidate surfaces include API documentation appended to a prompt, the retriever/API database, generated repository and model arguments, and supporting execution code. The authors do not define these as attack surfaces or evaluate attacker control, prompt injection, privilege misuse, data theft, or malicious repositories.
research.method: Closed-document analysis of all 22 supplied text pages and 16 supplied page renderings. The paper constructs APIBench, generates instruction–API pairs with GPT-4, fine-tunes LLaMA-7B with and without documentation, compares four retrieval settings, evaluates selected API structure using AST matching, and includes constraint, documentation-change, manual-execution, prompting, DocPrompting, and base-model analyses.
research.limitations: Reliability study rather than security evaluation; single-call scope; asymmetric HuggingFace scoring; conflicting dataset and result values; qualitative documentation-update examples; unspecified API-disjoint splits; single LLM runs; limited manual execution sample; absent separate supplements and uninspected artifacts. Research relevance is interpretive, not an author-reported security finding.

claims.statement: Gorilla is a retriever-aware fine-tuned LLaMA-7B model specialized for API calls, trained using instruction–API pairs.
RAT appends documentation to the prompt and is intended to teach the model to judge relevance; the authors explicitly acknowledge that retrieval can hurt performance.

Table 1 reports Gorilla no-retriever accuracy of 59.13% on Torch Hub, 71.68% on HuggingFace, and 83.79% on TensorFlow Hub; HuggingFace comparisons are qualified by different scoring for non-Gorilla models.

The evaluator defines hallucination as an API absent from its database and distinguishes this from selecting an existing API incorrectly; this is a database-relative API metric rather than a general security measure.

On 100 randomly sampled Gorilla generations, AST and human API accuracy were both 78%, whereas complete-code execution succeeded for 72%; correct API identity therefore did not guarantee executable surrounding code.
Figure 6 shows generated API calls changing after references change the model backbone or repository; the documentation-change evidence is qualitative and supplies no aggregate success rate.

The constraint experiment retains 65.26% of the Torch Hub dataset based on model-card accuracy metadata. Gorilla's zero-shot constraint accuracy is 47.88%, but it does not lead every retrieval condition.

In Table 7's HuggingFace comparison, Gorilla exceeds DocPrompting accuracy by 9.96 percentage points, calculated as 71.68 minus 61.72, and reduces hallucination by 6.41 points, calculated as 17.36 minus 10.95.
The authors report performing language-model experiments once because of GPU costs; repeated-run variability and confidence intervals are not characterized.
The paper focuses on one API call and explicitly places its execution system outside the main focus; its API results do not establish secure end-to-end autonomous task completion.

For the user's security question, retrieval and API generation identify a documentation-to-action influence path worth investigating. This is analyst inference: the paper does not test malicious documentation or directly compare web-agent vulnerability with standalone LLM vulnerability.
Dataset descriptions conflict: the main text reports 626 filtered TensorFlow Hub models, whereas Appendix A.1 reports 696 Tensor Hub APIs. The supplied material does not resolve the difference.

Table 2 shows zero accuracy without documentation for Gorilla trained with the oracle retriever, contrasting with strong no-document performance for the no-retriever-trained variant. The result is conditional on training and inference format.

quality.limitations: Quotation presence and page bounds do not prove claim entailment or full coverage.

research.title: InjecAgent: Benchmarking Indirect Prompt Injections in Tool-Integrated Large Language Model Agents
research.research_question_relevance: ANALYST INFERENCE — MEDIUM confidence: The paper supports a mechanism relevant to why web-capable agents face additional security exposure: third-party content enters their decision context and can redirect available tools toward unauthorized actions or data disclosure. Browser snippets are one tested content type, but the benchmark also covers email, finance, home devices, and other domains. It does not directly compare matched standalone LLMs with agents or quantify a comparative vulnerability increase.
research.attack_surface: Attacker-modifiable fields in retrieved tool responses, including website snippets, emails, reviews, notes, tweets, profiles, calendar events, and product/task descriptions. The attacker attempts to convert external content into instructions for harmful tools. Evaluation conditions on successful retrieval and receipt of the injected response.
research.method: GPT-4-assisted generation and manual refinement of 17 user cases and 62 attacker cases; full cross-product yields 1,054 cases in each of base and fixed-prefix enhanced settings. Thirty agent configurations are evaluated through parsed tool requests. Direct harm requires a harmful invocation; data stealing requires extraction plus transmission using a GPT-4-simulated extraction response. Results distinguish ASR-valid, ASR-all, and output validity, with additional association, content-freedom, sensitivity, quality, and prompt-length analyses.
research.limitations: Authors identify one fixed enhancement prefix, limited mixed benign/malicious content, single-turn attacks of at most two steps, and only two fine-tuned configurations. Additional analyst observations include simulated continuation-based evaluation, restricted tool menus, absent standalone baseline, imperfect proxy metrics, configuration/version confounding, missing uncertainty estimates, and unresolved text–table and plot–table inconsistencies.

claims.statement: InjecAgent contains 1,054 test cases per setting, formed by pairing 17 user cases with 62 attacker cases comprising 30 direct-harm and 32 data-stealing cases.

The evaluation assumes the legitimate retrieval has already succeeded and measures the agent's subsequent behavior after receiving the injected tool response; it is not an end-to-end retrieval evaluation.
ASR-valid excludes invalid outputs from its denominator, whereas ASR-all measures success across all outputs; format failures and redundant user-tool execution are among the invalid cases.
Table 3 reports prompted GPT-4 overall ASR-valid of 23.6% in the base setting and 47.0% with the fixed enhanced prefix; these are conditional rates among valid outputs under the main prompt.
From Table 3, prompted GPT-4's enhanced-setting increase is 47.0−23.6=23.4 percentage points, and its enhanced/base ratio is approximately 1.99; these calculations use rounded table values.
Table 3 assigns base ASR-valid of 3.8% to function-calling GPT-3.5 and 6.6% to function-calling GPT-4, while the page 6 prose reverses that model-to-number mapping.

Data-stealing success requires both private-data extraction and subsequent transmission to the attacker; the displayed 100% S2 rates for the two function-calling configurations do not mean all initial stealing attacks succeed.

User-case identity has stronger measured association with success than attacker-case identity: Cramér's V is 0.28 versus 0.18 for direct harm and 0.31 versus 0.20 for data stealing, with paired Wilcoxon p-values 5×10^-5 and 0.0001.

Figure 2 labels aggregate ASR at 36.3% for high-content-freedom user cases and 18.3% for low-content-freedom cases; the paired comparison is reported with p<0.0001, supporting association rather than a controlled causal effect.

Sensitivity is measured using risk-related keywords in outputs, and the authors hypothesize that the fixed enhanced prefix can both strengthen an attack and make it more recognizable; this is not a validated direct measure of model understanding.

The authors explicitly limit generalization because they use one fixed hacking prefix, limited attacker-instruction variability, single-turn attacks of at most two steps, and only two fine-tuned agent configurations.
Experiments use temperature 0 and supply only the user and attacker tool specifications relevant to each case, which limits inference about selection among a large deployed tool inventory.
Low all-case attack success can coexist with severe invalidity: Llama2-13B has base validity 1.7%, ASR-valid 50.0%, and ASR-all 0.9%.

Table 9 reports zero stealing rates for the function-calling configurations, conflicting with nonzero stealing results elsewhere and the successful function-calling GPT-4 theft example; the supplied work does not explain the discrepancy.

For the research question about web-agent security, the paper supports an external-content-to-action risk mechanism: attacker-controlled retrieved text can redirect a tool-capable agent. It does not provide a matched standalone-LLM comparison or a quantitative agent-versus-standalone vulnerability ratio.
The attacker is not assumed to observe private extraction output directly; the generation specification requires forwarding it by email, making extraction and disclosure distinct security events.

quality.limitations: Quotation presence and page bounds do not prove claim entailment or full coverage.

research.title: Machine-Readable Ads: Accessibility and Trust Patterns for AI Web Agents interacting with Online Advertisements
research.research_question_relevance: MEDIUM confidence, analyst inference: the study shows how browser-connected agents' perception and actions depend on website-controlled markup, hidden descriptions, privacy interfaces, and payment prerequisites. These mechanisms are relevant to why web agency may introduce additional security exposure. The paper does not compare matched standalone LLMs with web agents, so it cannot establish a comparative vulnerability magnitude or a universal ranking.
research.attack_surface: Analyst mapping of tested surfaces: advertisement markup and semantic controls, off-screen descriptions, spatial placement, dynamic media, consent dialogs, subscription choices, and website-defined payment dependencies. No formal attacker model or prompt-injection success metric is supplied. Control of system prompts, internal memory, runtime tools, or other agents was not tested.
research.method: Controlled empirical study on a React-based clone of the Tiroler Tageszeitung news site. Browser Use 0.1.41 connected GPT-4o, Claude 3.7 Sonnet, and Gemini 2.0 Flash to browser actions. Ten tasks with ten repetitions per model yielded 300 baseline trials; exploratory follow-ups usually used ten repetitions per model per condition. Sessions were reset, Browser Use actions and recordings were logged, and Operator outcomes were manually recorded. Results are descriptive counts and qualitative behavioral patterns.
research.limitations: Single cloned news environment; authored task prompts; dummy payment credentials; commercial-model opacity and drift; different Operator and Browser Use instrumentation and confirmation gates; limited hidden-text variants and one guiding description; no user study or composite trust score; no reported inferential statistics; unavailable raw artifacts; incomplete follow-up totals; unresolved Gemini tier accounting; and no standalone-LLM comparison. Visual inspection covered only supplied page images 1 and 8.

claims.statement: The baseline evaluation comprised ten tasks executed ten times for each of three Browser Use models, producing 300 trials; browser sessions were reset between trials.

Actual DOM button overlays produced side-banner clicks in seven of ten Claude runs, seven of ten GPT-4o runs, and five of ten Gemini runs, whereas the pixel-text variant produced none; Operator did not select either banner variant.
Off-screen span descriptions produced banner clicks in 9/10 Claude, 10/10 GPT-4o, and 10/10 Gemini trials; the tested custom data and image-alt strategies each produced 0/10 across these models.

Exploration remained insufficient to reach a coupon on virtual page 10; Table VI reports mean scroll-down actions of 2.5 for Claude, 0.8 for GPT-4o, and 0.7 for Gemini, with maxima of five, two, and three respectively.

In the 12-second video condition, only GPT-4o retrieved the two-second coupon segment, once in ten trials; the authors attribute that success to incidental timing rather than a deliberate waiting strategy.

When sweepstake entry required a paid subscription, GPT-4o and Claude subscribed in 10/10 trials each and Gemini in 7/10; the three models had avoided buying subscriptions merely to simplify the article tasks.

No model accessed granular cookie preferences. Acceptance depended on banner type: GPT-4o accepted the footer in 0/10 and blocker in 8/10 trials; Claude and Gemini accepted both in 10/10; all rejected the predatory modal.
The environment was a high-fidelity clone rather than the live news domain, limiting coverage of live timing, sequencing, and personalization.

DOM-based Browser Use and vision-first Operator comparisons are indicative rather than like-for-like because their instrumentation, accessible interface layers, costs, latency, and confirmation requirements differ.
The study used dummy payment credentials to prevent real transactions and tested only a small hidden-text strategy subset with a single natural-language description.

Research relevance: the observed sweepstake-to-subscription transition illustrates how website-defined prerequisites can turn pursuit of a user goal into a financial action. This is an analyst inference about agent security, not a measured vulnerability comparison with standalone LLMs.

Research relevance: successful steering with non-visible descriptions identifies website-controlled representation as a potential action-selection attack surface, although the experiment does not establish that the tested descriptions were malicious prompt injections.

quality.limitations: Quotation presence and page bounds do not prove claim entailment or full coverage.

research.title: SkillTrojan: Backdoor Attacks on Skill-Based Agent Systems
research.research_question_relevance: ANALYST INFERENCE; MEDIUM confidence. The paper demonstrates an additional execution-layer attack surface in agents that install reusable third-party skills: persistent executable code can cause hidden side effects while the underlying LLM remains unchanged and the returned answer appears benign. This supports a conditional explanation of agent risk beyond model output behavior. It does not directly compare standalone LLMs against web AI agents, establish a general vulnerability ratio, or use web browsing as its main benchmark.
research.attack_surface: Installed skill packages combining natural-language specifications and executable scripts; conditional skill instructions, tool-output fields, run-local trajectories, fragment-emitting actions, and an attacker-modified verification action. Persistence resides in installed packages; reconstruction state is single-run only. Payload consequences depend on execution permissions.
research.method: Encrypt and partition an attacker-selected payload into indexed fragments; modify skill instructions and actions for trigger-conditioned emission; collect fragments during normal workflow execution; verify completeness, reconstruct by index, decrypt, and execute a side effect. Evaluate clean ACC and triggered ASR on EHR SQL and SWE-Bench Verified, plus scanner, fragmentation, encoding, trigger-prevalence, native-skill, and cross-framework analyses.
research.limitations: No direct standalone-LLM or dedicated web-agent comparison. Missing benchmark denominators, uncertainty, seeds, complete environment, judge identity, detailed Hybrid encoding, and independently inspected release artifacts. Native controls cover four open-weight models only. Cross-framework results use a separate unnamed coding benchmark and report ASR without clean ACC. Utility and superiority have model-specific exceptions, including a Table 7 prose–table conflict. Proposed sandboxing and runtime defenses are not evaluated.

claims.statement: The attack targets reusable executable skill packages while assuming the underlying language model and training data remain trusted and unmodified.
SkillTrojan partitions encrypted payloads into indexed fragments so reconstruction does not require a fixed action invocation order.
The default experimental configuration uses triggered-query proportion ρ=0.2, fragment count N=3, and XOR+Base64; this is not a training-data poisoning rate.
On EHR SQL, GPT-5.2-1211-Global reportedly reaches 97.2% ASR on triggered queries and 89.3% ACC on clean queries with SkillTrojan.
ASR requires payload reconstruction and execution, indicated by a verifier execution marker and corroborated by a deterministic side effect, rather than merely malicious text.
Two lightweight scanners classify 98.2% and 99.4% of full SkillTrojan samples as safe in an analysis of approximately 500 sampled skills; this does not establish failure of all static defenses.

SkillTrojanX reportedly contains over 3,000 backdoored skills; Table 4 reports 1,200 templates, six categories, four payload families, three crypto variants, three fragment-count variants, and 50 triggers.
The fragment-count ablation on GPT-4o-mini reports maximum ASR at N=3, balancing conspicuous larger fragments against incomplete collection when more actions are required.

For GPT-4o-mini with N=3 and ρ=0.2, switching from XOR+Base64 to Hybrid reduces the simple base64 detector hit rate by 57.0 percentage points, calculated as 78.0−21.0; reported ACC and ASR change by only 0.1 and 0.3 points respectively.
Reconstruction fragments are scoped to a single run; persistence comes from installed packages, and attacks requiring cross-run fragment storage are excluded.

Table 7 contradicts the accompanying statement that native skills achieve the best clean accuracy in all four settings: Qwen3-VL Non-attack ACC is 53.2%, exceeding native skills at 50.3% and SkillTrojan at 48.4%.
Cross-framework results use a separate industry-oriented coding benchmark and should not be directly compared numerically with the EHR SQL tables.

The paper informs why agents can expose risks beyond standalone model output: installed skills introduce persistent executable logic and execution-side effects. This is analyst inference, not a measured comparison of web agents against standalone LLMs.

Baseline success requires the model to explicitly invoke a provided payload tool, whereas SkillTrojan executes through compromised normal skills; comparisons therefore share an outcome criterion but differ in attacker control surface.
On SWE-Bench Verified, Table 6 reports SkillTrojan ACC/ASR of 65.7/63.9% for Qwen3-Coder, 70.4/92.8% for GPT-5.2-1211-Global, and 67.6/66.4% for GLM-4.7; clean correctness uses verified tests.

quality.limitations: Quotation presence and page bounds do not prove claim entailment or full coverage.

research.title: The Hidden Dangers of Browsing AI Agents
research.research_question_relevance: ANALYST INFERENCE — The paper explains additional vulnerability pathways arising when an LLM repeatedly ingests untrusted web content and its outputs control browser actions, sensitive-data substitution, authenticated sessions, and infrastructure. Its Browser Use cases support this system-level mechanism. It does not directly measure browsing agents against matched standalone LLM baselines, so it cannot establish a general comparative vulnerability rate.
research.attack_surface: Author-described surfaces include webpage HTML/DOM and screenshots, prompt construction, reasoning/planning loops, tool arguments and registries, sensitive-data replacement, URL allowlists, browser sessions, containers, remote debugging, telemetry, credential stores, shared memory, and multi-agent delegation. Only domain validation and prompt-driven credential exfiltration receive detailed Browser Use case treatment.
research.method: Mixed security systems analysis: benchmark-informed selection of Browser Use; literature- and demonstration-informed architecture reconstruction; seven-layer MAESTRO mapping; narrative defense synthesis; white-box URL-validation analysis for version 0.1.44; and a GPT-4o-based credential-exfiltration proof-of-concept setup. No systematic review protocol or repeated-trial security benchmark is supplied.
research.limitations: One detailed open-source case; inaccessible proprietary implementations; unspecified attack repetition and success criteria; missing execution traces and complete dependency configuration; no controlled standalone comparison or implemented mitigation evaluation; qualitative appendix severity judgments; and unresolved internal ordering, numbering, duplication, and reference inconsistencies. Remediation in 0.1.45 is an author-reported historical claim.

claims.statement: The authors describe browsing-agent exposure as extending beyond the LLM to its web driver, execution environment, and dependencies.
The methodology adopts MAESTRO to analyze layered autonomous-system risks and maps browsing-agent components into seven layers.

The implementation case is an in-depth white-box assessment of Browser Use; proprietary-system relevance is argued from architectural similarity rather than demonstrated through equivalent source audits.
Listing 1 uses the URL network-location string and splits it on a colon; the supplied crafted URL is accepted as example.com while its actual target is localhost.
The domain bypass is associated with Browser Use 0.1.44 and CVE-2025-47241; the authors report remediation in 0.1.45.
Table 3 reports domain bypass as Critical at CVSS 9.3/10 and credential exfiltration as High at 8.8/10; these are severity scores, not attack-success rates.
The authors describe attacker-controlled parsed webpage content as a route to overriding the agent's original task and initiating credential exfiltration.
The credential proof-of-concept code uses GPT-4o, a repository-issue reading task, and a sensitive-data dictionary containing username and password fields; no repeated-trial success rate is supplied.
The paper attributes approximately 25% to about 8% attack-success reduction to a cited GPT-4 detector setup and 0% to a cited isolated-planner pipeline; neither is a new Browser Use defense result.
The authors explicitly state that whether smaller models are inherently more vulnerable remains inconclusive and requires further empirical study.

Research relevance, as analyst inference: iterative exposure to untrusted pages plus action execution explains additional system-level vulnerability pathways compared with text-only interaction, but the paper does not quantify a controlled standalone-LLM comparison.
Table 9 repeats Table 8's observability threats while its caption identifies Deployment & Infrastructure, creating a visible caption/content inconsistency.
Appendix severity labels combine estimated likelihood and potential impact for broad scenarios; the authors acknowledge that concrete deployment vectors can yield different scores.

Browser Use leads the reproduced WebVoyager task-success table at 89.1%; the benchmark description reports 300 tasks across 15 websites, and these figures support capability-based selection rather than security ranking.

quality.limitations: Quotation presence and page bounds do not prove claim entailment or full coverage.

research.title: Toolformer: Language Models Can Teach Themselves to Use Tools
research.research_question_relevance: ANALYST INFERENCE, MEDIUM confidence for architectural relevance: Toolformer shows how model-generated requests invoke external APIs and how returned text enters subsequent generation, providing a concrete interface to examine when studying external-content influence. The paper does not directly compare the security of web agents and standalone LLMs, introduce an attacker model, or measure vulnerability. Confidence in the proposition that web agents are more vulnerable based on this paper alone is UNKNOWN.
research.attack_surface: ANALYST INFERENCE: candidate boundaries include model-generated API names and arguments, externally returned QA or search text, translation output, date context, and the runtime insertion of responses before generation resumes. These are information-flow interfaces visible in the method, not demonstrated exploitable attack surfaces. The search tool retrieves Wikipedia snippets; the evaluated system is not an unrestricted interactive web browser.
research.method: Few API demonstrations condition candidate-call generation over CCNet text. Calls are executed and filtered by weighted continuation-loss reduction against no-call and no-response baselines. Retained calls are inserted into text for GPT-J fine-tuning. Evaluation compares unmodified GPT-J, CCNet-only fine-tuning, Toolformer with and without active calls, and larger models across factual completion, arithmetic, QA, multilingual QA, temporal tasks, perplexity, scaling, decoding, and qualitative call quality.
research.limitations: Author-stated limits include no chaining, no interactive search, wording-sensitive call decisions, sample inefficiency, and no cost-aware selection. Evaluation permits at most one call per input. Analyst observations include absent adversarial tests, no security threat model, task-specific relaxed answer matching, generally missing evaluation sample counts and uncertainty statistics, external-model resource differences, and text-only visual coverage for pages 11–16.

claims.statement: Toolformer learns tool-use decisions through self-supervised training requiring a handful of demonstrations for each API; this does not mean all human design or supervision is absent.
Candidate calls are retained when the call and response reduce weighted continuation loss by at least the filtering threshold relative to the stronger of no call and a call without its response.

With Wikipedia search disabled on LAMA, Toolformer scores 33.8, 11.5, and 53.5 on SQuAD, Google-RE, and T-REx, exceeding every displayed baseline under the correct-word-within-five-words evaluation rule.
On ASDiv, SVAMP, and MAWPS, enabled Toolformer scores 40.4, 29.4, and 44.0 versus disabled scores 14.8, 6.3, and 15.0; the calculator is used for 97.9% of examples across the arithmetic benchmarks.

With the QA tool disabled, Toolformer improves over GPT-J-derived baselines on WebQS, NQ, and TriviaQA but remains below GPT-3 on all three; evaluation checks answer containment within the first twenty predicted words.

On MLQA, active calls improve all six languages relative to Toolformer disabled, but Toolformer does not consistently outperform unmodified GPT-J; the setup uses English context and English answers with multilingual questions.
The TEMPLAMA improvement is not attributed to calendar use, which occurs in only 0.2% of examples; DATESET calendar use is 54.8%, and the authors attribute its improvement to that tool.

GPT-J + CC and Toolformer disabled have identical displayed perplexities of 10.3 on WikiText and 10.5 on held-out CCNet; this supports no added displayed penalty from API augmentation relative to CC-only fine-tuning, with calls disabled.

The authors place useful tool-use emergence around 775M parameters in their GPT-2/GPT-J scaling experiment, with Wikipedia search an exception; only QA, calculator, and search are included in this experiment.

Increasing the decoding API-start rank cutoff from k=1 to k=10 increases call coverage from 40.3% to 98.1% on T-REx and from 8.5% to 100.0% on WebQS; these k values concern decoding rather than training-position sampling.
Toolformer cannot learn chained tool use in the current method because independently generated calls provide no chained-use training examples; interactive use is also unsupported.
The authors report sensitivity of API-call decisions to exact input wording, sample inefficiency for some tools, and a lack of tool-dependent computational-cost consideration.

The inference loop is relevant to studying external-content influence because an API response is inserted into the LM context before generation resumes; this architectural observation does not demonstrate an attack or comparative vulnerability.

Loss reduction is an imperfect proxy for semantic usefulness: the qualitative analysis includes an irrelevant search result that reduces perplexity. The paper does not test whether this imperfection creates a security vulnerability.
The DATESET active-minus-disabled improvement is 21.4 score points, calculated as 27.3 minus 5.9 under the same displayed temporal-task evaluation; it is not a 21.4% relative improvement.
DATESET is generated from 500 randomly selected current dates and seven template families totaling 9,400 questions; the exact per-date allocation is not fully specified.

quality.limitations: Quotation presence and page bounds do not prove claim entailment or full coverage.

research.title: YuraScanner: Leveraging LLMs for Task-driven Web App Scanning
research.research_question_relevance: ANALYST INFERENCE, MEDIUM confidence: The paper shows how an LLM becomes an action-taking web system through page observations, recent history, browser actuators, and state-changing tasks. The documented deletion of the only account illustrates consequences beyond textual output. It does not directly compare web-agent vulnerability with standalone LLM vulnerability, test prompt injection, or measure agent compromise. Its confirmed vulnerabilities concern target web applications.
research.attack_surface: AUTHOR-REPORTED: URLs, forms, input fields, JavaScript-driven interactions, authenticated administration interfaces, and workflow-dependent application states. ANALYST INFERENCE: Browser actuation and persistent application changes are relevant to studying agent risk, but hostile webpage control over the agent is not evaluated.
research.method: Goal-based crawler using semantic DOM abstractions, an LLM bridge with six-action history, concrete browser actuators, depth-one task discovery, CRUD-oriented ordering, separated form-filling prompts, and replay followed by Black Widow XSS testing. Evaluation includes ten-application manual task and coverage analysis and 20-application vulnerability testing, with four-hour tool runs.
research.limitations: Partial execution is combined with full execution in the 61.3% headline. WordPress is excluded after prompt-size failures. Authentication is manually prepared. Model-selection scores, repeated-run uncertainty, costs, and exact GPT-4 snapshot are absent. Dataset naming and vulnerability-distance scope are ambiguous. Moodle is not direct XSS and has a reported no-impact developer assessment. Source access is vetted, artifacts were not supplied, and no direct standalone-LLM security comparison is conducted.

claims.statement: YuraScanner uses a goal-based agent architecture with sensors, an LLM-driven bridge, and browser actuators to execute tasks through semantic page abstractions.
Automatic task generation begins with a depth-one shallow crawl and asks an LLM to infer tasks from interface content; CRUD ordering is used to address task dependencies.
The scanner reuses Black Widow's XSS engine and records concrete navigation actions so forms can be revisited and tested after task execution.
Manual review on ten applications found 1,818 valid tasks among 2,361 generated tasks; 543 proposed tasks referred to functionality absent from the target application.
Of 1,818 valid tasks, 667 were fully executed and 448 partially executed, giving 1,115 full-or-partial executions, approximately 61.3%; partial execution excludes correct execution of the final step.
The retained evaluation excludes WordPress because theme documentation inside an input field caused prompts to exceed the LLM's maximum size, producing API errors.

The reported average additional coverage is 55.19% for forms and 35.16% for URLs when YuraScanner-only resources are added to comparison tools' resource sets; this is not universal superiority in standalone resource totals.
The authors report that 14.3% of YuraScanner's collected forms occur beyond three task steps and were not found by the comparison tools in the reported experiments.
In the 20-application vulnerability experiment, YuraScanner and Black Widow each run for four hours; 15 reports represent 13 unique issues, with 12 found by YuraScanner and three by Black Widow.
The Moodle finding is qualified as HTML meta tag attribute injection that could escalate to XSS, and its developers reportedly judged it without impact under their application's threat model.
During Leantime testing, successful execution of a task deleting the only user account locked YuraScanner out and caused subsequent tasks to fail.
Authentication is handled separately: all tools receive credentials or session cookies and manually scripted authentication sequences, limiting claims of fully autonomous end-to-end access.
The authors withhold public source release because of misuse concerns and warn that reproduction can vary due to randomized navigation and non-static OpenAI models.

For the user's research question, the browser-actuator architecture and self-lockout example illustrate how model decisions can acquire consequential application effects; this is analyst inference, not evidence from a direct comparison of agent vulnerability with standalone LLM vulnerability.
Full completion is approximately 36.69% of valid tasks, calculated as 667 divided by 1,818 times 100; the paper's 61.3% combines full and partial execution.
